title: Gene to protein, bond by bond
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A gene is the DNA sequence that codes for a functional product.

(나) The central dogma describes how that DNA sequence becomes a protein.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Transcription builds the RNA strand via phosphodiester bonds formed 5'→3'.
statements.explanation: Phosphodiester bonds link one nucleotide's phosphate to the next's 3'-OH, so synthesis always extends 5'→3'.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Translation builds the polypeptide via peptide bonds, which form by condensation, releasing water.
statements.explanation: Peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction: each new bond releases one water molecule as amino acids join.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: E. coli is convenient for studying this whole pathway because its DNA isn't separated from its ribosomes by a nuclear envelope.
statements.explanation: As a prokaryote, E. coli has no nucleus, so transcription and translation can occur in the same compartment, even on the same mRNA.

links: Central dogma · Gene definition · E. coli

title: ATP's double identity
stem: Read (A) and (B) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(A) ATP: adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups.

(B) cAMP and NAD are also built on a base + sugar + phosphate scaffold.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: ATP counts as a nucleotide structurally, even though it's never incorporated into a nucleic acid strand.
statements.explanation: The base+sugar+phosphate architecture is the structural definition of a nucleotide — nothing requires polymerization into DNA/RNA.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The "high energy" in ATP resides in the bonds between its second and third phosphate groups.
statements.explanation: The high-energy bonds are between the 2nd and 3rd phosphate groups (AMP→ADP→ATP) — this is exactly why hydrolyzing off a phosphate releases usable energy.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because (B) shares ATP's scaffold, "nucleotide" is a structural classification, not a statement about function.
statements.explanation: ATP, cAMP, and NAD are repurposed for energy transfer, signaling, and catalysis support respectively — all while remaining structural nucleotides.

links: ATP structure · Nucleotide as scaffold

title: One reaction pair, three macromolecules
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Peptide bond formation between two amino acids.

(나) Phosphodiester bond formation between two nucleotides.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Both (가) and (나) release one water molecule as they form.
statements.explanation: Both are condensation reactions — the defining feature of condensation is releasing water as monomers join.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Hydrolyzing the bond in (가) would release energy, since hydrolysis is the reverse of the energy-requiring condensation reaction.
statements.explanation: Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction: it consumes water and releases energy, rather than requiring it.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If a polysaccharide were built the same way as (가) and (나), a glycosidic bond would also form by releasing water.
statements.explanation: Glycosidic bonds form between monosaccharides by the same condensation logic, releasing water.

links: Condensation vs hydrolysis across macromolecules

title: Why a phospholipid and not a triacylglycerol
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Property 1 of a cell: membrane-enclosed cytoplasm.

(나) A phospholipid: glycerol + two fatty acid tails + one phosphate head group.

(다) A triacylglycerol: glycerol + three fatty acid tails.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) is amphipathic, which is why it self-assembles into a bilayer rather than a droplet like (다).
statements.explanation: Two hydrophobic tails plus one hydrophilic head makes (나) amphipathic; (다)'s three tails make it uniformly hydrophobic.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (다) would work just as well as (나) for satisfying (가), since both contain glycerol.
statements.explanation: (다) has no polar head group, so it just clumps into a droplet — it can't wrap around an aqueous cytoplasm the way a bilayer does.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The hydrophilic behavior of (나)'s head group would still occur even in a nonpolar solvent, since it's an inherent property of the head group alone.
statements.explanation: This is backwards — "hydrophilic" specifically describes favorable interaction with water's own polar/charged nature; the term is defined relative to water, not an isolated inherent property.

links: Amphipathic phospholipids · Membrane property

title: pH, charge, and the active site
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) An enzyme's active site depends on the protein's precise 3D fold.

(나) Amino and carboxyl R-groups are ionizable functional groups.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Moving the enzyme from its optimal pH into a strongly acidic solution changes the charge on the groups in (나).
statements.explanation: Ionizable groups' protonation state depends on H+ concentration — that's what pH measures.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: That charge change only affects surface-exposed groups, never residues that form the active site itself.
statements.explanation: Active-site residues are frequently ionizable and directly involved in catalysis (e.g. proton transfer) — they are especially, not immune to, pH-driven charge changes.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: This means an enzyme's function depends only on its amino acid sequence, never on the surrounding solution.
statements.explanation: The scenario itself shows the opposite — the surrounding solution's pH can disrupt function even with the sequence unchanged.

links: pH · Functional group charge · Protein folding

title: What an enzyme actually changes
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Glycolysis and the citric acid cycle are metabolic reactions (property 5).

(나) Enzymes catalyze these reactions.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) lowers the activation energy needed to reach the transition state.
statements.explanation: This is exactly what a catalyst does — it speeds the rate of reaching equilibrium.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) speeds the reaction by stabilizing the transition state, without being consumed itself.
statements.explanation: A catalyst lowers the energy barrier and emerges from the reaction unchanged, ready to catalyze again.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Without (나), reactions in (가) would still reach the same equilibrium eventually, just more slowly.
statements.explanation: Since the enzyme doesn't change the energetics, the same equilibrium is reached — only the rate differs.

links: Enzymes: rate vs energetics

title: Two kinds of reproduction, one tenet
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A bacterium reproducing by binary fission.

(나) A virus replicating inside a host cell.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) satisfies tenet 3 as long as the cell eventually splits in two, regardless of whether its DNA was duplicated first.
statements.explanation: Tenet 3 specifically requires DNA duplication before division — division alone, without a complete duplicated genome for each daughter cell, wouldn't satisfy it.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) also satisfies tenet 3, since new virus particles are produced from an existing one.
statements.explanation: The virus itself was never a cell, and no cell-to-cell division occurs — it hijacks host machinery instead.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나) is treated as an exception to cell theory specifically because it isn't a cell and cannot replicate without a host.
statements.explanation: This is exactly why viruses sit outside cell theory rather than being classified as unusual minimal cells.

links: Tenet 3 · Binary fission · Virus exception

title: Cytoskeleton and centrosome, non-EMS partners
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The cytoskeleton: a protein filament network, no membrane.

(나) The centrosome: organizes cytoskeletal filaments during division.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) is classified as EMS, unlike (나), because it physically contacts vesicles during transport.
statements.explanation: Contact isn't the criterion, and this is factually backwards — (가), the cytoskeleton, is classified non-EMS, exactly like (나).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Both fail the EMS criterion because neither participates in membrane-based vesicle trafficking.
statements.explanation: This is the actual EMS criterion — not "has a membrane," but participation in the trafficking network.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) is the one that organizes and directs the process, while (나) supplies the mechanical apparatus itself.
statements.explanation: The roles are reversed: the cytoskeleton supplies the mechanical apparatus; the centrosome organizes and directs it.

links: Cytoskeleton · Centrosome · Non-EMS

title: Where molecular diversity actually comes from
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Only six elements (C, H, N, O, P, S) make up nearly all biological molecules.

(나) Carbon can form up to four covalent bonds.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The huge diversity of biological molecules comes mainly from having many different elements to combine.
statements.explanation: The diversity comes from combinatorial arrangement (chains, rings, branches) enabled by (나), not from elemental variety — (가) explicitly says it's only six elements.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) is what lets carbon build the chains, rings, and branches underlying all four macromolecule classes.
statements.explanation: Four bonding sites give carbon an essentially unlimited structural scaffold.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Lipids don't qualify as organic molecules, since they aren't built from a repeating monomer.
statements.explanation: "Organic" just means "contains carbon" — lipids still contain carbon, they're simply the one macromolecule class that isn't a polymer.

links: CHNOPS · Carbon bonding · Organic definition

title: Arabidopsis walls and yeast walls
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Arabidopsis thaliana is widely used to study how plant cell walls are built.

(나) Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast), the "minimal model eukaryote," has cell walls that contain chitin.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because chitin is a modified polysaccharide, fully hydrolyzing a yeast wall's chitin would release modified sugar units, not amino acids.
statements.explanation: Hydrolysis breaks a polymer into its monomers, and a polysaccharide's monomers are sugars; chitin's are modified sugars, so no amino acids are released.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because both organisms have cell walls, findings about Arabidopsis walls should apply just as well to yeast walls.
statements.explanation: A model stands in for its close relatives. Yeast is a fungus with chitin in its walls, while plant walls are built from other polysaccharides such as cellulose.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Findings from Arabidopsis are expected to carry over to crops such as canola and tomatoes.
statements.explanation: Flowering plants are closely related, which is why Arabidopsis is their model; canola and tomatoes are flowering plants too.

links: Model organisms: Arabidopsis and yeast · Plant vs fungal walls · Hydrolysis of polysaccharides (Mod 2)

title: What Hooke's cork couldn't show
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Hooke (1665): observed empty cell walls in dead cork.

(나) Leeuwenhoek (1670s–1700): observed living "animalcules" in pond water.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) alone was sufficient evidence for "all life is made of cells," since he identified the walled compartments.
statements.explanation: Empty walls in dead tissue show structure, not life — a theory about living units needs evidence cells are alive.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) supplied what (가) was missing: direct visual evidence that cells contain a nucleus.
statements.explanation: Leeuwenhoek's contribution was observing live, moving organisms — direct evidence cells are living units — not resolving internal structures like the nucleus.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Electron microscopy would have revealed finer detail in both (가) and (나), because it uses a shorter-wavelength beam than light.
statements.explanation: A shorter wavelength gives electron microscopy far higher resolution than the light microscopes Hooke and Leeuwenhoek used.

links: Hooke · Leeuwenhoek · Electron microscopy

title: Three scientists, three separate gaps
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Schleiden (botanist): plant tissue is made of cells, embryos arise from one cell.

(나) Schwann (zoologist): confirmed the same pattern in animal tissue.

(다) Virchow (physician): cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) alone was enough to establish tenets 1 and 2 for all of life, plant and animal alike.
statements.explanation: One kingdom's observations don't generalize — that's exactly why (나)'s independent animal confirmation was still needed.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (다) addressed a logically separate question from (가) and (나): origin, not composition.
statements.explanation: Whether cells are made of cells (composition) is a different question from where new cells come from (origin).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because both unicellular and multicellular organisms needed confirming, (가)+(나)+(다) together were needed to establish the theory's claimed universality.
statements.explanation: No single scientist's observations at one complexity level or kingdom could generalize to the others.

links: Cell theory founders · Unicellular vs multicellular

title: Structure doesn't always track ancestry
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Archaea: isoprenoid cell membrane, often extreme environments.

(나) The three-domain tree places Eukarya as having descended from within Archaea.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Based on (나), Archaea is evolutionarily closer to Eukarya than Bacteria is.
statements.explanation: Branching from within Archaea means Eukarya shares more recent common ancestry with Archaea than with Bacteria.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Despite this close relatedness, Archaea still shares the defining prokaryotic trait of having no nucleus, just like Bacteria.
statements.explanation: Archaea remains structurally prokaryotic (no nucleus) even though it's evolutionarily closer to Eukarya than Bacteria is — relatedness and structure are separate axes.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Gross structural similarity is therefore not a reliable guide to evolutionary relatedness in this case.
statements.explanation: Eukarya's very different structure from Archaea, despite close relatedness, demonstrates exactly this.

links: Eukarya from within Archaea

title: Stripping plant cells down to protoplasts
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Plant biologists remove the walls from leaf cells by soaking them in wall-digesting enzymes, including cellulase, which breaks cellulose down into glucose. In a concentrated mannitol solution that keeps them from bursting, the cells survive as round "protoplasts."

(나) Animal cells have no cell wall at all.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Cellulase breaks down the wall's cellulose by hydrolysis, using one water molecule for each glycosidic bond it splits.
statements.explanation: Plant walls are polysaccharides such as cellulose, chains of glucose joined by glycosidic bonds; hydrolysis inserts a water molecule across each bond broken.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The protoplasts lost their plasma membranes along with their walls, since the enzymes digest the cell's outer layers.
statements.explanation: The cells survive because their plasma membranes remain: membranes are built of phospholipids and proteins, not cellulose, so the enzymes leave them intact.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The protoplasts in (가) and the animal cells in (나) are each enclosed by a plasma membrane, the one boundary every cell has.
statements.explanation: A plasma membrane encloses every cell; walls are extra outer layers found in plants, fungi, bacteria and many protists, but not in animals.

links: Plasma membrane is universal · Plant walls are polysaccharides · Hydrolysis and glycosidic bonds (Mod 2) · Real-world: plant protoplasts

title: The potato-blight water mold
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The potato-blight water mold absorbs nutrients from potato leaves and has no chloroplasts.

(나) Its walls are made of cellulose and other glucose polymers, with little or no chitin.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Its walls are more like a plant's than a fungus's, even though it feeds the way fungi do.
statements.explanation: Fungal walls contain chitin, while plant walls are polysaccharides such as cellulose; walls of cellulose and other glucose polymers with little or no chitin fit the plant pattern.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A chitin-digesting enzyme would leave the water mold's walls largely intact, since enzymes that speed hydrolysis are specific.
statements.explanation: Hydrolysis is sped up by specific enzymes, and these walls are mostly glucose polymers rather than chitin, so a chitin-digesting enzyme has little to act on.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because its walls contain cellulose, the water mold should be classified as a plant.
statements.explanation: Plants are multicellular autotrophs with chloroplasts, and this heterotroph has no chloroplasts, so it isn't one. Water molds are protists.

links: Fungal vs plant walls · Plants are autotrophs with chloroplasts · Enzyme specificity in hydrolysis (Mod 2) · Real-world: potato blight

title: The double-membrane trap
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Mitochondria: double membrane.

(나) Chloroplast: double membrane.

(다) The EMS is defined by membrane-based vesicle trafficking, not just "having a membrane."

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Since (가) and (나) both have a double membrane, they should be classified as EMS.
statements.explanation: Having multiple membranes is not the criterion — (다) says participation in the trafficking network is.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Based on (다), neither (가) nor (나)'s membranes are derived from or connected to the ER–Golgi trafficking network.
statements.explanation: Their membranes instead reflect endosymbiotic bacterial origin, not the vesicle-trafficking pathway.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: This makes (가) and (나) non-EMS despite being membrane-bound organelles.
statements.explanation: Membrane-bound but not trafficking-connected — exactly why both are classified non-EMS.

links: Mitochondria/chloroplast vs EMS criterion

title: Location inside the nucleus isn't the criterion
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The nucleolus: dense region inside the nucleus, no membrane of its own, site of rRNA synthesis.

(나) The nuclear envelope: double-membrane boundary of the nucleus.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) is part of the EMS because it's located inside the nucleus.
statements.explanation: Location doesn't matter — (가) has no membrane of its own, so it fails the EMS's membrane-trafficking criterion.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) is part of the EMS because it has a membrane continuous with the ER.
statements.explanation: The nuclear envelope's membrane connects to the trafficking network, unlike the nucleolus.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: By the same whole/boundary/region logic, cytosol relates to cytoplasm the way (가) relates to the nucleus.
statements.explanation: Nucleolus is a sub-region within the nucleus; cytosol is the fluid sub-portion within the broader cytoplasm — the same part-of-a-whole pattern.

links: Nucleolus vs nuclear envelope · Cytoplasm vs cytosol

title: Why only plant cells get turgor
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The vacuole: membrane-bound, formed via vesicle trafficking.

(나) A plant cell's vacuole fills with water and pushes against the cell wall.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) means the vacuole is classified as EMS.
statements.explanation: A membrane-bound compartment continuous with the ER/Golgi trafficking pathway meets the EMS criterion.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) describes turgor pressure, an example of property 6 (mechanical activities).
statements.explanation: This is a membrane-trafficked organelle producing a direct, whole-cell mechanical effect.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나) could also occur in an animal cell, since animal cells have vacuoles too.
statements.explanation: Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall to push against, so there's no comparable turgor-pressure effect.

links: Vacuole · Turgor pressure

title: Two shapes, two outcomes
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Methane (CH4): tetrahedral, symmetric.

(나) Water (H2O): bent, asymmetric.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: O–H bonds in (나) are more polar than C–H bonds in (가).
statements.explanation: O is more electronegative than C relative to H, making O–H bonds more polar than C–H bonds.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (가)'s symmetric geometry cancels out its (already weak) bond dipoles, leaving no net dipole.
statements.explanation: Four dipoles pointing outward symmetrically in a tetrahedron sum to zero.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나)'s bent geometry prevents its bond dipoles from cancelling, leaving a net dipole.
statements.explanation: Two genuinely polar O–H bonds at a bent angle don't cancel — a net dipole remains.

links: Methane vs water · Molecular geometry

title: One bond, two structural roles
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Cysteine's sulfhydryl group (-SH) can react with another cysteine's -SH to form a disulfide bond.

(나) Two cysteines sit on the same polypeptide chain.

(다) Two cysteines sit on separate polypeptide chains.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Under (나), the resulting disulfide bond stabilizes tertiary (3D) folding.
statements.explanation: A disulfide bond within one chain pulls that region together, stabilizing the fold.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Under (다), the resulting disulfide bond contributes to quaternary structure by linking the two chains.
statements.explanation: Covalently linking two separate polypeptide chains is exactly what quaternary structure means.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) could just as well occur between a cysteine's -SH and a hydroxyl group.
statements.explanation: Disulfide bonds are specifically S–S bonds, formed sulfhydryl-to-sulfhydryl — hydroxyl doesn't have the sulfur needed.

links: Disulfide bonds · Tertiary vs quaternary

title: A swapped base, an unswapped class
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) DNA uses thymine; RNA uses uracil instead.

(나) Both thymine and uracil are single-ring bases.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because of (나), thymine and uracil are both classified as pyrimidines, so the swap in (가) does not change the base-class present.
statements.explanation: Both thymine and uracil are single-ring pyrimidines — the swap changes the specific base, not the structural class.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: RNA's ribose sugar carries an extra -OH compared to DNA's deoxyribose, making RNA's backbone more reactive.
statements.explanation: That 2'-OH is the defining chemical difference between ribose and deoxyribose.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: This greater reactivity fits RNA's role as a disposable working copy, versus DNA's role as stable long-term storage.
statements.explanation: A more reactive, less stable backbone suits a molecule that isn't meant to last, unlike DNA.

links: Thymine/uracil swap · Ribose vs deoxyribose

title: Why a strand has a direction at all
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A phosphodiester bond links one nucleotide's phosphate to the next nucleotide's 3'-OH.

(나) A nucleic acid strand has a free 5' end and a free 3' end.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because of (가), new nucleotides are added onto the free 3' end of a growing strand.
statements.explanation: New nucleotides attach at the free 3'-OH end — this is exactly why synthesis always proceeds 5'→3'.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: This means both DNA replication and transcription proceed 5'→3'.
statements.explanation: Both processes build new strands by the same phosphodiester-bond mechanism, always extending toward the 3' end.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나)'s directionality exists because (가) always attaches at the same asymmetric location on each nucleotide.
statements.explanation: Because the bond always links phosphate-to-3'-OH, the two ends of the resulting strand are chemically distinct.

links: 5' to 3' directionality

title: Same formula, specific bond
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Glucose: aldehyde group.

(나) Fructose: ketone group.

(다) Both share the molecular formula C6H12O6.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Based on (다), glucose and fructose have identical numbers of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, despite differing in functional group.
statements.explanation: Sharing the formula C6H12O6 means identical atom counts — (가) and (나) differ in how those atoms are arranged (aldehyde vs ketone), not in how many there are.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Sucrose forms by a glycosidic bond specifically between glucose's C1 and fructose's C2 hydroxyl.
statements.explanation: This specific carbon-to-carbon linkage is what makes sucrose a defined, non-arbitrary structure.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) and (나) are isomers of each other.
statements.explanation: Same molecular formula, different atomic arrangement — exactly the definition of isomers.

links: Glucose/fructose isomers · Glycosidic bond

title: Same monomer, three different jobs
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Starch: branched glucose polymer, plant energy storage.

(나) Glycogen: branched glucose polymer + central protein, animal energy storage.

(다) Cellulose: glucose polymer, plant structural support.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가), (나), and (다) share the same monomer, but (다) has a different C:H:O ratio because its role is structural rather than storage.
statements.explanation: Elemental composition is tied to monomer identity, not biological role — all three share the same glucose monomer and therefore the same 1:2:1 ratio regardless of function.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Since they share a monomer, (가), (나), and (다) must also share the same biological role.
statements.explanation: The box itself states three different roles — storage in two different kingdoms, plus structural support.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Their different roles must therefore come from a variable other than monomer identity — specifically, how the monomers are linked and branched.
statements.explanation: Linkage and branching pattern, not monomer choice, is what determines a polysaccharide's biological role.

links: Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose

title: No shared structure, still both lipids
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Cholesterol: four fused carbon rings.

(나) Triacylglycerol: glycerol + three fatty acid tails.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) and (나) share no structural similarity at all, yet both are classified as lipids.
statements.explanation: No glycerol backbone in (가), no ring system in (나) — structurally unrelated.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: This is possible because lipids are classified by a shared physical property (hydrophobicity), not shared structure.
statements.explanation: Hydrophobicity, not structure, is what unites the lipid class.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) cannot serve as a precursor to any other molecule, unlike (나).
statements.explanation: Cholesterol is specifically the precursor to steroid hormones like cortisol.

links: Steroids · Lipid classification

title: What a double bond changes, and what it doesn't
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A saturated fatty acid: no carbon–carbon double bonds.

(나) An unsaturated fatty acid: one or more carbon–carbon double bonds.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: A triacylglycerol built purely from (나) would have the same 3-tail, glycerol-backbone architecture as one built from (가).
statements.explanation: Saturation only affects the fatty acid tails themselves, not the overall triacylglycerol architecture.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나)'s double bonds introduce a kink, since a double bond doesn't allow free rotation.
statements.explanation: Restricted rotation at each double bond produces a bend in the chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Swapping one of (가) or (나)'s tails for a phosphate head group would turn the molecule into a steroid.
statements.explanation: That substitution produces a phospholipid, not a steroid — steroids have an entirely different four-ring architecture.

links: Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids

title: What makes a group hydrophilic, precisely
stem: Read (가)–(다) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Water: partial negative charge on O, partial positive on each H.

(나) A hydroxyl group (-OH): polar.

(다) A methyl group (-CH3): nonpolar.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) can hydrogen-bond with (가), which is what makes it hydrophilic.
statements.explanation: A polar group interacting with water's partial charges is exactly what "hydrophilic" means.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (다) cannot hydrogen-bond with (가), which is why it is hydrophobic instead.
statements.explanation: Methyl is nonpolar — it has no charge for water to interact with, so it can't engage in the same interactions as (나).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: "Hydrophilic" is therefore defined by whether a group can engage in the same polarity-driven interactions that (가) itself exhibits.
statements.explanation: Hydrophilicity isn't independent — it's defined relative to water's own polarity.

links: Water polarity · Hydrophilic functional groups

title: Why E. coli beats yeast for this one job
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) E. coli: no nucleus, single circular chromosome.

(나) S. cerevisiae: true nucleus, chromatin packaging.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Property 2 (genetic program) is physically implemented at the nucleotide level in both (가) and (나).
statements.explanation: Both are DNA-based organisms — the genetic program property applies universally at the nucleotide level.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (가) is the more tractable system for studying that nucleotide-level chemistry directly, mainly because it replicates its DNA faster than (나) does.
statements.explanation: The tractability comes from structural simplicity — no nuclear envelope or chromatin packaging to navigate — not from replication speed.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나) is therefore never used as a model organism for anything related to DNA.
statements.explanation: Overreach — yeast is the standard model for the cell cycle, which is itself deeply tied to DNA replication and segregation.

links: E. coli vs yeast tractability

title: One molecule, two charges at once
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) An amino acid has 4 groups on its alpha carbon: -COOH, -NH2, H, and R.

(나) At physiological pH, -NH2 gains a proton and -COOH loses one.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) describes the amino acid existing as a zwitterion — both a positive and negative charge at once.
statements.explanation: Simultaneously protonated amino and deprotonated carboxyl is exactly the zwitterion state.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: All 20 amino acids have identical R groups, differing only in how (가)'s COOH and NH2 are arranged.
statements.explanation: This is backwards — COOH, NH2, and H are the shared, invariant groups across all 20 amino acids; R is specifically the one group that varies.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나) means the amino acid has zero net charge overall at physiological pH, regardless of R group.
statements.explanation: Zwitterion means both charges are present, not that they always cancel — a charged R group would shift the net charge.

links: Zwitterion · Amino acid structure

title: Support, transport, and what they're not
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A structural protein in the extracellular matrix.

(나) A membrane protein that transports glucose into the cell.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) is an example of the "support" function of proteins.
statements.explanation: Extracellular-matrix structural proteins are a textbook example of the support function.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (나) is an example of the "transport" function of proteins.
statements.explanation: Moving a specific molecule across the membrane is the transport function by definition.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Both (가) and (나) are also, by definition, enzymes.
statements.explanation: Support and transport are separate functional categories from the enzymatic (catalytic) function — neither example catalyzes a reaction.

links: Protein functional categories

title: Two properties, not one
stem: Read (가) and (나) below. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Property 2: genetic program based on DNA.

(나) Property 8: self-regulation.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) is implemented through the central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein.
statements.explanation: This is exactly the molecular mechanism behind the genetic-program property.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Loss of (나) is specifically linked to uncontrolled cell growth, i.e. cancer.
statements.explanation: Self-regulation failing is the basis for uncontrolled growth described in the notes.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) and (나) are actually the same property described two different ways.
statements.explanation: They're two distinct, independently listed properties in the list of 8 — one about information, one about growth control.

links: Genetic program vs self-regulation

title: Founders of cell theory
prompt: Match each scientist to their specific, documented contribution.

pairs.right: Observed empty cell walls in dead cork and coined the term "cells"
First observed living "animalcules" moving in pond water
Showed all plant tissue is made of cells and embryos arise from one cell
Independently confirmed the same cellular organization in animal tissue
Added that cells arise only from pre-existing cells (tenet 3)

explanation: Note the order matters: Hooke's dead-cell observation came roughly two centuries before the formal theory; Leeuwenhoek's living cells filled the gap Hooke couldn't; Schleiden and Schwann each covered one kingdom; Virchow closed the theory with the origin question neither had addressed.
links: Hooke · Leeuwenhoek · Schleiden · Schwann · Virchow

title: Domains and cell-type roots
prompt: Match each term to its defining feature.

pairs.right: Literally "before nucleus" — no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles
Literally "true nucleus" — membrane-bound nucleus and organelles
Prokaryotic domain: cell wall, often plasmids, single circular chromosome
Prokaryotic domain: isoprenoid cell membrane, often extreme environments

explanation: Eukarya is hypothesized to have evolutionarily descended from within Archaea, making Archaea our closer prokaryotic relative despite the huge structural gap between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
links: Tree of Life · Prokaryote vs eukaryote · Bacteria vs Archaea

title: Sort every organelle: EMS or non-EMS?
prompt: Classify each structure by the EMS's actual criterion — membrane-based vesicle trafficking — not just "has a membrane."

pairs.right: EMS
EMS
EMS
EMS
EMS
EMS
EMS
EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS
Non-EMS

explanation: The trap: mitochondria and chloroplast both have a double membrane, but neither membrane is continuous with, or trafficked by, the ER–Golgi vesicle network — so "has a membrane" is not the criterion. The nucleolus and cytoskeleton have no membrane at all, which is a separate reason they're non-EMS.
links: EMS criterion · Mitochondria/chloroplast trap · Vacuole

title: Picking the model organism for the job
prompt: Match each research goal to the model organism best suited to it.

pairs.left: Work out how a cell copies its DNA and reads its genes, using a simple cell with no nucleus
pairs.right: Escherichia coli

pairs.left: Learn how a eukaryotic cell controls when it divides, using a minimal, single-celled eukaryote
pairs.right: Saccharomyces cerevisiae

pairs.left: Find a gene that controls flowering, expecting it to work similarly in other flowering plants
pairs.right: Arabidopsis thaliana

pairs.left: Know in advance which cells each cell of an embryo will give rise to
pairs.right: Caenorhabditis elegans

pairs.left: Test what a gene does in a mammal before studying it in people
pairs.right: Mus musculus

explanation: In the notes, E. coli is the model for DNA replication, transcription and translation, and yeast, the 'minimal model eukaryote', for the cell cycle. Every C. elegans cell's location, lineage and fate is known, Arabidopsis stands in for the closely related flowering plants, and the mouse is the 'model mammal' with well-understood genetics.
links: Model organisms: matching organism to purpose

title: Sorting eukaryotes by their traits
prompt: Each organism belongs to a different eukaryotic group. Match each one to its group, using its traits rather than its appearance.

pairs.left: Baker's yeast: single cells with chitin in their walls, absorbing sugars from bread dough
pairs.right: Fungi

pairs.left: Volvox: photosynthetic cells that live together as a colony
pairs.right: Protists

pairs.left: A moss: multicellular, with chloroplasts and polysaccharide cell walls
pairs.right: Plants

pairs.left: A sponge: multicellular, no cell walls, filtering food particles from seawater
pairs.right: Animals

explanation: Yeast is a fungus even though it is single-celled, and Volvox is a protist (an alga) even though it photosynthesizes: protists are a diverse group, mostly single cells but some forming colonies. A sponge is multicellular, has no walls and takes in food, so it is an animal even though it doesn't move.
links: Protists, fungi, plants and animals · Classifying by traits

title: Exceptions to the cell theory
prompt: Match each exception to what it is actually made of.

pairs.right: Nucleic acid + protein coat; inert outside a host
Circular RNA only, no protein coat
Infectious protein only — no nucleic acid at all

explanation: They form a gradient of "how little can still spread": a virus keeps genetic material and a coat; a viroid drops the coat; a prion drops genetic material entirely and spreads by inducing misfolding, not replication.
links: Virus · Viroid · Prion

title: The 8 basic properties of a cell
prompt: Match each property to what it actually means.

pairs.right: Cytoplasm and cytosol are bounded by a plasma membrane
DNA directs the cell via the central dogma
The cell duplicates its own DNA before dividing
Bioenergetics — e.g. building and spending ATP
Metabolism — e.g. glycolysis, the citric acid cycle
Transport and movement, largely via the cytoskeleton
Detects and reacts to signals via receptors
Controls its own growth; loss of this property underlies cancer

explanation: These 8 aren't independent — they interlock: property 2's genetic program is what specifies the enzymes that carry out property 5, and losing property 8 (regulation) is specifically what happens when growth control fails.
links: 8 basic cell properties

title: Nucleus, cytoplasm, and cell-boundary terminology
prompt: Match each term to its precise definition — several are easy to confuse with a neighboring term.

pairs.right: The whole membrane-bound organelle containing the chromosomes
Specifically the nucleus's double-membrane boundary (part of the EMS)
A dense, non-membrane region inside the nucleus — rRNA synthesis / ribosome assembly
Everything inside the plasma membrane, organelles included
Just the fluid portion of the cytoplasm, excluding organelles
Rigid external layer — NOT universal (absent in animal cells)
Universal boundary present in every cell, all three domains

explanation: The recurring pattern here is whole-vs-boundary-vs-region: nucleus/nuclear envelope/nucleolus and cytoplasm/cytosol both follow it. Cell wall vs plasma membrane is a different distinction entirely — universality, not scale.
links: Nucleus vs nuclear envelope vs nucleolus · Cytoplasm vs cytosol · Cell wall vs plasma membrane

title: Functional groups and their charge behavior
prompt: Match each functional group to its charge / polarity behavior.

pairs.right: Acts as a base; positively charged at cellular pH
Acts as an acid; negatively charged at cellular pH
Negatively charged
Polar, uncharged — hydrophilic
Polar; forms S–S disulfide bonds
Nonpolar — hydrophobic
Polar; links monomers (e.g. cyclizes sugars)

explanation: Notice the pattern: every group that's polar or charged is hydrophilic (can hydrogen-bond or electrostatically interact with water's own partial charges); methyl is the one group here with neither property, which is exactly why it's the odd one out — hydrophobic.
links: Functional groups · Hydrophilic vs hydrophobic

title: The four macromolecule classes
prompt: Match each macromolecule class to its monomer and primary biological role.

pairs.right: Amino acids → structure and catalysis (enzymes)
Nucleotides → encode and transmit genetic information
Monosaccharides → structure and energy source
Not a polymer — grouped by hydrophobicity, not a monomer

explanation: Lipids break the pattern on purpose: the other three are monomer-built polymers via condensation, but lipids are the one macromolecule class that isn't a polymer at all — they're united by a shared physical property instead of a shared structure.
links: Four macromolecule classes · Lipids as the exception

title: Purines vs. pyrimidines
prompt: Sort each nitrogenous base by its ring structure.

pairs.right: Purine (double ring)
Purine (double ring)
Pyrimidine (single ring)
Pyrimidine (single ring)
Pyrimidine (single ring)

explanation: The DNA↔RNA thymine/uracil swap doesn't change ring class — both are pyrimidines, so the purine/pyrimidine split (2 purines, 3 pyrimidines) holds identically in DNA and RNA.
links: Purine vs pyrimidine

title: DNA vs. RNA, feature by feature
prompt: Sort each feature by which nucleic acid it belongs to.

pairs.right: DNA
RNA
DNA
RNA
DNA
RNA

explanation: These aren't independent facts — they're causally linked: ribose's extra 2'-OH makes RNA's backbone more reactive and less stable than DNA's deoxyribose backbone, which is exactly why RNA suits a disposable working copy and DNA suits long-term archival storage.
links: DNA vs RNA

title: Nucleotide chemistry vocabulary
prompt: Match each term to its precise meaning.

pairs.right: Base + sugar only
Base + sugar + one or more phosphates
Links one nucleotide's phosphate to the next's 3'-OH
Nucleotide repurposed as the cell's energy currency
Nucleotide repurposed as a signaling molecule
Nucleotide repurposed as an electron-carrying coenzyme

explanation: ATP, cAMP, and NAD are all structurally nucleotides (base+sugar+phosphate) even though none of them ever gets incorporated into a DNA or RNA strand — "nucleotide" is a structural classification, not a statement about function.
links: Nucleoside vs nucleotide · ATP/cAMP/NAD

title: Monosaccharides and polysaccharides
prompt: Match each carbohydrate to its identifying feature.

pairs.right: Aldehyde group; product of photosynthesis
Aldehyde group; found in dairy products
Ketone group; commercial sweetener
Branched glucose polymer; plant energy storage
Branched glucose polymer attached to a central protein; animal energy storage
Glucose polymer; plant structural support

explanation: Glucose, galactose, and fructose are all isomers of C6H12O6 — same formula, different arrangement. Starch, glycogen, and cellulose are all glucose polymers too, yet one is storage in plants, one in animals, and one is structural — proof that a polysaccharide's role comes from its linkage pattern, not its monomer.
links: Glucose/galactose/fructose · Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose

title: Lipid types and their structural features
prompt: Match each lipid-related term to its structural feature.

pairs.right: Glycerol + three fatty acid tails
Glycerol + two fatty acid tails + one phosphate head group
Many carbons fused into four rings — no glycerol at all
No carbon–carbon double bonds
One or more carbon–carbon double bonds
The specific steroid that's also a precursor to steroid hormones

explanation: Phospholipid vs triacylglycerol is a one-substitution difference — swap one fatty acid tail for a phosphate head — but that swap is what turns a hydrophobic storage molecule into an amphipathic, membrane-forming one.
links: Triacylglycerol vs phospholipid · Steroids · Saturated vs unsaturated

title: Bond types on the electronegativity spectrum
prompt: Match each bond type / molecule to its position on the electronegativity-difference spectrum.

pairs.right: ~0 electronegativity difference — equal sharing
Moderate difference — unequal sharing, partial charges
Large difference — full electron transfer
Nonpolar overall: weak bond dipoles cancel in a symmetric tetrahedron
Polar overall: bent shape prevents the O–H dipoles from cancelling
Dissolves as water's δ− oxygen surrounds Na+ and δ+ hydrogens surround Cl−

explanation: Nonpolar, polar, and ionic aren't three different mechanisms — they're one continuum (electronegativity difference) at three different magnitudes.
links: Electronegativity spectrum · Methane vs water geometry

title: Reaction and water-chemistry vocabulary
prompt: Match each term to its precise definition.

pairs.right: The starting materials of a chemical reaction
What a chemical reaction converts the reactants into
Joins two monomers; releases water; requires energy
Breaks a bond; consumes water; releases energy
Weak attraction between an electronegative atom and an H bonded elsewhere
Logarithmic 0–14 scale of H+ concentration

explanation: Condensation and hydrolysis are exact opposites of each other, both defined by what happens to water — one produces it, the other consumes it — which is why the same reaction pair can both build and break every polymer class.
links: Condensation vs hydrolysis · Hydrogen bonds · pH scale

box: A researcher wants to visualize a live neuron's mitochondria without killing the cell, using a fluorescent dye that binds only mitochondrial membranes.
claim: This approach relies on fluorescence microscopy's ability to selectively label one structure while leaving the rest of the cell dark.
explanation: Fluorescence microscopy uses molecule-specific labels so only the tagged structure lights up against a dark background — exactly the selective-labeling advantage it offers over standard light microscopy.
links: Fluorescence microscopy

box: A student examines a sample under electron microscopy and finds far greater structural detail than a colleague sees on the same sample under light microscopy.
claim: This difference in resolution occurs because electron microscopy uses a shorter-wavelength beam, which is why living cells can be imaged this way in real time.
explanation: The shorter wavelength does give EM higher resolution, but EM requires a vacuum and typically a fixed/dead sample — it cannot image living cells in real time, unlike light microscopy.
links: Electron vs light microscopy

box: Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork in 1665 and described empty box-like compartments; Anton van Leeuwenhoek later observed moving "animalcules" in pond water.
claim: Hooke's observation alone was enough to demonstrate tenet 1 of cell theory, since he had already identified that life is organized into discrete units.
explanation: Hooke observed dead, empty cell walls in cork — structure without evidence of life. Tenet 1 (all life is made of cells) needed evidence those units are alive, which Leeuwenhoek's living, moving cells supplied.
links: Hooke · Leeuwenhoek · Tenet 1

box: A scientist examines a tissue sample and confirms every cell within it arose by division from a pre-existing cell, with no evidence of spontaneous generation.
claim: This observation, by itself, is what Virchow's contribution to cell theory specifically established.
explanation: "Cells arise only from pre-existing cells" (rejecting spontaneous generation) is precisely Virchow's tenet 3 contribution.
links: Virchow · Tenet 3

box: A viroid consists of a short circular RNA molecule with no protein coat, and it can still cause disease in an infected plant.
claim: Because a viroid contains genetic material (RNA) capable of directing disease, it satisfies the basic cell definition and should be counted as a minimal cell.
explanation: Having genetic material isn't sufficient — a viroid has no membrane-enclosed cytoplasm, no ribosomes, and no independent metabolism. It's an exception to cell theory precisely because it isn't a cell despite carrying genetic material.
links: Viroid exception

box: A prion is a misfolded protein that can induce normal copies of the same protein to also misfold, with no nucleic acid involved in the process at all.
claim: A prion's ability to "reproduce" its misfolded shape means it satisfies cell theory's tenet 3 in a protein-only form.
explanation: Tenet 3 concerns cells arising from pre-existing cells via DNA-based division — a prion isn't a cell, and its spread is a conformational templating effect, not cellular reproduction. It's classified as an exception to cell theory.
links: Prion exception

box: A cell is treated with a drug that specifically blocks its ability to duplicate its DNA before division, but leaves all other cellular machinery untouched.
claim: This cell would still satisfy property 3 (self-reproduction) as long as it can still physically pinch into two cells.
explanation: Property 3 specifically requires duplicating DNA before division so each daughter cell gets a complete genome — physical division alone, without duplicated DNA, doesn't satisfy self-reproduction.
links: Property 3: self-reproduction

box: A tumor cell has lost the normal checkpoints that would otherwise stop it from dividing when it shouldn't.
claim: This is a direct example of a failure in property 8 (self-regulation), which is specifically linked to uncontrolled growth like cancer.
explanation: Loss of self-regulation (property 8) causing uncontrolled division is exactly the cancer link described among the 8 basic cell properties.
links: Property 8: self-regulation

box: A cell converts glucose into usable cellular energy through glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.
claim: This process demonstrates property 4 (acquire and use energy) but not property 5 (chemical reactions/metabolism), since those are two separate, unrelated properties.
explanation: Glycolysis and the citric acid cycle are themselves the metabolic chemical reactions referenced in property 5 — energy acquisition/use (property 4) and metabolism (property 5) are closely linked, not unrelated; this scenario illustrates both together.
links: Property 4 vs property 5

box: A newly discovered single-celled organism has a circular chromosome, no membrane-bound nucleus, and plasmids, and it thrives in a boiling hydrothermal vent using an isoprenoid-based membrane.
claim: Based on these features together, this organism is best classified as Bacteria rather than Archaea.
explanation: The isoprenoid membrane and extreme-environment tolerance are specifically Archaea's hallmark features; Bacteria typically have ester-linked membrane lipids. This organism fits Archaea.
links: Archaea vs Bacteria features

box: The three-domain tree of life places Eukarya as branching from within Archaea, rather than as a sibling group equally distant from both Bacteria and Archaea.
claim: This placement means Bacteria is the domain most distantly related to Eukarya.
explanation: If Eukarya branches from within Archaea, Bacteria diverged earlier from that lineage — making Bacteria the most distant of the three domains from Eukarya.
links: Three-domain tree

box: Rod-shaped E. coli cells are treated with A22, a compound that breaks up the filaments MreB forms just inside the cell membrane. The treated cells keep making cell wall, but they grow as spheres instead of rods.
claim: This result shows that, besides its cell wall, E. coli needs an internal protein framework to keep its rod shape.
explanation: Prokaryotes rely primarily on the cell wall and an internal rigid protein framework for support. Without MreB filaments, which guide where new wall is added, the cells still make wall but lose their rod shape; MreB is one of the cytoskeleton-like proteins bacteria have.
links: Prokaryote support: wall and protein framework · Real-world: A22 and bacterial shape

box: Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite that causes sleeping sickness, is a single eukaryotic cell with no cell wall. It swims through its host's blood with a flagellum and takes in nutrients from it.
claim: Since it has no cell wall and gets its carbon from another organism, it should be classified as an animal.
explanation: Trypanosoma is a protist (one of the protozoa): animals are multicellular, with a distinct mode of early development, so having no wall and feeding on another organism isn't enough.
links: Protists vs animals · Unicellular vs multicellular · Real-world: sleeping sickness

box: A fungal cell absorbs nutrients from its environment through its cell wall rather than ingesting food particles.
claim: Since fungi absorb nutrients rather than photosynthesizing, their cell walls must be made of cellulose, just like plant cell walls.
explanation: Fungal walls contain chitin, a modified polysaccharide, while plant walls are built from polysaccharides such as cellulose. Feeding by absorption says nothing about what a wall is made of, so the 'must' doesn't follow.
links: Fungi vs plants: cell wall material

box: An animal cell and a plant cell are compared side by side.
claim: The animal cell can be distinguished from the plant cell by the presence of a cell wall in the animal cell and its absence in the plant cell.
explanation: This is exactly backwards — plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells characteristically lack a cell wall entirely.
links: Animal vs plant cell walls

box: A protein is synthesized on a ribosome attached to the rough ER, folded and modified as it passes through the Golgi, and packaged into a vesicle for secretion.
claim: Every structure this protein passes through during its journey (rough ER, Golgi, vesicle) is classified as EMS.
explanation: Rough ER, Golgi, and the transport vesicle are all part of the membrane-trafficking pathway — the defining criterion for EMS classification.
links: EMS: secretory pathway

box: Mitochondria and peroxisomes are both membrane-bound organelles found in the same eukaryotic cell.
claim: Because both are membrane-bound, both must be classified as EMS.
explanation: Having a membrane isn't the criterion — EMS specifically means participation in membrane-trafficking (the ER–Golgi–vesicle pathway). Neither mitochondria nor peroxisomes participate in that pathway, so both are non-EMS despite being membrane-bound.
links: Non-EMS: membrane ≠ EMS

box: A cell's cilia beat rhythmically to move fluid across its surface, and its centrosome organizes microtubules during division.
claim: Both structures are classified as EMS because they are essential to the cell's mechanical activity (property 6).
explanation: Cilia and centrosomes are both non-EMS — mechanical/structural importance isn't the EMS criterion; only participation in membrane-based vesicle trafficking is, and neither structure does that.
links: Non-EMS: cilia & centrosome

box: A researcher wants to study flower development and needs a fast-growing plant with a fully sequenced genome and well-established genetic tools.
claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is the standard model organism for this purpose.
explanation: Arabidopsis is the standard flowering-plant model organism, chosen for its fast life cycle, small genome, and extensive genetic toolkit.
links: Arabidopsis

box: A geneticist wants to study how a single gene mutation affects development and behavior, using an organism with a short generation time, easily visible mutant phenotypes, and a century of established genetic techniques.
claim: Mus musculus (the mouse) is the best-suited model organism for this purpose, since it's the most extensively studied model organism overall.
explanation: Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) is the classic choice for classical genetics — short generation time, easy visible mutations, and a huge genetic toolkit built up over a century. Mice are preferred when findings need to translate to mammalian biology specifically, not for rapid genetic screening.
links: Drosophila vs mouse

box: A model organism is chosen specifically because it is small, fast-reproducing, and representative of broader biological principles — not because it's the most complex organism available.
claim: This selection logic explains why E. coli, despite being one of the structurally simplest organisms studied, remains one of the most widely used model organisms in molecular biology.
explanation: Simplicity and tractability, not complexity, drive model-organism selection — E. coli's simple structure is exactly why it's so useful for studying fundamental DNA/RNA/protein processes directly.
links: Model organism selection logic

box: Nearly all biological molecules are built from just six elements: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur.
claim: This small elemental "alphabet" is possible because every element's outermost electron shell holds a maximum of 8 electrons, giving every element identical bonding behavior.
explanation: Bonding behavior comes from how many valence electrons an atom needs to complete its outer shell, which differs by element (carbon needs 4, oxygen needs 2, etc.) — elements do not have identical bonding behavior.
links: CHNOPS · Valence electrons

box: A carbon atom has 4 valence electrons and an oxygen atom has 6 valence electrons in its outer shell.
claim: Because oxygen's outer shell is closer to full, it typically forms fewer covalent bonds than carbon does.
explanation: Oxygen needs only 2 more electrons to complete its outer shell (forming 2 bonds), while carbon needs 4 more (forming up to 4 bonds) — fewer electrons needed means fewer bonds typically formed.
links: Valence electrons and bond count

box: An atom's electrons are organized into orbitals, each of which can hold a maximum of 2 electrons.
claim: This 2-electron-per-orbital limit is what ultimately constrains how many covalent bonds an atom can form.
explanation: The number of unpaired (bonding-available) electrons an atom has sets its bonding capacity — carbon's four singly-occupied orbitals are exactly why it forms up to four bonds.
links: Orbitals and bonding capacity

box: Sodium (Na) has 1 valence electron; chlorine (Cl) has 7 valence electrons. When they react, sodium transfers its electron to chlorine.
claim: This electron transfer, rather than sharing, is what makes NaCl an example of a covalent bond.
explanation: Full electron transfer (not sharing) between atoms of very different electronegativity is the definition of an ionic bond — NaCl is a textbook ionic bond, not covalent.
links: Ionic bond · NaCl

box: Water is placed in a beaker with table salt (NaCl), and the salt fully dissolves.
claim: This happens because water molecules, being polar, surround each Na+ and Cl- ion with oppositely-charged ends, forming hydration shells that pull the ions apart.
explanation: Water's partial charges orient toward the ions' opposite charges, forming hydration shells that stabilize separated ions — exactly why water is a strong solvent for ionic compounds.
links: Water dissolving NaCl

box: A carbon atom forms a bond with another carbon atom, and a separate carbon atom forms a bond with an oxygen atom.
claim: Both bonds are equally nonpolar, since both involve carbon.
explanation: C–C bonds are nonpolar (identical electronegativity), but C–O bonds are polar covalent, since oxygen is more electronegative than carbon and pulls shared electrons toward itself unequally.
links: Polar vs nonpolar covalent bonds

box: A solution has a pH of 3, and another solution has a pH of 6.
claim: The pH-3 solution has 1,000 times more H+ ions than the pH-6 solution.
explanation: pH is a negative log scale, so each whole-number drop means a 10-fold increase in H+ concentration; a 3-unit difference (6→3) is 10³ = 1,000-fold.
links: pH scale is logarithmic

box: An enzyme normally functions at pH 7. It's placed into a solution at pH 2.
claim: This change cannot affect the enzyme's shape, since pH only affects small molecules, not large proteins like enzymes.
explanation: Proteins contain ionizable functional groups (like -NH2 and -COOH) whose charge depends on pH; a large pH shift changes these charges, which can disrupt the folded structure and impair function.
links: pH and protein structure

box: Two water molecules are near each other, with a partially positive hydrogen on one weakly attracted to a partially negative oxygen on the other.
claim: This weak attraction is a hydrogen bond, and it depends on both atoms involved being electronegative.
explanation: A hydrogen bond forms between a hydrogen (already bonded to an electronegative atom) and a separate electronegative atom with a lone pair — the hydrogen itself isn't electronegative; it's the atom pulling on the hydrogen's electron density that must be electronegative.
links: Hydrogen bond definition

box: A molecule contains an -NH2 group attached to its backbone.
claim: At physiological pH, this group tends to gain a proton and carry a positive charge.
explanation: The amino group is basic — it readily accepts a proton (H+) at physiological pH, becoming positively charged (-NH3+).
links: Amino functional group

box: A molecule has a -COOH group and a separate molecule has a -CH3 group.
claim: Both groups are hydrophilic, since both are common functional groups found in biological molecules.
explanation: Being a common functional group doesn't make something hydrophilic — -COOH is polar/ionizable and hydrophilic, but -CH3 (methyl) is nonpolar and hydrophobic.
links: Carboxyl vs methyl: hydrophilic?

box: Two amino acids join together, and separately, two monosaccharides join together.
claim: Only the amino acid reaction forms a bond through a specific functional-group linkage (the amide/peptide bond); the sugar-sugar reaction doesn't involve any specific functional group.
explanation: Both are functional-group-mediated condensation reactions — amino acids link via the amide (peptide) bond between carboxyl and amino groups, while monosaccharides link via a glycosidic bond formed from a hydroxyl group; both are specific, not generic.
links: Peptide bond vs glycosidic bond

box: A carbonyl group (C=O) appears in the middle of a carbon chain in one molecule, and at the end of a carbon chain in another molecule.
claim: Both are still built around the same core carbonyl group, but the two positions give the group different names (ketone vs. aldehyde respectively).
explanation: A carbonyl (C=O) at an internal carbon is a ketone; at a terminal carbon it's an aldehyde — same core functional group, positional difference gives it a more specific name (exactly the fructose/ketone vs. glucose/aldehyde distinction).
links: Carbonyl: aldehyde vs ketone

box: A cell needs to break down a stored polysaccharide into individual glucose monomers for energy.
claim: This breakdown reaction consumes a water molecule for each bond broken, and releases energy.
explanation: Hydrolysis (breaking a polymer) consumes water and releases energy — the reverse of the energy-requiring, water-releasing condensation reaction that built the polymer.
links: Hydrolysis

box: An enzyme catalyzes a reaction, lowering the activation energy required.
claim: Because the enzyme lowers activation energy, the reaction also becomes more energetically favorable overall (releases more net energy) than it would without the enzyme.
explanation: Enzymes change the rate of a reaction (how fast equilibrium is reached) by lowering activation energy — they do not change the overall energy difference between reactants and products.
links: Enzymes: rate vs energetics

box: A polypeptide chain folds into a specific 3D shape based on interactions between its R groups.
claim: If a single amino acid in the sequence is changed, the protein's 3D shape and function could be altered, even though only one R group changed.
explanation: Amino acid sequence determines 3D shape — even a single R-group change can disrupt the pattern of interactions (charge, hydrophobic, disulfide, etc.) that stabilizes the fold, altering shape and function.
links: Sequence determines shape

box: A functional protein is composed of four separate polypeptide chains held together by non-covalent interactions and disulfide bonds.
claim: This description specifically matches the definition of quaternary structure.
explanation: Quaternary structure is exactly the association of multiple separate polypeptide chains into one functional protein.
links: Quaternary structure

box: A protein acts as an enzyme in the cytoplasm, but the same protein also has a separate moonlighting role providing structural support to the cytoskeleton.
claim: Because it can act as an enzyme AND provide support, this contradicts the idea that proteins are classified by discrete functional categories (enzyme, transport, signal, movement, support, defense).
explanation: A single protein having more than one function doesn't invalidate the functional categories themselves — the categories describe what a protein can do, and one protein can occupy more than one category at once.
links: Protein functional categories

box: A nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and one or more phosphate groups. A nucleoside consists of just the base and the sugar.
claim: Removing the phosphate group(s) from a nucleotide would leave a nucleoside.
explanation: This is exactly the structural difference — a nucleoside is a nucleotide minus its phosphate group(s).
links: Nucleoside vs nucleotide

box: DNA contains the bases adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine; RNA contains adenine, uracil, guanine, and cytosine.
claim: Adenine and guanine are purines (double-ring), while thymine, uracil, and cytosine are all pyrimidines (single-ring).
explanation: This is the correct purine/pyrimidine split — two purines (A, G) and three pyrimidines (T, U, C) across DNA and RNA.
links: Purines vs pyrimidines

box: A phosphodiester bond links the phosphate group of one nucleotide to a specific carbon on the sugar of the next nucleotide.
claim: This linkage always connects to the 5' carbon of the next nucleotide's sugar, which is why strands grow in the 3'→5' direction.
explanation: The phosphodiester bond links to the next nucleotide's 3'-OH, not 5' — which is exactly why strands grow 5'→3', the reverse of this claim.
links: Phosphodiester bond direction

box: Glucose and galactose share the exact same molecular formula (C6H12O6) but differ in the 3D arrangement of one hydroxyl group.
claim: This relationship makes glucose and galactose isomers of each other, just like glucose and fructose are.
explanation: Same molecular formula, different atomic/spatial arrangement is the definition of isomers — this applies to glucose/galactose just as it does to glucose/fructose.
links: Six-carbon sugar isomers

box: A cell links three glucose molecules together into a short chain via glycosidic bonds.
claim: Because it contains only three monomers, this molecule is correctly classified as a polysaccharide.
explanation: A chain of only a few monomers (here, three) is an oligosaccharide; "polysaccharide" refers to much longer chains — classification here depends specifically on monomer count.
links: Disaccharide vs oligo vs polysaccharide

box: Starch (plant storage), glycogen (animal storage), and cellulose (plant structural support) are all polymers built entirely from glucose monomers.
claim: Despite sharing the same monomer, they serve different biological roles because of differences in how the glucose units are linked and branched.
explanation: Same monomer, different linkage/branching pattern — this is exactly what determines each polysaccharide's distinct biological role.
links: Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose

box: A steroid hormone like testosterone is built from four fused carbon rings, with no glycerol backbone or fatty acid tail anywhere in its structure.
claim: Because it lacks the glycerol-and-fatty-acid architecture typical of other lipids, testosterone should not be classified as a lipid at all.
explanation: Lipids are grouped by a shared physical property (hydrophobicity), not shared structure — a steroid's ring structure is just as valid a lipid architecture as a glycerol-based one.
links: Steroids as lipids

box: A fatty acid tail contains two carbon-carbon double bonds along its chain.
claim: These double bonds prevent free rotation at those points, introducing kinks that make the molecule it's part of pack less tightly than a fully saturated version would.
explanation: Double bonds restrict rotation and introduce a bend in the chain — exactly why unsaturated fats pack more loosely (and tend to be liquid at room temperature) compared to saturated fats.
links: Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids

box: A lipid molecule has a glycerol backbone attached to two fatty acid tails and one phosphate-containing head group.
claim: This structure is amphipathic, and would spontaneously arrange itself in water with its tails facing outward, toward the water.
explanation: The molecule (a phospholipid) is amphipathic, but the hydrophobic tails orient away from water (facing inward, toward each other), while the hydrophilic phosphate heads face outward, toward the water — the claim reverses the orientation.
links: Phospholipid orientation in water

box: Cell theory states that (1) all living things are composed of cells, and (2) the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. A bacterium is a single cell that performs every life function alone; a human liver is made of billions of cells, each performing its own functions as part of the larger organism.
claim: Both the bacterium and the human liver illustrate tenets 1 and 2 together — life is cellular, and the cell (whether alone or as part of a larger body) is the basic functional unit — applying equally to unicellular and multicellular organisms.
explanation: Tenet 1 (all life is cellular) and tenet 2 (the cell is the basic structural/functional unit) hold regardless of whether an organism is a single cell (unicellular) or built from many cooperating cells (multicellular) — both examples satisfy both tenets.
links: Tenets 1 & 2 · Unicellular vs multicellular

box: A drop of vegetable oil is added to a glass of water and does not mix in, clumping into a separate layer; a spoonful of sugar added to the same glass dissolves completely and disappears.
claim: Both outcomes are explained by water's behavior as a "universal solvent" — it dissolves the oil via the hydrophobic effect and dissolves the sugar via hydrophilic interactions.
explanation: Water does NOT dissolve the oil — the hydrophobic effect describes exactly why nonpolar molecules like oil clump together and separate from water, rather than being dissolved by it. Water's strength as a solvent (shown by the dissolved sugar) applies specifically to polar/hydrophilic substances, not universally to everything.
links: Water as solvent: hydrophilic vs hydrophobic

box: A particular stretch of DNA contains the instructions to build a functional enzyme, and this stretch is passed down from parent to offspring.
claim: This stretch of DNA fits the definition of a gene, since a gene is specifically defined as a DNA sequence that codes for a functional product.
explanation: This is exactly the definition of a gene used in this course — a DNA sequence that codes for a functional product (here, an enzyme).
links: Gene definition

box: A bacterial cell duplicates its single circular chromosome, then elongates and pinches inward at its midpoint, splitting into two genetically identical daughter cells.
claim: This process is called binary fission, and it is the standard mode of reproduction for prokaryotic cells.
explanation: This is exactly binary fission — chromosome duplication followed by division into two identical cells — the standard prokaryotic reproduction method.
links: Binary fission

box: A student claims that "organic," in the biological/chemical sense used in this course, means "naturally occurring" or "healthy," similar to how the word is used on food packaging.
claim: In this course, "organic molecule" simply means any molecule that contains carbon — unrelated to the food-packaging sense of the word.
explanation: In this context, "organic" has a specific chemical meaning — containing carbon — unrelated to the "natural/healthy" connotation from food marketing.
links: "Organic" = contains carbon

box: An amino acid's alpha carbon is bonded to four groups: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group.
claim: At physiological pH, this same amino acid typically exists as a zwitterion, with both the amino and carboxyl groups carrying opposite charges simultaneously.
explanation: The standard amino acid structure (alpha carbon + NH2 + COOH + H + R) is correct, and at physiological pH the amino group is protonated (positive) while the carboxyl group is deprotonated (negative) — the simultaneous-charge zwitterion state.
links: Amino acid structure · Zwitterion

box: A single neuron embedded in the human brain and a single amoeba living independently in a pond both carry out digestion, energy production, and response to stimuli using the same basic cellular toolkit.
claim: This shared capability across such different cells — one embedded in a multicellular brain, one living alone — is exactly what tenet 2 of cell theory (the cell as the basic structural and functional unit of life) describes.
explanation: Tenet 2 states the cell — regardless of whether it's embedded in a multicellular organism or living independently — is the basic unit carrying out life's functions; both examples show this.
links: Tenet 2: the cell as basic unit

box: A biology textbook describes water as the "universal solvent" of life, noting that most of the biochemistry inside a cell happens in an aqueous (water-based) environment.
claim: This label reflects water's ability to dissolve a very wide range of polar and ionic (hydrophilic) substances, not a literal ability to dissolve absolutely everything, including nonpolar substances.
explanation: "Universal solvent" describes water's unusually broad ability to dissolve hydrophilic substances via hydrogen bonding and charge interactions — it does not mean water dissolves nonpolar (hydrophobic) substances, which instead clump together via the hydrophobic effect.
links: "Universal solvent" — what it actually means

stem: A researcher needs to observe the general shape and arrangement of cells in a tissue sample quickly and cheaply, without needing to resolve internal organelle structure. Which technique best fits this need?
options: Electron microscopy
Fluorescence microscopy with organelle-specific antibody labeling
X-ray crystallography
Light microscopy
Mass spectrometry
explanation: Light microscopy is the fastest, cheapest option and is sufficient when only gross cell shape/arrangement is needed; EM and fluorescence labeling are reserved for finer detail or specific structures, and the other two techniques aren't microscopy methods at all.
links: Choosing a microscopy technique

stem: An infectious particle consists only of nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat. It has no ribosomes, no metabolism, and cannot reproduce without hijacking a host cell's machinery. Which of the following best classifies this particle under cell theory?
options: An exception to cell theory (not a cell)
A minimal prokaryotic cell
A eukaryotic cell lacking EMS organelles
An example of tenet 3 in action
A cell missing only property 1
explanation: No ribosomes, no independent metabolism, and no ability to reproduce without a host means this particle fails the basic cell definition entirely — it's a virus, treated as an exception to cell theory rather than an unusual minimal cell.
links: Virus as cell theory exception

stem: Which of the following is the best example of property 7 (respond to stimuli)?
options: A cell duplicating its DNA before dividing
A cell breaking down glucose via glycolysis
A cell's ribosome translating mRNA into protein
A cell's checkpoint halting division after DNA damage
A cell's receptor binding a hormone and triggering an internal signaling cascade
explanation: Property 7 specifically concerns detecting and reacting to external signals via receptors — a receptor binding a hormone and triggering a response is the textbook example; the other options illustrate reproduction, metabolism, the genetic program, and self-regulation instead.
links: Property 7: respond to stimuli

stem: A microbiologist finds an organism with a single circular chromosome, plasmids, a peptidoglycan-based cell wall, and standard ester-linked membrane lipids, living in ordinary soil. Which domain does this organism most likely belong to?
options: Archaea
Bacteria
Eukarya
Protista
It cannot be a member of any of the three domains
explanation: Peptidoglycan cell walls and ordinary ester-linked membrane lipids (rather than isoprenoid) in a non-extreme environment are hallmarks of Bacteria, not Archaea.
links: Identifying Bacteria vs Archaea

stem: Which combination of features would correctly identify an organism as belonging to Fungi rather than Plantae?
options: Cellulose cell wall, autotrophic, chloroplasts present
No cell wall, heterotrophic by ingestion
Chitin cell wall, heterotrophic by absorption, no chloroplasts
Cellulose cell wall, heterotrophic by absorption
Chitin cell wall, autotrophic, chloroplasts present
