explanation: Using Module 3's definitions: cytoplasm = all cell contents except the nucleus, organelles included; cytosol = the fluid region outside the organelles but inside the plasma membrane.
links: Cytoplasm vs cytosol · Real-world: cell fractionation

box: The enzymes of glycolysis are dissolved in the fluid outside the organelles, while the enzymes of the citric acid cycle are inside the mitochondrial matrix.
claim: Both sets of enzymes are in the cytoplasm, but only the glycolysis enzymes are in the cytosol.
explanation: Using Module 3's definitions, the cytoplasm is everything in the cell except the nucleus, mitochondria included, while the cytosol is only the fluid outside the organelles. So matrix enzymes are cytoplasmic but not cytosolic.
links: Cytoplasm vs cytosol · Mitochondrial matrix

title: Assembly line in the Golgi
stem: Read (가) and (나) about how the Golgi apparatus modifies a membrane glycoprotein. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The enzyme that adds sugar Y is found only in cisternae that the protein reaches after the cisternae holding the enzyme that adds sugar X.

(나) Sugar Y can be attached only to a sugar chain that already carries sugar X.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Glycosylation links the sugars to the protein by hydrogen bonds, so the chains can easily fall off later.
statements.explanation: Glycosylation joins carbohydrates covalently to lipids or to specific amino acids of proteins; the chains are stable.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Placing different enzymes in different regions of the Golgi lets modifications occur in a set order as the protein moves through.
statements.explanation: Each modification step happens in a different region with its own enzymes, so X is added before Y by position.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Once the protein reaches the plasma membrane, its sugar chains will face the extracellular fluid, because the inside of the Golgi corresponds to the outside of the cell after vesicle fusion.
statements.explanation: A vesicle's inner face becomes the outer face of the plasma membrane when it fuses — which is why membrane carbohydrates all face outward.

links: Golgi cisternae · Glycosylation · Membrane orientation · Carbohydrates face outward

box: Plasma cells, the immune cells that secrete thousands of antibody (protein) molecules per second, have cytoplasm filled with stacked sheets of rough ER.
claim: Because antibodies are secreted, they are most likely made by free ribosomes in the cytosol, while all that rough ER mainly makes membrane lipids.
explanation: Proteins for secretion are built by ribosomes on the rough ER and then travel ER → Golgi → secretory vesicles → exocytosis; the huge rough-ER area is where the antibodies are made. Lipid synthesis is the smooth ER's job.
links: Rough vs smooth ER · Secretory route · Real-world: antibody-secreting cells

stem: A wilted houseplant is watered, and its leaves become firm again within hours. Which structure is most directly responsible for restoring firmness?
options: The chloroplasts, which make extra sugars that stiffen the leaf's cell walls
The cell wall, which actively contracts to pull the leaf back into shape
The smooth ER, which makes new phospholipids so each cell can quickly grow larger again
The central vacuole, which fills with water and presses the cell against its wall
The lysosomes, which break down and clear away the damaged, wilted tissue
explanation: Water entering by osmosis swells the vacuole, pressing the membrane against the wall; that turgor pressure — not the wall on its own — keeps soft plant tissue firm.
links: Vacuole · Turgor pressure · Cell wall

title: One system, two kinds of connection
stem: Which statements in <보기> about how the endomembrane system is connected are correct?
box:
(가) The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER membrane.

(나) Material travels from the ER to the Golgi, and from the Golgi to the plasma membrane, only inside vesicles.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (가) is a permanent membrane bridge, while (나) is a transient connection made by vesicles budding from one compartment and fusing with another.
statements.explanation: Endomembrane compartments are linked either physically by membrane bridges or transiently by vesicles.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A phospholipid made in the smooth ER could reach the plasma membrane without ever leaving a membrane.
statements.explanation: It stays in the bilayer as vesicles bud and fuse, moving from the ER membrane to the Golgi membrane to the plasma membrane.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The nucleus is the innermost organelle of this system, and the plasma membrane belongs to the same system.
statements.explanation: The endomembrane system includes the nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles, and the plasma membrane; the nucleus is its innermost organelle.

links: Endomembrane system · Membrane bridges vs vesicles · Smooth ER lipids

box: Ribosomes are found both bound to the rough ER and free in the cytosol.
claim: Because ribosomes can bind the ER membrane, they are membrane-enclosed organelles that belong to the endomembrane system.
explanation: Ribosomes have no membrane of their own; they are non-endomembrane structures that attach to the rough ER's cytosolic face or float free in the cytosol.
links: Ribosomes · EMS vs non-EMS

stem: A glycoprotein receptor ends up in the plasma membrane with its sugar chains facing outside the cell. Using the diagram, which route did it take?
options: Rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane
Free ribosome in the cytosol → Golgi → plasma membrane
Smooth ER → lysosome → plasma membrane
Rough ER → Golgi through a permanent membrane bridge → plasma membrane
Golgi → rough ER → vesicle → plasma membrane
explanation: Membrane proteins are made on rough-ER ribosomes, carried by vesicle to the Golgi (not physically attached to the ER), where sugars are added, then shipped by vesicle to the plasma membrane.
links: Secretory pathway · Golgi sorting · Glycosylation

stem: Lysosomes keep their interior near pH 5, while the cytosol stays near pH 7. Which result would best support the course's explanation of why lysosomal contents must be kept separate from the rest of the cell?
options: Lysosomal enzymes released into the cytosol digest the cell's ribosomes
Cytosolic proteins unfold and stop working at pH 5 but not at pH 7
Lysosomal enzymes are made on the rough ER and then sorted in the Golgi
Cytosolic proteins keep their shape and activity at every pH from 3 to 11
Lysosomes stay acidic only while their proton pumps are supplied with ATP
explanation: The course's reason is that the cytosol's proteins and organelles suit pH 7 and would be damaged at pH 5, so the matching test exposes cytosolic proteins to pH 5, with pH 7 as the control. Enzyme digestion is a different reason; the other results are unrelated or contradict the claim.
links: Why lysosomes are kept separate · Experimental logic

stem: Two cells of equal volume are compared. In cell X, the ER is a highly folded network of tubules and flattened sacs; in cell Y, the ER is a few round, unfolded sacs enclosing the same total volume. Which prediction follows?
options: Cell Y has more ER membrane area, because round sacs have the most surface for their volume
Both cells have the same ER membrane area, because their ER encloses the same volume
Folding reduces the ER's membrane area but greatly increases the space enclosed inside it
Folding matters only for mitochondria; the shape of the ER doesn't affect its output
Cell X has far more ER membrane area, so more surface on which to make lipids and proteins
explanation: For a given enclosed volume, a round shape has the least surface; folding into tubules and flattened sacs packs much more membrane into the same space. That large membrane area is where the ER makes lipids and proteins.
links: ER structure · Membrane surface area

box: Nuclear pores perforate the nuclear envelope, letting molecules move between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
claim: Away from the pores, a single lipid bilayer separates the nucleus from the cytosol, just as the plasma membrane separates the cell from its surroundings.
explanation: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane — an inner and an outer membrane, the outer one continuous with the ER — so two bilayers separate the nucleus from the cytosol everywhere except at the pores.
links: Nuclear envelope · Double membrane

stem: Away from any pores or channels, how many lipid bilayers separate each of these spaces from the cytosol: the inside of the nucleus, the mitochondrial matrix, and the inside of a lysosome?
explanation: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane, and a mitochondrion has an outer and an inner membrane; a lysosome is a specialized vesicle bounded by a single membrane.
links: Nuclear envelope · Mitochondrial membranes · Lysosome membrane

stem: Electron micrographs show ribosomes attached to the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope, just as they are attached to the rough ER. Which fact best explains this?
options: The nuclear envelope is part of the Golgi apparatus
The outer nuclear membrane is physically continuous with the ER membrane
Ribosomes are assembled in the nucleolus and stick to the envelope as they leave
Nuclear pores are lined with ribosomes that carry out export
The inner nuclear membrane is where the cell's lipids are made
explanation: The outer nuclear membrane and the ER form one continuous membrane, so the outer nuclear membrane can behave like rough ER, with ribosomes bound to its cytosolic face.
links: Nuclear envelope–ER continuity

box: A drug blocks all vesicle traffic from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
claim: Newly made lysosomal enzymes would still reach the lysosomes, since lysosomes collect their enzymes directly from the rough ER.
explanation: Lysosomal enzymes are made in the rough ER, sorted in the Golgi, and only then packaged into lysosomes. The Golgi isn't physically attached to the ER, so blocking ER-to-Golgi vesicles keeps the enzymes from ever reaching lysosomes.
links: Lysosomal enzyme route · ER-to-Golgi vesicles

title: If this organelle failed…
prompt: Match each failing structure in an animal cell to its most direct consequence.

pairs.right: Proteins destined for secretion or the plasma membrane are no longer made
Proteins leave the ER but are not modified, given sugars, or sorted to their destinations
Worn-out proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids pile up undigested
Far less ATP is made from the energy stored in sugars
The cell loses the protein scaffold that gives it its structure

explanation: Each structure has one main job in the animal cell: the ER makes proteins and lipids, the Golgi modifies and sorts them, lysosomes break down macromolecules, mitochondria harness energy, and the cytoskeleton is the cell's protein scaffold.
links: Organelle roles in an animal cell

box: A student argues that mitochondria belong to the endomembrane system because they are surrounded by membranes and sit in the cytoplasm next to the ER and Golgi.
claim: The student is right, because what qualifies an organelle for the endomembrane system is being enclosed by a membrane.
explanation: Membership depends on connection — by membrane bridges or vesicle traffic — not on having a membrane. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are membranous but are not part of the endomembrane system.
links: EMS membership · Mitochondria and chloroplasts are non-EMS

title: Locating events in the two energy organelles
prompt: Using the diagram's labels, match each compartment to the scenario that happens there or depends on it.

pairs.right: A small dye molecule crosses easily through large, nonselective channels
Where that dye stops if it cannot cross the next, more selective membrane
A toxin that blocks ATP synthase acts here
Where mitochondrial genes are transcribed and translated
Where chlorophyll absorbs light energy
Reached after crossing the chloroplast's outer and inner membranes, without entering any thylakoid

explanation: Porins make the outer membrane nonselective, so the inner membrane is the real barrier. The ETC and ATP synthase sit in the inner membrane; DNA and ribosomes are in the matrix; pigments are in thylakoid membranes; the stroma is the fluid around the thylakoids.
links: Mitochondrial compartments · Chloroplast compartments

title: Counting membranes to the destination
stem: Two molecules start in the cytosol. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Molecule X must reach the lumen of a thylakoid.

(나) Molecule Y, a charged molecule such as ADP, must reach the mitochondrial matrix.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: X and Y must each cross the same number of membranes: two.
statements.explanation: X crosses three — the chloroplast's outer (A), inner (B), and thylakoid (C) membranes — while Y crosses two, the mitochondrial outer (1) and inner (3) membranes.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Once Y passes through the porins of the outer membrane, it will reach the matrix without needing any other transport protein.
statements.explanation: Porins make only the outer membrane nonselective; the inner membrane is a separate, selective barrier that charged molecules cross only through transport proteins.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The chloroplast stroma occupies the position that corresponds to the mitochondrial matrix: the space enclosed by the inner membrane.
statements.explanation: Both are the innermost space bounded by the inner membrane; the chloroplast simply adds thylakoids inside it.

links: Double membranes · Thylakoid as a third membrane · Porins

box: Heart muscle cells use ATP nonstop. Their mitochondria have much more densely folded inner membranes than the mitochondria of less active cells.
claim: The extra folding would be expected to support faster ATP production, because it increases the membrane area available for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
explanation: The ETC and ATP synthase are located in the inner membrane; folding packs more of that membrane — and more ATP-making machinery — into each mitochondrion.
links: Inner membrane folding · ATP synthase · Real-world: heart muscle

title: Bacteria inside our cells
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> about the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts are correct?
box:
(가) Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular genomes and ribosomes, and they grow and divide semi-autonomously.

(나) Mitochondria resemble proteobacteria, and chloroplasts resemble cyanobacteria, in organization and biochemistry.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Their circular genomes support an endosymbiotic origin, since bacteria typically have a single circular chromosome.
statements.explanation: Circular DNA, their own ribosomes, and independent division are bacterial traits kept from free-living ancestors.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Under both hypotheses, mitochondria descend from a proteobacterium; the hypotheses differ in whether the nucleus formed before or after that partnership.
statements.explanation: Hypothesis 1: infolding makes the nucleus and EMS first, then a proteobacterium is engulfed. Hypothesis 2: the partnership comes first and infolding makes the nucleus later.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Under Hypothesis 1, the proteobacterium was engulfed by a host cell that had not yet formed a nucleus.
statements.explanation: That describes Hypothesis 2. In Hypothesis 1, the archaeon forms its nucleus and endomembrane system by infolding before engulfing the proteobacterium.

links: Endosymbiosis · Two hypotheses for eukaryote origin · Semi-autonomous organelles

box: Hypothesis 2 in the diagram begins with an archaeon host living in partnership with a proteobacterium symbiont inside it.
claim: Hypothesis 2 implies that, for a time, a cell contained the ancestor of mitochondria but did not yet have a nucleus.
explanation: In Hypothesis 2 the symbiosis comes first and membrane infolding produces the nucleus later — so there was a stage with a symbiont inside a still nucleus-free archaeal host. Hypothesis 1 predicts the opposite order.
links: Hypothesis 1 vs Hypothesis 2 · Prokaryotes lack a nucleus

box: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both contain their own circular genomes and ribosomes, and both grow and divide independently within the cell.
claim: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from the same engulfed bacterium, which later specialized into two kinds of organelle.
explanation: They come from two different endosymbiotic events: mitochondria from a proteobacterium, and chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium engulfed later by a eukaryotic cell that already had mitochondria.
links: Endosymbiosis: two separate partners

stem: Chloramphenicol, an antibiotic that blocks bacterial ribosomes, can cause serious side effects (such as bone-marrow suppression) by also blocking protein synthesis inside one human organelle. Which organelle is it, and why is it vulnerable?
options: Mitochondria — they descend from bacteria and keep bacteria-like ribosomes
Rough ER — its ribosomes are attached to a membrane, like some bacterial ones
Nucleus — it holds the cell's DNA, which the drug stops cells from reading
Golgi apparatus — it modifies newly made proteins, so it depends on ribosomes
Lysosomes — their digestive enzymes are proteins that need constant replacement
explanation: Mitochondria originated as endosymbiotic proteobacteria and keep their own DNA and ribosomes in the matrix, so a drug aimed at bacterial ribosomes can hit them too; cytosolic and rough-ER ribosomes are the eukaryotic type.
links: Mitochondrial ribosomes · Endosymbiosis · Real-world: antibiotic side effects

box: A leaf cell contains both chloroplasts and mitochondria.
claim: Because chloroplasts already make sugars, a leaf cell would be expected to rely on its chloroplasts, rather than mitochondria, to harness the energy in those sugars as ATP.
explanation: Chloroplasts capture light energy to make sugars; mitochondria then harness the energy in sugars to make ATP. Plant cells need both — mitochondria are present in almost all eukaryotic cells.
links: Chloroplasts make sugars · Mitochondria make ATP

stem: In autumn, the green colour drains from many leaves as their chlorophyll is broken down. Where in the chloroplast is this pigment being lost, and which process does the loss directly weaken?
options: The stroma — capturing light energy to make sugars
The outer membrane — the barrier controlling what enters the chloroplast
The thylakoid membranes — converting sugars into ATP
The lumen — storing the sugars made in summer
The thylakoid membranes — capturing light energy to make sugars
explanation: Light-collecting pigments, mostly chlorophyll, sit in the thylakoid membrane, so losing them weakens light capture for photosynthesis. Converting sugars into ATP is the mitochondrion's job.
links: Thylakoid pigments · Photosynthesis · Real-world: autumn leaves

box: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria (and no nucleus), yet they still need ATP — for example, to run their Na+/K+ pumps.
claim: Red blood cells must make their ATP without the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain.
explanation: The citric acid cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, and the ETC and ATP synthase sit in the inner membrane; with no mitochondria, red cells rely on ATP-making reactions in the cytosol (glycolysis).
links: Mitochondrial compartments · Real-world: red blood cells

box: Both the ER and the inner mitochondrial membrane are highly folded.
claim: In both cases, folding is valuable mainly because it increases the volume of the compartment the membrane encloses.
explanation: Folding increases membrane area, not enclosed volume. More ER membrane means more room for making lipids and proteins; more inner mitochondrial membrane means more room for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
links: Membrane folding and surface area · ER · Inner mitochondrial membrane

stem: A small dye added to the cytosol can pass through porins but cannot cross a lipid bilayer on its own or use any other mitochondrial protein. Where in the mitochondrion will it be found?
options: In the matrix
In both the matrix and the intermembrane space
In the intermembrane space
Nowhere — porins are in the inner membrane
In the thylakoid lumen
explanation: Porins sit in the outer membrane, so the dye passes into the intermembrane space; with no way across the inner membrane, it never reaches the matrix. Thylakoids belong to chloroplasts, not mitochondria.
links: Porins · Intermembrane space · Inner-membrane barrier

stem: A single-celled green alga contains both mitochondria and chloroplasts. Which sequence of events best explains how it came to have both?
options: A single engulfed proteobacterium later divided into both mitochondria and chloroplasts
A cyanobacterium engulfed a proteobacterium, and together the pair became the first alga
A cell that already had mitochondria later engulfed a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast
Chloroplasts formed first by infolding of the cell membrane, and mitochondria were engulfed later
Mitochondria came from an engulfed cyanobacterium, and chloroplasts from a proteobacterium
explanation: Two separate endosymbioses: mitochondria came from a proteobacterium; later, in the lineage leading to green algae and plants, a cell that already had mitochondria engulfed a cyanobacterium. That is why nearly all eukaryotes have mitochondria but only some have chloroplasts.
links: Endosymbiosis: mitochondria and chloroplasts

title: Two hormones, two strategies
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Testosterone, a steroid hormone (a lipid), binds receptor proteins inside its target cells.

(나) Insulin, a protein hormone, binds receptor proteins on the outer surface of its target cells.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Testosterone can reach receptors inside the cell because, being nonpolar, it crosses the bilayer by simple diffusion.
statements.explanation: Nonpolar molecules such as lipids pass directly through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Insulin stays outside because it is nonpolar and gets trapped in the bilayer's hydrophobic core.
statements.explanation: Insulin is a large, polar macromolecule — too large to cross the bilayer at all — so it signals through a surface receptor instead.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A small fragment of insulin that kept many charged side chains could cross the bilayer as freely as water.
statements.explanation: Shrinking helps only if the molecule is also uncharged; charged groups are still blocked by the hydrophobic core.

links: Selective permeability · Simple diffusion · Receptors · Real-world: steroid vs protein hormones

box: Cells produce CO2 continuously as a waste product of metabolism.
claim: CO2 leaves the cell by simple diffusion, without a transport protein, and its net movement stays outward as long as its concentration inside the cell is higher than outside.
explanation: Small gases like CO2 cross the bilayer directly. Net diffusion runs from high to low concentration and continues while the gradient exists — and producing CO2 inside keeps that gradient going.
links: Simple diffusion · Concentration gradient

box: A membrane permeable to urea separates two compartments. After an hour, the urea concentration is the same on both sides.
claim: At this point, urea molecules have stopped crossing the membrane.
explanation: Only the net movement stops. Random motion continues in both directions, so influx and efflux still happen — they are simply equal.
links: Diffusion equilibrium · Influx and efflux

stem: A radioactive tracer shows that 500 molecules of solute X enter a cell each second while 200 leave each second. Which description is correct?
options: Influx is 500/s, efflux is 200/s, and the net flux is 700/s into the cell
Influx is 500/s, efflux is 200/s, and the net flux is 300/s into the cell
Influx is 200/s, efflux is 500/s, and the net flux is 300/s out of the cell
There is no net flux, because molecules are moving in both directions
The net flux is 300/s out of the cell, since efflux always opposes influx
explanation: Influx = movement in, efflux = movement out, and net flux = the difference when one exceeds the other: 500 − 200 = 300/s inward.
links: Influx · Efflux · Net flux

title: Reading uptake curves
stem: Uptake of two molecules into cells is measured as their outside concentration is raised. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Uptake of X rises at first but levels off at high outside concentrations; a drug that locks X's transport protein in one shape blocks uptake. X always moves from high to low concentration.

(나) Uptake of Y rises in direct proportion to its outside concentration, never levels off, and needs no protein.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: X crosses by facilitated diffusion through a carrier: each molecule must bind and trigger a shape change, so uptake stops rising once all the carriers are busy.
statements.explanation: Carriers bind specific molecules and change conformation to release them on the other side; a limited number of carriers caps the rate, and locking the shape blocks transport.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because X's uptake levels off, X must be moving against its concentration gradient using energy.
statements.explanation: Leveling off reflects a limited number of carriers, not the direction of movement; X moves down its gradient, so this is passive.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Y is most likely a small uncharged or nonpolar molecule crossing by simple diffusion.
statements.explanation: Simple diffusion needs no protein, so nothing saturates — the rate just tracks the concentration gradient.

links: Carrier proteins · Simple vs facilitated diffusion · Passive transport

box: Aquaporins are channel proteins that let water cross membranes much faster than through the bilayer alone. When the body needs to conserve water, kidney cells insert more aquaporins into their membranes.
claim: With enough aquaporins, kidney cells can move water against its concentration gradient back into the body.
explanation: A channel only provides an aqueous pore — facilitated diffusion. Water still moves by osmosis, down its own concentration gradient (toward the side with more solute); aquaporins change the rate, not the direction.
links: Channel proteins · Osmosis · Real-world: kidney water conservation

box: In cystic fibrosis, a chloride-ion channel in airway cells fails to work, so fewer Cl- ions move out of the cells into the thin fluid layer that lines the airways. Patients' airway mucus becomes thick and sticky.
claim: The thick mucus is explained by osmosis: with less solute moving into the airway fluid, less water follows it out of the cells.
explanation: Water moves toward the side with more solute (lower water concentration). When Cl- secretion fails, the airway fluid gains less solute, so less water leaves the cells and the mucus dehydrates.
links: Ion channels · Osmosis · Real-world: cystic fibrosis

title: The wrong IV bag
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic to red blood cells and is safe to infuse into a vein.

(나) By mistake, a large volume of pure water is infused into a patient's vein.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In normal saline, water molecules stop crossing the red cell membrane.
statements.explanation: Isotonic means no net flow; water still crosses in both directions at equal rates.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Red blood cells exposed to the pure water would swell and could burst (hemolysis), because water moves into the cells, where the solute concentration is higher.
statements.explanation: Pure water is hypotonic to the cells: water enters by osmosis, the cells swell, and animal cells, having no wall, can lyse.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A plant cell placed in pure water would swell but not burst, because its wall resists the pressure; it becomes turgid.
statements.explanation: The wall pushes back against the swelling vacuole and membrane, producing turgor instead of lysis.

links: Tonicity · Hemolysis · Turgor · Real-world: IV fluids

stem: Lettuce left in a salty dressing turns limp. What happened in its cells?
options: The dressing is hypotonic, so water rushed into the cells until their walls burst
Salt entered the cells by simple diffusion, making the cells swell and then collapse
The dressing is isotonic, so the limpness must come from the vinegar dissolving the walls
Water left the cells (hypertonic dressing), so their membranes pulled off the walls: plasmolysis
The dressing is hypertonic, so the cells shrivelled by crenation, just as red blood cells do
explanation: Higher solute outside (hypertonic) pulls water out by osmosis. In plant cells the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis) and turgor is lost; 'crenation' is the term for animal cells, which have no wall.
links: Hypertonic solution · Plasmolysis vs crenation · Real-world: wilting salad

box: Paramecium, a single-celled protist with no cell wall, lives in pond water that is hypotonic to its cytoplasm.
claim: Without a way to pump out the water that constantly enters, Paramecium would swell and burst, like a red blood cell in pure water.
explanation: In a hypotonic solution water keeps entering by osmosis; with no wall to resist the pressure, the cell would lyse — so wall-less freshwater protists must actively expel water (with contractile vacuoles).
links: Hypotonic environment · Lysis · Real-world: freshwater protists

stem: A cell whose internal solute concentration is 0.3 M is placed in a 0.5 M solution of a solute that cannot cross its membrane. Which statement is correct?
options: The solution is hypertonic, and water leaves the cell because the water concentration is higher inside the cell than outside
The solution is hypertonic, and water leaves the cell because water moves from high solute concentration to low solute concentration
The solution is hypotonic, and water enters the cell because the cell's solute concentration is lower
The solute diffuses in until both sides reach 0.4 M, so no water moves
No water moves until the cell uses ATP to pump the solute out
explanation: More solute outside means less free water outside; water diffuses from higher [H2O] (inside) to lower [H2O] (outside) — that is, toward the higher solute concentration. The solute can't cross, so only water moves.
links: Osmosis as water diffusion · Tonicity

box: Glucose enters most body cells through GLUT carrier proteins, always moving from higher to lower glucose concentration.
claim: Because a protein is required, this glucose uptake is powered by ATP.
explanation: Needing a protein doesn't settle it — facilitated-diffusion carriers and ATP-driven pumps are both proteins. Direction does: GLUT moves glucose down its gradient, so this is facilitated diffusion, which is passive and uses no ATP.
links: Facilitated diffusion · Passive vs active

title: Name that transport mode
prompt: Match each example to the transport mode it uses.

pairs.left: O2 entering a red blood cell in the lungs
pairs.right: Simple diffusion

pairs.left: K+ leaving a nerve cell through a pore that opens only when triggered
pairs.right: Facilitated diffusion through a gated channel

pairs.left: Glucose moving down its gradient into a muscle cell by binding a carrier that changes shape
pairs.right: Facilitated diffusion through a carrier

pairs.left: Na+ pushed out of a cell against its gradient by a pump that hydrolyzes ATP
pairs.right: Primary active transport

pairs.left: Glucose pulled into an intestinal cell against its gradient as Na+ flows in
pairs.right: Secondary active transport

pairs.left: A white blood cell engulfing a whole bacterium
pairs.right: Phagocytosis (bulk transport)

explanation: Ask two questions: is a protein needed, and is the solute moving with or against its gradient? Down the gradient = passive (no protein = simple; protein = facilitated). Against it = active (ATP directly = primary; another ion's gradient = secondary). Whole particles need bulk transport.
links: Passive vs active · Channels vs carriers · Primary vs secondary · Bulk transport

box: Solution A is hypertonic to red blood cells, and red blood cells are hypertonic to solution B.
claim: If A and B were separated by a membrane permeable only to water, net water flow would be from B into A.
explanation: Solute concentrations rank A > cells > B. Water moves from the lower-solute (higher-water) side toward the higher-solute side, so from B into A. Tonicity is always relative to something.
links: Tonicity is relative · Osmosis

title: Same physics, different cells
prompt: Match each real situation to what happens to the cells.

pairs.left: Red blood cells dropped into distilled water
pairs.right: They swell and burst (lysis)

pairs.left: Red blood cells placed in concentrated salt water
pairs.right: They shrivel (crenation)

pairs.left: Spinach leaves soaked in strong brine
pairs.right: Their membranes pull away from the cell walls (plasmolysis)

pairs.left: Cells of a wilted plant after the soil is watered
pairs.right: They swell against their walls and become turgid

pairs.left: Red blood cells suspended in normal (0.9%) saline
pairs.right: No net water movement; they keep their normal shape

explanation: First decide whether the outside is hypertonic, hypotonic, or isotonic to the cells; water then moves toward the higher solute concentration. The cell wall is the only reason plant and animal outcomes differ.
links: Tonicity · Crenation · Plasmolysis · Turgor

title: A heart drug that slows a pump
stem: Digoxin, used to treat some heart conditions, partially blocks the Na+/K+ pump in heart muscle cells. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The Na+/K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, keeping Na+ low inside the cell.

(나) Heart cells also have a Na+/Ca2+ antiporter: as Na+ flows in down its gradient, it pushes Ca2+ out of the cell.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: With fewer working pumps, Na+ would slowly build up inside the heart cells.
statements.explanation: The pump is what keeps intracellular Na+ low; slowing it lets the Na+ that leaks in accumulate.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Digoxin would therefore let Ca2+ accumulate inside the heart cells, because the weakened Na+ gradient powers less Ca2+ removal.
statements.explanation: The antiporter is secondary active transport driven by the Na+ gradient; a smaller gradient pushes out less Ca2+, and the extra Ca2+ strengthens contraction.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Since the antiporter uses no ATP directly, it would keep removing Ca2+ at its normal rate however much the pump is blocked.
statements.explanation: Secondary active transport runs on the gradient that primary active transport builds; weaken the pump and everything that depends on its gradient weakens too.

links: Na+/K+ pump · Secondary active transport · Antiporter · Real-world: digoxin

box: A mutant Na+/K+ pump can be phosphorylated by ATP (step 2 in the diagram) but can never release its phosphate (step 4).
claim: The mutant pump will release Na+ outside and bind K+, but it can never carry K+ into the cell or begin another cycle.
explanation: Phosphorylation opens the pump outward (Na+ out, K+ binds). Releasing the phosphate is what snaps the pump back to face inward and releases K+ inside; without it, the cycle stops after step 3.
links: Na+/K+ pump cycle · Conformational change

stem: Based on the diagram, what is the net movement of positive charge across the plasma membrane for each ATP the Na+/K+ pump uses?
options: Five positive charges move out of the cell
One positive charge moves into the cell
No net charge moves, since Na+ and K+ both carry +1
Two positive charges move out of the cell
One positive charge moves out of the cell
explanation: Each cycle moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in: 3 − 2 = one net positive charge out, which helps make the inside negative relative to the outside.
links: Pump stoichiometry · Electrochemical gradient

box: Plant cells, like animal cells, maintain ion gradients across their plasma membranes.
claim: Plant cells build these gradients with proton (H+) pumps rather than a Na+/K+ pump, which is found only in animal cells.
explanation: The Na+/K+ pump occurs only in animal cells. Plant cells use ATP-driven proton pumps, and the resulting H+ gradient powers their secondary active transport.
links: Na+/K+ pump · Proton pumps

title: Two forces on every ion
stem: The diagram shows the two forces on Na+ and on K+ in a resting animal cell, whose inside is negative relative to the outside. Apply the same reasoning to other ions and conditions. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Ca2+ is far more concentrated outside the cell than inside, and so is Cl-.

(나) For a brief moment, the inside of the cell becomes positive relative to the outside.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: When Ca2+ channels open in a resting cell, Ca2+ rushes in, because both its concentration gradient and the charge difference push it inward.
statements.explanation: Like Na+, Ca2+ is concentrated outside (chemical force inward) and positively charged, so the negative interior attracts it (electrical force inward); the forces add.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: For Cl- in a resting cell, the charge difference also pulls it inward, adding to its concentration gradient.
statements.explanation: Like charges repel: a negative interior pushes the anion outward, opposing its inward concentration gradient.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: During (나), the charge force on Na+ would point outward, so the total inward push on Na+ would be weaker than at rest.
statements.explanation: With the inside positive, the electrical force now repels Na+; only its concentration gradient still pushes it in, so the total inward drive shrinks.

links: Electrochemical gradient · Chemical vs electrical force · Charge of the ion

box: A plant cell uses ATP to pump H+ out across its plasma membrane.
claim: The H+ gradient it builds stores energy in its concentration difference but not in any charge difference across the membrane.
explanation: H+ carries a positive charge, so pumping it builds a charge difference as well as a concentration difference — an electrochemical gradient, which can then drive secondary active transport.
links: Proton pump · Electrochemical gradient

title: Why oral rehydration solution contains sugar
stem: Cholera causes severe diarrhea, but the intestinal Na+/glucose symporter keeps working. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Oral rehydration solution (ORS) — water with both Na+ and glucose — has saved millions of cholera patients.

(나) Plain water, or salt water without sugar, rehydrates cholera patients much less effectively.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The symporter hydrolyzes ATP to move glucose against its gradient.
statements.explanation: It is secondary active transport: Na+ flowing down its gradient drives glucose uphill. The ATP is spent by the basal Na+/K+ pump.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: ORS works because Na+ and glucose absorbed together through the symporter raise the solute concentration inside intestinal cells, and water follows by osmosis.
statements.explanation: Moving solute into the cells (and on into the blood) creates the osmotic pull that draws water out of the gut.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the basal Na+/K+ pumps stopped, glucose uptake from the gut would eventually fail even though the symporter itself uses no ATP.
statements.explanation: The pump keeps Na+ low inside the cell; without it the Na+ gradient runs down and the symporter loses its driving force.

links: Na+/glucose symport · Primary vs secondary active · Osmosis · Real-world: oral rehydration therapy

stem: In the diagram, glucose enters the intestinal cell through a symporter coupled to Na+ but leaves across the basal membrane through a uniporter. Why can the exit step be passive?
options: The basal uniporter hydrolyzes ATP itself, so the exit step is really a form of active transport
Cell glucose exceeds blood glucose, so exit is downhill; lumen glucose is lower, so entry is uphill
Glucose is nonpolar, so it diffuses freely through the basal membrane without any protein
Na+ in the blood drives glucose out of the cell through the basal uniporter by symport
The apical membrane has no transport proteins, so only the basal exit step needs one
explanation: Direction relative to the gradient decides the mechanism: lumen (low) → cell (high) needs secondary active transport, while cell (high) → blood (lower) is facilitated diffusion through a uniporter.
links: Symporter vs uniporter · Facilitated diffusion · Glucose absorption

title: Who moves what, and on whose energy?
prompt: Match each transport protein to its correct classification.

pairs.right: Secondary active symporter — both solutes move the same way; the Na+ gradient powers it
Secondary active antiporter — solutes move opposite ways; the Na+ gradient powers it
Uniporter — one solute moving down its gradient (facilitated diffusion)
Primary active antiporter — ATP hydrolysis moves two ions in opposite directions
Primary active pump for a single solute — ATP moves H+ into an organelle against its gradient

explanation: Every transporter gets an energy word (primary, secondary, passive) for what powers it; direction words say whether it moves one solute (uniport) or two in the same (symport) or opposite (antiport) directions.
links: Symport · Antiport · Uniport · Primary vs secondary

box: A carrier protein for facilitated diffusion and an active transporter both bind their solute and change shape.
claim: Because both work by changing shape, both would be expected to move their solute from higher to lower concentration.
explanation: Only the carrier follows the gradient. An active transporter couples its shape change to an energy source, so it moves its solute in one direction — against the gradient.
links: Carrier vs active transporter

box: Cyanide stops mitochondria from making ATP. In a poisoned cell, the Na+/K+ pumps slow, and the Na+ and K+ gradients across the plasma membrane gradually run down.
claim: Secondary active transport in this cell would also decline, even though secondary transporters never use ATP themselves.
explanation: Secondary transporters run on ion gradients that primary (ATP-driven) pumps build. When ATP runs out, the gradients fade — and so does everything they drive.
links: Primary vs secondary active transport · Real-world: cyanide poisoning

stem: A bacterium uses ATP to pump H+ out of the cell. A drug-efflux antiporter in the same membrane lets H+ flow back in while pushing an antibiotic out — a common cause of antibiotic resistance. Which change would most directly stop the antiporter from expelling the antibiotic?
options: Adding more glucose to the medium so the bacterium can make more ATP
Raising the antibiotic concentration outside the bacterial cell
Blocking the bacterium's ribosomes for a few seconds with another drug
Making the membrane leaky to H+, so the H+ gradient collapses
Adding a second antibiotic that targets the cell wall
explanation: The antiporter is secondary active transport: its energy comes from H+ moving down its electrochemical gradient. Remove the gradient, and the drug can no longer be pushed out against its own gradient.
links: Proton gradient · Antiporter · Real-world: antibiotic efflux pumps

stem: Each cycle of the Na+/K+ pump removes one more ion than it brings in, offsetting the Na+ that constantly leaks into an animal cell. What would happen to the volume of a cell whose pumps were completely blocked by the poison ouabain?
options: It would shrink, because K+ stays trapped inside and draws water out of the cell
It would stay the same size, because Na+ and K+ carry the same positive charge
It would swell: Na+ that leaks in accumulates, so water follows it in by osmosis
It would shrink, because a blocked pump can no longer let water into the cell
It would burst at once, because the pump is also the cell's main route for water
explanation: Na+ (with Cl- following) keeps leaking in but is no longer pumped out, so internal solute rises; water follows by osmosis and the cell swells. The pump is part of how wall-less animal cells control their volume.
links: Na+/K+ pump · Osmosis · Cell volume

box: The Na+ and K+ gradients across an animal cell's membrane always favour Na+ moving in and K+ moving out, yet the Na+/K+ pump steadily moves Na+ out and K+ in.
claim: What keeps the pump's cycle running in this direction is its coupling to ATP: phosphorylation and phosphate release force its shape changes to occur in one fixed order.
explanation: An active transporter changes conformation when it binds its solutes; here each change is tied to ATP — phosphorylation after Na+ binds inside, phosphate release after K+ binds outside — so the cycle runs one way, uphill for both ions. ATP hydrolysis supplies more energy than the gradients store.
links: Active transporters move solutes one way · Na+/K+ pump cycle

title: When LDL can't get in
stem: LDL particles carry cholesterol in the blood and are taken into cells by receptor-mediated endocytosis. In familial hypercholesterolemia, the LDL receptor is defective, and blood cholesterol stays very high. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Normal cells gather LDL receptors in coated pits and take LDL in efficiently, even at low blood levels.

(나) Patients' cells can still take up small amounts of LDL.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The small uptake in (나) could occur by pinocytosis, which brings in whatever molecules are dissolved in the engulfed fluid without recognizing them.
statements.explanation: Pinocytosis is nonspecific 'cell drinking', so some LDL enters with the fluid — far less efficiently than through concentrated receptors.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In normal cells, LDL taken in through coated pits is delivered first to early endosomes near the cell periphery, then to late endosomes deeper inside.
statements.explanation: Receptor-mediated cargo goes into a network of endosomes: early (peripheral), then late (interior), which also receive material from the Golgi.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Clathrin on the outer face of the coated pit is what recognizes and binds LDL.
statements.explanation: Receptors on the extracellular side bind LDL; clathrin coats the cytoplasmic side and helps bring the vesicle in.

links: Receptor-mediated endocytosis · Clathrin · Endosomes · Real-world: familial hypercholesterolemia

box: Neutrophils engulf bacteria by phagocytosis, and the phagosome then fuses with a lysosome whose contents include lysozyme. The antibiotic penicillin kills bacteria by blocking the construction of their cell walls.
claim: Lysozyme attacks the same bacterial structure that penicillin targets.
explanation: Lysozyme degrades bacterial cell walls, while penicillin blocks wall construction. Human cells have no wall, so both strategies hit bacteria without harming our own cells.
links: Phagocytosis · Lysozyme · Bacterial cell wall

stem: A cell takes in a dissolved dye for which it has no receptor. Which process brings the dye in, and must the resulting vesicle fuse with a lysosome?
options: Phagocytosis; yes — every engulfed particle is digested
Receptor-mediated endocytosis; yes — cargo always goes to lysosomes first
Pinocytosis; yes — fluid can only be released after digestion
Exocytosis; no — the dye enters by vesicle fusion
Pinocytosis; no — the small vesicle need not merge with a lysosome
explanation: Without a receptor, uptake is nonspecific pinocytosis ('cell drinking'), which forms small vesicles that don't need to merge with a lysosome; phagocytosis is for large, recognized particles.
links: Pinocytosis · Phagocytosis · Endocytosis

box: A cell takes up a fluorescent dye by endocytosis. Moments later, the dye appears inside the cell as small bright dots.
claim: At that moment, the dye is still separated from the cytosol by a membrane that came from the plasma membrane.
explanation: Endocytosis never breaks membrane continuity: the infolded membrane becomes the vesicle wall, so the cargo stays enclosed — still 'outside' the cytosol.
links: Endocytosis · Membrane continuity

title: Releasing messages by the vesicle-load
stem: Which statements in <보기> about exocytosis are correct?
box:
(가) Nerve cells release chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) stored in vesicles by exocytosis.

(나) During intense activity, a single nerve terminal can release hundreds of vesicles per second.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The messengers reach the outside of the cell without the cytosol ever being exposed to the extracellular fluid.
statements.explanation: Fusion keeps membranes continuous; only the vesicle's interior opens to the outside.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A nerve cell releasing many vesicles would steadily gain plasma-membrane area unless it took membrane back in by endocytosis.
statements.explanation: Each fusion adds membrane; cells balance this by retrieving membrane through endocytosis.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Vesicles that carry secreted proteins to the cell surface bud from the Golgi, part of the endomembrane system.
statements.explanation: Exocytosis delivers the contents of vesicles that bud off the endomembrane system into the extracellular space.

links: Exocytosis · Membrane continuity · Real-world: neurotransmitter release

title: Disarming a phagocyte
prompt: Each neutrophil below has one defect. Match each defect to its most direct consequence.

pairs.left: No surface receptors for a particular bacterium
pairs.right: The bacterium is never recognized, so it isn't engulfed

pairs.left: Phagosomes that cannot fuse with lysosomes
pairs.right: Bacteria are enclosed but never exposed to hydrolytic enzymes
Bacterial cell walls are not broken down

pairs.left: Phagosomes lacking oxidases on their inner surface
pairs.right: No H2O2 is made to kill bacteria

pairs.left: Lysosomes whose proton pump has failed
pairs.right: Microorganisms normally killed by acidic pH survive

explanation: Phagocytic defense is a chain — recognition, engulfment into a phagosome, fusion with a lysosome, then killing by lysozyme, acidic pH, and H2O2. Breaking any one link leaves a specific gap; in single-celled organisms, the same pathway provides nutrition.
links: Phagocytosis · Lysosomes · Immune defense

stem: Vitamin B12 travels in the blood bound to a carrier protein at very low concentration, yet cells take it in efficiently and selectively. Which feature best explains this?
options: Receptors that bind the carrier gather in coated pits, capturing it even from dilute fluid
Pinocytosis takes in extracellular fluid, so it collects the vitamin in proportion to its concentration
The vitamin–carrier complex is small enough to diffuse straight across the lipid bilayer
Phagocytosis engulfs the vitamin–carrier complexes as large, recognized particles
Exocytosis pulls the complex into the cell each time a vesicle fuses with the membrane
explanation: Receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates specific cargo: receptors gather in clathrin-coated pits, so the cell takes up far more of the target than nonspecific pinocytosis would at that concentration.
links: Receptor-mediated endocytosis · Coated pits · Real-world: vitamin uptake

box: Pinocytic vesicles are smaller than phagosomes and carry dissolved molecules rather than whole cells.
claim: Like phagocytosis, pinocytosis begins when the plasma membrane recognizes a specific target.
explanation: Pinocytosis takes up extracellular fluid without recognition — whatever is dissolved comes in. Recognition through receptors is a feature of phagocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis.
links: Pinocytosis vs phagocytosis

title: Which way in or out?
prompt: Match each scenario to the bulk-transport process it uses.

pairs.left: A macrophage engulfs a worn-out red blood cell and digests it
pairs.right: Phagocytosis

pairs.left: A cell samples the surrounding fluid, taking in whatever solutes it contains
pairs.right: Pinocytosis

pairs.left: A liver cell captures cholesterol-carrying LDL particles through clathrin-coated pits
pairs.right: Receptor-mediated endocytosis

pairs.left: A pancreatic cell releases insulin stored in vesicles
pairs.right: Exocytosis

explanation: Ask what is moving and whether it is recognized: large recognized particles → phagocytosis; fluid with no recognition → pinocytosis; specific cargo through receptors and clathrin → receptor-mediated endocytosis; outward delivery by vesicle fusion → exocytosis.
links: Bulk transport modes

box: A newly made lysosomal enzyme leaves the Golgi apparatus. Minutes earlier, LDL particles were taken into the same cell by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
claim: The enzyme and the LDL could meet in late endosomes, which receive material both from early endosomes and from the Golgi apparatus.
explanation: Endocytosed cargo passes from early endosomes (near the periphery) to late endosomes (deeper inside), which also receive material from the Golgi — a meeting point of the inward and outward routes.
links: Early and late endosomes · Golgi delivery

box: A macrophage takes in material by endocytosis many times a minute.
claim: Each round of endocytosis removes a little membrane from the cell surface — the reverse of what exocytosis does.
explanation: The plasma membrane folds inward and pinches off to form each vesicle, so endocytosis takes surface membrane into the cell, while exocytosis adds vesicle membrane back; busy cells balance the two.
links: Endocytosis · Exocytosis · Membrane balance

title: What the mice and the enzymes proved
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Griffith, 1928: heat-killed virulent bacteria alone do not kill a mouse, but mixed with live nonvirulent bacteria they do, and live virulent bacteria are recovered from the mouse.

(나) Avery, MacLeod and McCarty, 1944: an extract of heat-killed virulent cells still transforms nonvirulent cells after RNase or protease treatment, but not after DNase treatment.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (가), the virulent cells recovered from the mouse must have come from live nonvirulent cells that picked up something from the dead virulent cells.
statements.explanation: Dead cells can't revive, and nonvirulent cells alone are harmless; the only source of live virulent cells is nonvirulent cells transformed by a molecule in the debris.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Griffith's experiment by itself identified DNA as the transforming molecule.
statements.explanation: Griffith showed that some molecule in the debris carried the genetic information for virulence, but it wasn't identified until Avery's enzyme experiments. (The notes' opening line credits Griffith with showing that DNA is the genetic material; strictly, his experiment showed only that something transforms, and Avery's team identified it as DNA.)

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the DNase-treated extract in (나) had still transformed the cells, DNA could not have been the molecule required for transformation.
statements.explanation: The logic is elimination: destroying the true genetic material must block transformation, and only destroying DNA did.

links: Griffith's transformation · Avery's enzyme experiment · Experimental logic

box: The virulent bacteria recovered from Griffith's fourth mouse were grown in culture, and their descendants were virulent too.
claim: This shows that transformation changed the bacteria's heritable genetic information, rather than just coating them temporarily with material from the dead cells.
explanation: A temporary coating would be diluted away as cells divide; virulence passed on for generations means the information was stored and copied — the defining jobs of genetic material.
links: Transformation · Genetic material stores and copies information

stem: Suppose Avery's team had found the opposite pattern: the protease-treated extract failed to transform the nonvirulent cells, while the DNase- and RNase-treated extracts still transformed them. What would they have concluded?
options: DNA is the genetic material, since DNase didn't stop transformation
RNA is the genetic material, since RNase didn't stop transformation
Protein, not DNA, is the transforming (genetic) material
Both DNA and protein are required, since some treatments worked
Nothing can be concluded, since heat-killed cells were used
explanation: Each enzyme destroys one candidate; the treatment that blocks transformation identifies the molecule that is required — in this hypothetical, protein. The real result (only DNase blocked it) pointed to DNA.
links: Avery, MacLeod & McCarty · Logic of elimination

title: Chargaff by the numbers
stem: Two double-stranded DNA samples of equal length are analyzed. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Sample 1 is 30% adenine.

(나) Sample 2 is 60% G + C.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Chargaff's rule %A = %T would hold just as well for the genome of a virus made of single-stranded DNA.
statements.explanation: The rule comes from complementary pairing between two strands; a single strand has no partner forcing A to equal T.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Sample 1 is 20% guanine.
statements.explanation: %A = %T = 30%, so A + T = 60% and G + C = 40%; since %G = %C, guanine is 20%.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Sample 2 would need more heat than sample 1 to separate its strands.
statements.explanation: Sample 1 is only 40% G + C. Each G–C pair has three hydrogen bonds versus two for A–T, so G–C-rich DNA holds together more strongly.

links: Chargaff's rules · Hydrogen bonds per base pair · Complementary pairing

box: One strand of a 10-base-pair DNA segment reads 5'-GGCATGCCAT-3'.
claim: The two strands of this segment are held together by 25 hydrogen bonds.
explanation: Count the pairs: 6 G–C pairs (G, G, C, G, C, C) × 3 = 18, plus 4 A–T pairs × 2 = 8, for 26 hydrogen bonds.
links: Hydrogen bonds: G–C = 3, A–T = 2

stem: What is the complementary strand of 5'-ATGCCT-3', written in the standard 5'→3' direction?
options: 5'-TACGGA-3'
5'-TCCGTA-3'
3'-AGGCAT-5'
5'-UACGGA-3'
5'-AGGCAT-3'
explanation: Pair each base (A–T, G–C) to get 3'-TACGGA-5', then rewrite it from its 5' end, because the strands are antiparallel: 5'-AGGCAT-3'.
links: Antiparallel strands · Complementary pairing · Writing sequences 5'→3'

box: A DNA sequence is written simply as GATTC, with neither end labeled.
claim: By convention, the C at the right-hand end carries the strand's free 5' phosphate.
explanation: An unlabeled sequence is written 5'→3', so the left end (G) is the 5' end; the C on the right carries the free 3'-OH.
links: Sequence convention · Strand polarity

title: Reading the ladder
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Every rung joins a two-ring base to a one-ring base.

(나) The sugar-phosphate backbones run along the outside of the ladder, and the bases point inward.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Pairing a purine with a pyrimidine on every rung keeps the helix a constant 2 nm wide.
statements.explanation: Two rings (A, G) plus one ring (C, T) always gives the same rung length; two purines would bulge the helix and two pyrimidines would pinch it.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: With the backbones outside, the negatively charged phosphates face the surrounding water while the bases are tucked inside.
statements.explanation: The ionized phosphates are hydrophilic and sit on the outside; the bases stack in the interior.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because the strands are antiparallel, the left strand's 5' end sits across from the right strand's 5' end.
statements.explanation: Antiparallel means opposite directions: the left strand's 5' end faces the right strand's 3' end, as the diagram shows.

links: Purine–pyrimidine pairing · Antiparallel strands · Backbone outside

box: A gene is 3,000 base pairs long. Use the helix dimensions given in the diagram.
claim: Stretched out as a double helix, this gene makes about 300 complete turns and is about 1 µm (1,000 nm) long.
explanation: 3,000 bp ÷ 10 bp per turn = 300 turns; 300 × 3.4 nm = 1,020 nm ≈ 1 µm.
links: Helix dimensions: 3.4 nm and 10 bp per turn

stem: About 2 m of DNA must fit inside a human nucleus only a few micrometres across. Which is the first level of packing in the condensation series?
options: The DNA double helix folds directly into a 1,400 nm condensed chromatid
DNA wraps around histone proteins, forming the 10 nm nucleosome fiber
The DNA coils into a 30 nm fiber before any proteins bind to it
RNA molecules wrap around the DNA to shorten it before it folds
Phospholipids coat the DNA so that it can be folded more tightly
explanation: Packing proceeds stepwise: 2 nm DNA → 10 nm nucleosome fiber (DNA wound around histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4) → 30 nm chromatin fiber → 300 nm → 700 nm → 1,400 nm condensed chromatid.
links: Chromosome condensation · Nucleosomes · Histones

title: Carbon numbers matter
stem: Which statements in <보기> about nucleotide structure are correct?
box:
(가) In a DNA nucleotide, the base attaches to the 1' carbon of deoxyribose and the phosphate to the 5' carbon.

(나) Deoxyribose has no oxygen at its 2' carbon.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The next nucleotide attaches at the 2' carbon, which is why losing the 2' oxygen defines DNA.
statements.explanation: Attachment is always at the 3'-OH. The missing 2' oxygen is simply what makes the sugar deoxyribose.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A nucleoside (base + sugar only) can be joined directly into a growing chain, since the base alone decides pairing.
statements.explanation: Joining needs phosphates: incoming units are nucleoside triphosphates, whose phosphate forms the phosphodiester link and supplies the energy. A nucleoside has none.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: When two nucleotides join, the phosphate on the incoming nucleotide's 5' carbon bonds to the 3'-OH of the previous nucleotide, forming a phosphodiester bond.
statements.explanation: That 5'-phosphate-to-3'-OH link is the phosphodiester bond, which is why each strand has a 5' end and a 3' end.

links: Nucleotide carbons · Phosphodiester bond · Nucleotide vs nucleoside

box: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments are loaded into wells in a gel held at about pH 8, and an electric field is applied across it.
claim: The DNA fragments will migrate toward the negative electrode.
explanation: Negatively charged DNA is attracted to the positive electrode. The ionized phosphate groups of the backbone give DNA its uniform negative charge.
links: Negatively charged backbone · Real-world: gel electrophoresis

box: Many DNA-binding proteins, including transcription factors, recognize specific base sequences without unzipping the double helix.
claim: This is possible because the helix's outer surface forms major and minor grooves in which the edges of the paired bases are exposed.
explanation: The uneven grooves leave part of each base pair accessible from outside, so proteins can 'read' a sequence such as a promoter while the DNA stays double-stranded.
links: Major and minor grooves · DNA-binding proteins

stem: Which statement best describes what holds the two strands of the double helix together and stabilizes it?
options: Covalent bonds that form between the paired bases on the two strands
Ionic bonds between the negatively charged phosphate groups of the two strands
Phosphodiester bonds that cross the middle from one strand to the other
Many weak H-bonds between paired bases, plus stacking between neighbouring bases
Hydrogen bonds alone, since neighbouring bases on a strand don't interact
explanation: Base pairs are joined by hydrogen bonds — weak one by one but strong in number — and stacking interactions between adjacent bases on each strand add stability. Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides only within a strand.
links: Hydrogen bonds · Base stacking · Phosphodiester bonds

box: In PCR, DNA is heated to about 95 °C so its two strands separate; on cooling, short complementary DNA pieces (primers) pair with the separated strands.
claim: Heating separates the strands by breaking the phosphodiester bonds that link the two strands, and these bonds re-form when the sample cools.
explanation: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides within each strand and stay intact. Heat breaks the weak hydrogen bonds between paired bases (base stacking along each strand adds stability), which is what lets DNA 'unzip' down the middle.
links: Unzipping DNA · Real-world: PCR

stem: Watson and Crick built their double-helix model from other researchers' results. Which pairing of evidence and inference is correct?
options: Franklin and Wilkins' X-ray data revealed the helix's shape and size; Chargaff's ratios pointed to A–T, G–C pairing
Chargaff's ratios revealed the helical shape and dimensions; Franklin and Wilkins' X-ray data showed which bases pair
Franklin and Wilkins' X-ray data showed that A pairs with G; Chargaff's ratios showed that the strands run parallel
Chargaff's ratios showed that the helix is left-handed; Franklin and Wilkins' X-ray data placed the bases on the outside
Griffith's and Avery's experiments revealed the helical shape; Chargaff's ratios showed that the backbone lies inside
explanation: X-ray crystallography (Franklin and Wilkins) gave the helical structure; Chargaff's equal ratios implied complementary pairing. The resulting model: a right-handed, antiparallel double helix with backbones outside and bases inside.
links: Watson & Crick · Franklin & Wilkins · Chargaff

box: The two strands of a DNA double helix are complementary.
claim: So the two strands have identical sequences when each is read 5'→3'.
explanation: Complementary means paired, not identical: the partner of 5'-ATGCCT-3' reads 5'-AGGCAT-3'. Only special palindromic sequences, such as 5'-GAATTC-3', read the same on both strands.
links: Complementary vs identical · Antiparallel strands

box: Erwin Chargaff found that %A = %T and %G = %C in DNA from many species; Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins obtained X-ray crystallography images of DNA.
claim: Chargaff's ratios alone were enough for Watson and Crick to conclude that DNA is a helix of two strands.
explanation: The ratios suggested which bases pair, but the helical shape and its dimensions came from the X-ray data. Watson and Crick needed both lines of evidence.
links: Evidence behind the double helix

title: Structure explains function
prompt: Match each feature of DNA structure to the property it explains.

pairs.right: Each strand can serve as a template to rebuild its partner
The strands can be 'unzipped' without breaking either backbone

pairs.left: A purine always paired with a pyrimidine
pairs.right: The helix keeps a constant 2 nm width
The charged, hydrophilic part of DNA faces the surrounding water
Proteins can read base sequences without unwinding the helix

explanation: DNA's two jobs — storing information and copying it — follow from its structure: complementary, weakly paired strands make copying possible, while the regular, stable helix protects the stored sequence.
links: DNA structure and function

box: A single DNA strand is 12 nucleotides long, and each nucleotide was built with a phosphate on its 5' carbon.
claim: The strand therefore has two 5'-phosphate ends, one at each end.
explanation: Phosphodiester bonds link each nucleotide's 5' phosphate to the previous one's 3'-OH, so only one end keeps a free 5' phosphate; the other end has a free 3'-OH. That difference gives every strand its polarity.
links: Strand polarity · Phosphodiester bonds

box: A student builds a DNA model whose two strands twist around each other to the left, with the sugar-phosphate backbones running down the middle and the bases pointing outward.
claim: Apart from the backbones and bases being swapped, the model is correct, including its left-handed twist.
explanation: The twist is wrong too: DNA's two strands form a right-handed helix. So the model has two errors — a left-handed twist, and backbones inside instead of outside with the bases pointing inward.
links: Right-handed helix · Backbones outside, bases inside

box: A liver cell and a nerve cell from the same person make very different sets of proteins.
claim: As it developed, the nerve cell must have lost the genes for liver proteins from its genome.
explanation: Both cells carry the same genome. Gene expression is regulated: each cell type turns on a different subset of genes, so the liver genes are present but switched off in the nerve cell.
links: Genome · Regulated gene expression

stem: Why is RNA synthesis called 'transcription' while protein synthesis is called 'translation'?
options: Transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm, so the two names simply record where each step occurs
Transcription copies DNA into new DNA before division, while translation converts that DNA into RNA for export
Transcription is carried out by ribosomes reading DNA, while translation is carried out by RNA polymerase reading mRNA
Transcription copies within one nucleic-acid 'language'; translation converts it into another: amino acids
Transcription keeps the two DNA strands together, while translation separates them so each can be read into protein
explanation: DNA and RNA are both nucleic acids, so making RNA from DNA is copying in the same language; making protein from mRNA's code changes the language to amino acids. Location differs only in eukaryotes and isn't the reason for the names.
links: Central dogma · Transcription vs translation

box: HIV carries its genome as RNA. After infecting a cell, it makes a DNA copy of that RNA, which is inserted into the host's DNA.
claim: The host cell's RNA polymerase carries out this step by running in reverse.
explanation: RNA polymerase makes RNA from a DNA template. Making DNA from an RNA template — reverse transcription, an exception to the central dogma — requires the virus's own RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase.
links: Reverse transcription · Central dogma exception

title: Small differences, big consequences
stem: Which statements in <보기> about how RNA differs from DNA are correct?
box:
(가) Ribose, RNA's sugar, carries an -OH on its 2' carbon, where deoxyribose has only -H.

(나) The 5' end of a newly made RNA typically carries three phosphates, while the 5' end of DNA typically carries one.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The 2'-OH makes RNA less stable than DNA, which suits RNA as a short-lived working copy and DNA as long-term storage.
statements.explanation: The extra hydroxyl makes RNA more reactive and less stable — fine for a message that should be temporary.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Uracil has an extra methyl group compared with thymine, which is why it pairs with A.
statements.explanation: Uracil has an -H where thymine has a methyl (-CH3); both pair with A.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: RNA's 5' triphosphate is left over from the first nucleotide, which was never joined to a previous nucleotide and so never lost its outer phosphates.
statements.explanation: Each later nucleotide loses two phosphates (as pyrophosphate) when it is joined to the chain; the first one keeps its full triphosphate at the 5' end.

links: Ribose vs deoxyribose · RNA 5' triphosphate · Uracil vs thymine

box: A nucleic acid isolated from a cell is 120 nucleotides long, contains ribose, and folds into a compact three-dimensional shape in which several short stretches are base-paired with one another.
claim: Because parts of it are base-paired, the molecule must be double-stranded, like DNA.
explanation: Ribose identifies RNA, which is usually single-stranded; it folds into complex shapes when stretches of the same strand pair with each other. Base pairing alone doesn't make a molecule double-stranded.
links: RNA folding · DNA vs RNA

stem: A purified nucleic acid, 2,000 nucleotides long, has this base composition: 20% A, 30% U, 25% G, 25% C. What is the best conclusion?
options: It is double-stranded RNA, since its G and C percentages are equal
It is single-stranded DNA, since 2,000 nucleotides is too long for RNA
It is double-stranded DNA, since its G and C percentages are equal
It is double-stranded RNA, since in RNA adenine always pairs with uracil
It is single-stranded RNA: it contains uracil, and A does not equal U
explanation: Uracil means RNA. In a double strand every A would pair with a U, forcing %A = %U; 20% ≠ 30%, so it is single-stranded (G = C here is a coincidence).
links: RNA vs DNA · Base-pairing ratios

box: Like DNA, each RNA strand has a 5'-phosphate end and a 3'-hydroxyl end.
claim: RNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3'-OH end, so the 5' end of an RNA is the first part made.
explanation: All nucleic acids grow by addition at the 3' end, so the 5' end is where synthesis started — and in RNA it still carries its triphosphate.
links: RNA polarity · Growth at the 3' end

box: The notes define a gene as 'the DNA sequence that corresponds to a specific protein'. Muscle cells and liver cells both transcribe gene X, but their mature X mRNAs differ by one exon.
claim: The two cells make different but related proteins from gene X, so 'one gene, one specific protein' is an oversimplification.
explanation: The same primary transcript is spliced differently in the two cells (alternative splicing), so one gene's DNA sequence corresponds to more than one related protein.
links: Gene definition · Alternative splicing

box: A mutation changes one base in the protein-coding part of a gene.
claim: For this change to alter the protein's amino-acid sequence, it must first be copied into mRNA by transcription, because ribosomes read mRNA, not DNA.
explanation: In the central dogma, protein synthesis depends on the code carried by mRNA; a DNA change reaches the protein only through its RNA copy.
links: Central dogma · mRNA carries the code

box: AZT, one of the first HIV drugs, is a thymidine nucleoside whose sugar carries an azide group in place of the 3'-OH. Cells add phosphates to it, and HIV's reverse transcriptase then incorporates it into viral DNA.
claim: Once AZT is added to a growing viral DNA strand, no further nucleotide can be attached, so viral DNA synthesis stops at that point.
explanation: Nucleotides can only be added to a free 3'-OH. AZT has none, so it ends the chain — which is how it blocks HIV from copying its RNA into DNA.
links: 3'-OH requirement · Nucleoside vs nucleotide · Real-world: AZT

title: Templates and products
prompt: Match each process to its template and product.

pairs.right: DNA template → RNA
mRNA code → polypeptide
RNA template → DNA
DNA template → DNA

explanation: Transcription, reverse transcription, and replication all copy nucleic-acid information by complementary base pairing (by RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase, and DNA polymerase), always adding nucleotides at the 3' end; only translation, on ribosomes, changes the 'language'.
links: Central dogma · Reverse transcription · Replication

box: A student writes: 'A gene is a protein that determines a trait.'
claim: The student's definition is acceptable, because the protein made from a gene is what actually determines the trait.
explanation: The protein is the gene's product. A gene is the DNA sequence — the unit of heredity — that corresponds to that protein; making the protein is gene expression.
links: Gene vs gene product

stem: RNA polymerase builds a 100-nucleotide RNA from ribonucleoside triphosphates. How many phosphate groups does the finished RNA contain?
explanation: Each nucleotide after the first loses two phosphates (as pyrophosphate) when joined and keeps one in the backbone: 99. The first nucleotide keeps its whole triphosphate at the 5' end: 3. Total = 102.
links: RNA 5' triphosphate · Pyrophosphate release

box: Adenosine is adenine joined to ribose. ATP is adenosine carrying three phosphate groups.
claim: Adenosine and ATP are both nucleotides, since each contains a base and a sugar.
explanation: Base + sugar alone is a nucleoside (adenosine); adding phosphate makes a nucleotide, and ATP is one. Only nucleoside triphosphates like ATP can be joined into RNA by RNA polymerase.
links: Nucleoside vs nucleotide · ATP

stem: In the diagram, which nucleotide will RNA polymerase add next at the '?' slot?
options: CTP
dGTP
GTP
UTP
ATP
explanation: The template base opposite the slot is C, so the RNA needs G. RNA polymerase builds with ribonucleoside triphosphates, so the building block is GTP, not the DNA precursor dGTP.
links: Template reading · Ribonucleotide triphosphates

title: Reading a transcription bubble
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Top strand: 5'-CATGACCGTA-3'. Bottom strand: 3'-GTACTGGCAT-5'.

(나) The RNA made so far, 5'-CAUGACC, is paired with the bottom strand, and the polymerase moves to the right.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The polymerase reads the bottom (template) strand in the 5'→3' direction as it moves right.
statements.explanation: The template runs 3'→5' from left to right, so a polymerase moving right reads it 3'→5' while the RNA grows 5'→3'.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The RNA has the same sequence as the top (nontemplate) strand, with U in place of T.
statements.explanation: RNA is complementary to the template, so it matches the nontemplate strand except that U replaces T.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: When all 10 positions shown have been transcribed, the RNA will read 5'-CAUGACCGUA-3'.
statements.explanation: Copy the nontemplate strand and swap T for U: CATGACCGTA → CAUGACCGUA.

links: Template vs nontemplate · Read 3'→5', grow 5'→3'

box: The transcription bubble is about 14 base pairs long, but the RNA–DNA duplex inside it is only about 8 base pairs.
claim: So, as the polymerase advances, older RNA must peel away from the template and exit, while the two DNA strands re-pair behind the polymerase.
explanation: Only the newest ~8 nucleotides stay paired with the template. The polymerase has channels for the RNA to exit and for the DNA to enter and leave, and the unwound DNA rejoins after transcription.
links: Transcription bubble · Polymerase channels

title: Starting a eukaryotic gene
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A gene's promoter contains 5'-TATAAA-3', and transcription starts about 25 base pairs away from it.

(나) An activator protein bound to an enhancer several thousand base pairs upstream strongly increases transcription of the gene.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: General transcription factors bind the TATA box region of the promoter and help RNA polymerase II assemble there.
statements.explanation: At least six general transcription factors bind the promoter; together with Pol II they form the initiation complex.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The distant activator can affect transcription because the DNA loops, letting the activator contact the mediator, the general transcription factors, and Pol II at the promoter.
