statements.explanation: Looping brings enhancer-bound activators into contact with promoter-bound proteins through the mediator complex.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Deleting the TATA box would leave the start site unchanged, because Pol II recognizes the +1 nucleotide directly.
statements.explanation: The +1 site is set by the promoter complex about 25 bp from the TATA box; Pol II does not find it on its own.

links: TATA box · General transcription factors · Enhancers and DNA looping

box: Bacteria have a single type of RNA polymerase; a sigma factor associated with it recognizes promoter sequences.
claim: A bacterium could switch on a different set of genes by making a different sigma factor that recognizes a different promoter sequence.
explanation: Since promoter recognition is the sigma factor's job, swapping sigma factors redirects the same polymerase to other promoters — bacteria do exactly this, for example, when responding to heat stress.
links: Sigma factor · Promoter recognition · Regulated gene expression

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts transcription initiation in bacteria and in eukaryotes?
options: Bacteria: RNA polymerase II with general transcription factors. Eukaryotes: one polymerase guided by a sigma factor
Bacteria: one RNA polymerase guided by a sigma factor. Eukaryotes: ≥6 general transcription factors plus Pol II for mRNA
Both use sigma factors to find promoters, but eukaryotes also have three different RNA polymerases
Eukaryotic Pol II binds the TATA box with no other proteins, while bacteria need activators bound to enhancers
Bacteria have three RNA polymerases for different genes, while eukaryotes have one, guided by a sigma factor
explanation: In bacteria, a sigma factor lets the single RNA polymerase recognize promoters. In eukaryotes, general transcription factors bind the promoter, Pol II makes mRNA, and activators on enhancers act through the mediator.
links: Initiation: bacteria vs eukaryotes

box: Genes X and Y lie next to each other on the same chromosome.
claim: Because both genes are on the same DNA molecule, they must use the same strand as their template.
explanation: Which strand is transcribed can differ from one gene to the next, depending on each gene's promoter orientation — neighbouring genes can be transcribed in opposite directions.
links: Template-strand choice · Promoter orientation

title: Building RNA in a test tube
stem: Three test tubes each contain a DNA template with a promoter, RNA polymerase, and any factors it needs. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Tube 1 also contains ATP, GTP, CTP, and UTP.

(나) Tube 2 contains dATP, dGTP, dCTP, and dTTP instead. Tube 3 is like tube 1 but lacks UTP.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Tube 1 makes RNA; its nucleoside triphosphates supply both the building blocks and the energy for polymerization.
statements.explanation: Transcription needs a DNA template, RNA polymerase, and ribonucleoside triphosphates, which provide the monomers and the energy.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Tube 2 also makes RNA, because only base pairing matters to the polymerase.
statements.explanation: RNA polymerase builds RNA from ribonucleotides; deoxyribonucleotides are DNA building blocks.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In tube 3, RNA synthesis stalls at the first template position holding A.
statements.explanation: An A in the template must be paired with U; without UTP, the polymerase can't add the next nucleotide there.

links: Transcription requirements · NTPs vs dNTPs · Template pairing

box: The 3'-OH at the end of a growing RNA attacks the innermost phosphate of the incoming nucleotide, and the outer two phosphates leave as pyrophosphate.
claim: Because this chemistry needs a free 3'-OH on the growing chain, RNA — like DNA — can only be extended in the 5'→3' direction.
explanation: The incoming nucleotide brings the triphosphate (on its 5' carbon) and the chain supplies the 3'-OH, so every nucleic acid grows at its 3' end.
links: Polymerization chemistry · 5'→3' growth

stem: Cordycepin triphosphate looks like ATP, but its sugar lacks the 3'-OH (3'-deoxyadenosine triphosphate). Using the diagram, what happens if RNA polymerase uses it opposite a template T?
options: It cannot be added at all, because the incoming nucleotide's own 3'-OH performs the attack
It can be added, but then nothing more can be attached, so the RNA ends there
It is added, and elongation then continues normally from the cordycepin's end
It is released whole as pyrophosphate without ever joining the chain
It makes the RNA grow in the 3'→5' direction from that point on
explanation: Joining uses the chain's 3'-OH and the incoming nucleotide's innermost phosphate, so cordycepin can be added; but it provides no 3'-OH for the next attack, so it terminates the chain.
links: 3'-OH requirement · Chain termination · Real-world: cordycepin

box: Each phosphodiester bond in RNA forms as an incoming ribonucleotide releases its outer two phosphates as pyrophosphate.
claim: The energy for each new bond comes from a separate ATP molecule hydrolyzed by the polymerase, not from the incoming nucleotide.
explanation: The incoming nucleoside triphosphate supplies its own energy: the 3'-OH attacks its innermost phosphate, and splitting off pyrophosphate drives bond formation — which is why the building blocks must be triphosphates.
links: NTPs carry their own energy · Polymerization

title: One nucleotide, three checkpoints
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Read from top to bottom, the template strand shown is 3'-TGAA-5'.

(나) The incoming nucleotide in the diagram is UTP.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The incoming UTP would be joined even if the next template base were G, since the polymerase checks only that it is a ribonucleotide.
statements.explanation: An incoming NTP is kept only if it base-pairs correctly with the template base; opposite G, only C fits.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The RNA shown so far reads 5'-ACU-3', and adding the incoming U will make it 5'-ACUU-3'.
statements.explanation: Template T, G, and A pair with RNA A, C, and U; the incoming UTP pairs with the next template A.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Releasing pyrophosphate makes this a hydrolysis reaction, since a molecule splits off.
statements.explanation: Hydrolysis uses water to split a bond. Here the chain's 3'-OH — not water — attacks the innermost phosphate and a new phosphodiester bond forms, a condensation-type joining. (Module 2 draws this joining as releasing water; in cells the leaving group is pyrophosphate.)

links: Base-pair checking · Phosphodiester bond formation · Condensation vs hydrolysis

box: Transcription of a gene begins at its promoter and continues until RNA polymerase reaches a terminator sequence.
claim: A mutation that deletes a gene's terminator would be expected to produce abnormally long RNA transcripts that continue into the DNA beyond the gene.
explanation: Termination is the third stage, after initiation and elongation, and it happens when the polymerase reaches the terminator; without one, elongation runs on past the gene's normal end.
links: Initiation · Elongation · Termination

stem: A mutation narrows the channel through which ribonucleoside triphosphates enter RNA polymerase. Which stage of transcription is most directly slowed?
options: Initiation, because the promoter can no longer be recognized by the polymerase
Termination, because the terminator sequence can no longer be read
Splicing, because introns can no longer be removed from the RNA
Elongation, because each added nucleotide must enter through that channel
Capping, because the 5' cap can no longer be added to the RNA
explanation: During elongation, RNA polymerase unwinds the DNA and adds nucleotides that enter through a dedicated channel; other channels let DNA in and out and let the RNA exit. Promoter recognition and RNA processing don't depend on NTP entry.
links: Elongation · RNA polymerase channels

box: RNA polymerase moves along the template strand as the RNA grows 5'→3'.
claim: The polymerase therefore travels toward the 3' end of the template strand.
explanation: The template is read 3'→5', so the polymerase travels toward the template's 5' end. Because the strands are antiparallel, that keeps the new RNA growing 5'→3'.
links: Template read 3'→5' · RNA grows 5'→3'

title: Knock it out, see what breaks
prompt: Match each transcription element to the result of damaging or moving it.

pairs.right: Nothing can bind to start the gene, so it is not transcribed at all
Transcription can still occur but no longer starts at a fixed site about 25 bp downstream
Moved thousands of bp away, it still boosts transcription as long as the DNA can loop
Activator signals no longer reach the general transcription factors and Pol II
A bacterium's RNA polymerase can no longer recognize its promoters
Transcripts run on past the end of the gene

explanation: A promoter decides whether a gene can be transcribed at all; the TATA box fixes where transcription starts; enhancers and the mediator adjust how much; sigma factors are bacteria's promoter-recognition tool; terminators set where it stops.
links: Promoter · TATA box · Enhancer · Mediator · Sigma factor · Terminator

title: Two poisons, two polymerases
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Rifampin, a tuberculosis drug, blocks bacterial RNA polymerase.

(나) α-Amanitin, the toxin of the death-cap mushroom, blocks eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Rifampin stops bacteria from making new mRNA, so production of new bacterial proteins soon stops too.
statements.explanation: Bacteria use a single type of RNA polymerase for all transcription; block it and no new mRNA is available for translation.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: α-Amanitin halts mRNA production in a victim's liver cells, while RNAs made by the other two RNA polymerases are less directly affected.
statements.explanation: Eukaryotes have three distinct RNA polymerases, and Pol II is the one that makes mRNA.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Rifampin can be given to patients because the single bacterial RNA polymerase differs from the RNA polymerases in human nuclei.
statements.explanation: Selective toxicity comes from structural differences between bacterial and eukaryotic polymerases.

links: Bacterial vs eukaryotic RNA polymerases · Real-world: rifampin and death-cap poisoning

stem: Genes A and B lie on the same chromosome, but gene A is transcribed rightward and gene B leftward. Which statement is correct?
options: They use opposite DNA strands as templates, and each RNA still grows 5'→3'
They use the same template strand, but gene B's RNA grows 3'→5'
Gene B must lie on a different chromosome, since one chromosome is read in only one direction
RNA polymerase reads gene A's template 3'→5' and gene B's template 5'→3'
Both RNAs have the same sequence, since they come from the same DNA molecule
explanation: Which strand is the template can differ from gene to gene, set by each promoter's orientation. Because the strands are antiparallel, reading each template 3'→5' sends the polymerases in opposite directions — but every RNA grows 5'→3'.
links: Template-strand choice · Antiparallel strands · 5'→3' growth

stem: RNA polymerase has made a 30-nucleotide RNA and is still transcribing the gene. About how many of those 30 nucleotides have already separated from the DNA template?
options: About 8
About 16
None
All 30
About 22
explanation: Inside the transcription bubble (about 14 bp), the RNA–DNA hybrid is only about 8 bp, so just the newest ~8 nucleotides stay paired; the other ~22 have peeled off and left through the exit channel. (16 comes from wrongly subtracting the whole bubble.)
links: Transcription bubble · RNA–DNA hybrid

stem: A drug lets RNA polymerase bind promoters and begin transcribing normally, but the polymerase stalls partway through each gene, long before it reaches the terminator. Which stage of transcription does the drug block?
options: Initiation
Termination
Elongation
Splicing
Polyadenylation
explanation: Initiation (binding at the promoter and starting) works; the failure happens while nucleotides are being added along the gene, which is elongation. Termination would be the problem only if the polymerase reached the terminator but failed to stop there.
links: Initiation · Elongation · Termination

title: Two cells, two timelines
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In E. coli, ribosomes attach to an mRNA and start translating while RNA polymerase is still transcribing it.

(나) In a human cell, the primary transcript is processed in the nucleus before it is exported.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (나), the primary transcript itself is the mRNA that ribosomes translate.
statements.explanation: That is true of prokaryotes. A eukaryotic primary transcript must first be processed (cap, splicing, poly(A) tail) into export-ready mRNA.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The overlap in (가) is possible only because no nuclear envelope separates the DNA from the ribosomes.
statements.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus, so transcription and translation share the cytoplasm and can be coupled.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A single E. coli mRNA can carry the information for several genes.
statements.explanation: Prokaryotic primary transcripts can be polycistronic, coding for more than one protein.

links: Coupled transcription–translation · Primary transcript · Polycistronic mRNA

box: A company copies a human gene directly from genomic DNA — introns included — places it behind a bacterial promoter, and puts it into E. coli to produce a human protein.
claim: E. coli would likely make a faulty protein, because bacteria don't splice out introns, so its mRNA would still contain the intron sequences.
explanation: In prokaryotes the primary transcript is the mRNA — there is no splicing step — so intron sequences would be translated as if they were coding sequence.
links: Introns and splicing · Prokaryotic mRNA · Real-world: recombinant proteins

stem: To make a human protein in E. coli, biotechnologists want a DNA version of the gene with no introns. Which approach produces it?
options: Use reverse transcriptase to copy the mature, spliced mRNA into DNA
Use RNA polymerase to copy the primary transcript back into DNA
Add a 5' cap to the genomic gene so bacteria will process it
Add a poly(A) tail to the gene so that the bacteria will splice it out
Use a sigma factor to cut the introns out of the genomic DNA
explanation: Mature mRNA has already had its introns spliced out; reverse transcriptase (an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) turns that RNA into intron-free DNA (cDNA). Placed behind a bacterial promoter, it can be expressed correctly in E. coli.
links: Reverse transcriptase · Spliced mRNA · Real-world: cDNA cloning

title: Caps and tails
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A 5' cap (7-methylguanosine) is added to the 5' end of the primary transcript.

(나) About 250 adenines are added to the 3' end (polyadenylation).

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The poly(A) tail helps export the mRNA to the cytoplasm and protects its 3' end from exonucleases.
statements.explanation: Per the notes, the poly(A) tail aids export to the cytoplasm and protects the 3' end from exonucleases; it also plays a role in transcription termination.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because it is added to the 5' end, the cap protects the mRNA from exonucleases that attack its 3' end.
statements.explanation: The cap guards the 5' end (its unique 5'-to-5' linkage leaves no ordinary free 5' end); the 3' end is protected by the poly(A) tail.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: An mRNA lacking its cap would still be translated normally; it would just break down sooner.
statements.explanation: Without the cap, the ribosome would not recognize the mRNA, so translation could not occur.

links: 5' cap · Poly(A) tail · mRNA stability and translation

stem: Using the diagram's gene (exons E1–E4), suppose instead — unlike mRNA 2 in the diagram — that E1 and E4 are always kept, while E2 and E3 can each be included or skipped independently (exon order never changes). How many different mRNAs can be made?
explanation: Two independent include/skip choices give 2 × 2 = 4 mRNAs: E1-E4, E1-E2-E4, E1-E3-E4, and E1-E2-E3-E4 — four different, related proteins from one gene.
links: Alternative splicing · Exon combinations

box: In the diagram, mRNA 1 (E1-E2-E4) and mRNA 2 (E1-E2-E3) come from the same primary transcript.
claim: Proteins A and B would share the amino-acid sequence encoded by E1 and E2 but differ in the part encoded by E3 versus E4.
explanation: Shared exons give shared protein segments, and the swapped exon changes one region — which is why alternative splicing yields different but related proteins.
links: Alternative splicing · Related proteins

box: In some forms of β-thalassemia, a single base change at an intron–exon boundary of the β-globin gene stops that intron from being removed correctly.
claim: Because the mutation lies partly in an intron, which is cut out of the mRNA anyway, it cannot affect the β-globin protein.
explanation: Boundary sequences guide splicing. If an intron is kept or the wrong piece is cut, the mRNA's coding sequence changes, and the protein is abnormal or missing.
links: RNA splicing · Real-world: β-thalassemia

stem: Which best explains why eukaryotic primary transcripts must be processed while prokaryotic transcripts generally are not?
options: Prokaryotes have no RNA polymerase, so their ribosomes read the DNA directly and no transcript needs processing
Eukaryotic ribosomes can read only DNA, so each RNA must be converted back into DNA before it is exported
Prokaryotic transcripts are double-stranded, which already protects them from the enzymes that degrade RNA
Eukaryotes transcribe their genes in the cytoplasm, where unprocessed RNA would be translated too early
A nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation, so the transcript must be modified before export
explanation: The nuclear membrane adds a step between transcription and translation: the message must be processed so it can move from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and be recognized there. Prokaryotic primary transcripts are already mRNA.
links: Why RNA processing exists

title: What goes wrong without it?
prompt: Match each feature of gene expression to the consequence of losing it.

pairs.right: Ribosomes fail to recognize the mRNA, and its 5' end is exposed to exonucleases
Export to the cytoplasm suffers, and the 3' end is exposed to exonucleases
Intron sequences stay in the mRNA and are read as if they were coding sequence
Each gene can make only one version of its protein
Processed mRNA cannot leave the nucleus to reach the ribosomes

explanation: Each processing step solves a problem created by the nucleus — protecting the message, getting it out, and removing non-coding introns — while alternative splicing adds variety.
links: RNA processing · mRNA export

box: A polycistronic mRNA carries the information for several genes on one molecule.
claim: Polycistronic mRNAs are typical of human cells, where alternative splicing produces them.
explanation: Polycistronic mRNAs are a prokaryotic feature. Alternative splicing is different: it makes several mRNAs from one gene, not one mRNA from several genes.
links: Polycistronic mRNA vs alternative splicing

title: Designing a vaccine mRNA
stem: mRNA vaccines deliver a lab-made mRNA encoding a viral protein into the cytoplasm of human cells, where it is translated. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Manufacturers give the synthetic mRNA a 5' cap and a poly(A) tail.

(나) The synthetic mRNA contains no introns.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The cap is needed so the cell's ribosomes recognize the mRNA and translate it.
statements.explanation: Without a cap, ribosomes would not recognize the mRNA; the cap also protects it from exonucleases.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Leaving out introns makes sense because the mRNA goes straight to the cytoplasm, while splicing happens in the nucleus.
statements.explanation: Processing, including intron removal, happens in the nucleus before export, so an mRNA delivered to the cytoplasm must already be mature.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The vaccine mRNA must be converted into DNA and enter the nucleus before any protein can be made.
statements.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA directly in the cytoplasm; nothing needs to be copied into DNA.

links: 5' cap · Splicing happens in the nucleus · Real-world: mRNA vaccines

box: Lysosomes keep their interior near pH 5, while the surrounding cytosol stays near pH 7.
claim: Since pH 5 is only two units below pH 7, the lysosome holds only about twice the H+ concentration of the cytosol, so maintaining it takes little energy.
explanation: pH is a log scale: two units is a 10² = 100-fold difference in [H+]. Keeping H+ 100× more concentrated inside requires the lysosome's proton pump to move H+ against its gradient — active transport powered by ATP.
links: pH log scale (Mod 2) · Lysosome proton pump · Active transport

title: Why DNA hugs histones
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Histone proteins are rich in amino acids whose R groups contain amino groups, which are positively charged at cellular pH (Module 2).

(나) DNA wraps around histones to form nucleosomes, the 10 nm fiber (Module 4).

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The binding works through hydrogen bonds to specific bases, so histones wrap only particular DNA sequences.
statements.explanation: The attraction is to the backbone phosphates, which are the same along every sequence, so histones package DNA largely regardless of sequence.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Neutralizing DNA's phosphate charges would make it bind histones even more tightly.
statements.explanation: Removing the negative charges would remove the electrostatic attraction, loosening the DNA–histone interaction.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Attraction between the histones' positive charges and DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone helps the DNA wrap tightly.
statements.explanation: Opposite charges attract: the ionized phosphates on the outside of the helix meet the positive amino groups of the histones.

links: Amino-group charge (Mod 2) · Negative backbone · Nucleosomes

title: Macromolecules in one membrane
stem: Using the diagram and Module 2, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Phospholipids and cholesterol, channel and peripheral proteins, and sugar chains all appear in the diagram.

(나) Module 2 grouped biological macromolecules into carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Three of the four macromolecule classes are structural parts of the plasma membrane; nucleic acids are not.
statements.explanation: Membranes are made of lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Cholesterol, a steroid with four fused rings, is completely nonpolar, so it sits entirely inside the hydrophobic core.
statements.explanation: Cholesterol has a polar OH group that sits near the phospholipid heads; only its rings and tail are buried among the tails.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The sugar chains are built from monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds and are covalently attached to lipids or proteins on the extracellular side.
statements.explanation: Glycolipids and glycoproteins carry covalently attached carbohydrates, and all of them face the extracellular fluid.

links: Membrane components · Glycosidic bonds (Mod 2) · Cholesterol structure

box: When phospholipids are shaken in water, they spontaneously form closed bilayer vesicles. If the water is replaced by a nonpolar solvent such as hexane, the vesicles fall apart.
claim: This shows that the bilayer is held together mainly by water's tendency to exclude the nonpolar tails, not by bonds joining the phospholipids to one another.
explanation: In water, the hydrophobic effect pushes the tails together and the heads outward; take the water away and nothing holds the arrangement, because no covalent bonds join neighbouring phospholipids. The same effect makes the bilayer self-healing.
links: Hydrophobic effect (Mod 2) · Self-assembly · Self-healing

stem: During its cycle, the Na+/K+ pump is phosphorylated by ATP. Which description of the energy source fits the Module 1–2 picture of ATP?
options: The bond between adenine and ribose is broken, releasing the base to power the pump
ATP is added whole to the pump, which then uses all three phosphates at once
Its outermost phosphate bond breaks, that phosphate goes to the pump, and ADP is released
ATP transfers two of its phosphates to the pump, leaving AMP behind
No bond is broken; ATP simply binds the pump and acts as a signal
explanation: ATP stores energy in the bonds between its phosphates. Hydrolysis of the terminal bond (ATP → ADP + Pi) releases energy; here the Pi is transferred to the pump, and phosphorylation switches the pump's conformation.
links: ATP structure (Mod 1–2) · Na+/K+ pump phosphorylation

title: Cell properties, molecular machinery
stem: Module 1 listed basic properties shared by cells. Which statements in <보기> correctly link a property to Module 3–4 machinery?
box:
(가) Cells respond to stimuli.

(나) Cells acquire and use energy, and they follow a genetic program.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Acquiring and using energy relies on mitochondria, which count as part of the endomembrane system because they are enclosed by membranes.
statements.explanation: Mitochondria do convert energy from sugars into ATP, but they are not part of the endomembrane system; membership depends on bridge or vesicle connections, not on having membranes.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Responding to a protein hormone relies on receptor proteins in the plasma membrane, because the hormone cannot cross the bilayer.
statements.explanation: Receptors let the cell receive signals from macromolecules that stay outside.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Following a genetic program relies on the central dogma, in which information flows from DNA to RNA to protein.
statements.explanation: Genes (DNA) are transcribed into RNA, and mRNA is translated into the proteins that carry out the program.

links: Basic cell properties (Mod 1) · Receptors · Mitochondria · Central dogma

box: HIV consists of an RNA genome and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, packed inside a protein coat and an outer envelope.
claim: Because HIV carries its own genetic material and its own enzyme, it can reproduce on its own outside a host cell.
explanation: Viruses are exceptions to the cell theory: outside a host they are inert. HIV must use the host cell's machinery — nucleotides, RNA polymerase, ribosomes — to make new viruses.
links: Viruses as exceptions (Mod 1) · Reverse transcription

stem: Both hypotheses in the diagram begin with an archaeon as the host cell. How does that fit Module 1's three-domain tree of life?
options: It conflicts: the tree places Eukarya within Bacteria
It conflicts: archaea have no membranes that could fold inward
It fits only if mitochondria came from archaea rather than from proteobacteria
It fits: the tree has Eukarya branching from within Archaea
It is irrelevant: the tree includes only prokaryotes
explanation: Module 1's tree has Eukarya branching from within Archaea, matching an archaeal host; the mitochondria themselves were added from proteobacteria, which are Bacteria.
links: Three-domain tree (Mod 1) · Origin of eukaryotes

box: Ribosomal subunits are assembled in the nucleolus (Module 1), a region of the nucleus without its own membrane, from rRNA and proteins.
claim: Because ribosomal subunits are large RNA–protein complexes, they must leave the nucleus through nuclear pores by active transport rather than by passive diffusion.
explanation: Small molecules and ions diffuse through nuclear pores, but large proteins and RNA — and complexes of the two — require active transport.
links: Nucleolus (Mod 1) · Nuclear pores · Ribosomes

title: Why study E. coli?
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Module 1 lists E. coli as a model organism for studying DNA replication, transcription, and translation.

(나) In E. coli, transcription and translation are coupled.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because E. coli has no nucleus, it has no RNA polymerase and uses its ribosomes to copy DNA into RNA.
statements.explanation: E. coli has a single type of RNA polymerase that transcribes all its genes; ribosomes translate.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In E. coli, a researcher could see ribosomes translating an mRNA that is still attached to its DNA through RNA polymerase — something never seen inside a human nucleus.
statements.explanation: Coupling is possible only without a nuclear envelope; in human cells translation happens in the cytoplasm after export.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: E. coli is a poor model for human transcription, since transcription works completely differently in prokaryotes.
statements.explanation: Despite the difference in location, transcription is a similar process in prokaryotes and eukaryotes — which is why E. coli is a useful model.

links: Model organisms (Mod 1) · Coupled transcription–translation

box: Soft-stemmed plants wilt when they run short of water, even though their cellulose cell walls remain intact (Module 1).
claim: Their upright posture depends on turgor pressure from water-filled vacuoles pushing against the walls, so losing water weakens support even with intact walls.
explanation: A wall resists expansion but can't hold a soft plant up by itself; water entering by osmosis keeps the cells turgid, and wilting is the loss of that pressure.
links: Plant wall and vacuole (Mod 1) · Turgor

stem: Food chemists hydrogenate vegetable oils, converting C=C double bonds in the fatty acid tails to single bonds (Module 2). If a cell's membrane phospholipids were changed the same way, what would happen?
options: The tails would kink even more, making the membrane more fluid
The heads would lose their charge, so the bilayer would fall apart in water
Nothing would change, since fluidity depends only on cholesterol content
The membrane would become much more permeable to ions such as Na+
The tails would straighten and pack tightly, making the membrane less fluid
explanation: Removing double bonds makes saturated, straight tails that pack tightly and restrict lateral movement — the same reason saturated fats are solid at room temperature.
links: Saturated vs unsaturated (Mod 2) · Membrane fluidity · Real-world: hydrogenated oils

title: Building a pore from amino acids
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In a channel protein, the amino acids lining the pore have polar or charged R groups, while those on the outer surface facing the lipid tails have nonpolar R groups.

(나) A mutation replaces one charged, pore-lining amino acid with a nonpolar one.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The nonpolar outer surface lets the protein sit stably within the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer.
statements.explanation: Nonpolar R groups interact favourably with the lipid tails, anchoring the integral protein.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The polar lining creates an aqueous pore through which ions can pass without contacting the lipid tails.
statements.explanation: Channels are integral proteins surrounding an aqueous pore — the hydrophilic path that ions need.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because the changed amino acid lines the pore, the mutant protein can no longer insert into the membrane.
statements.explanation: Insertion depends on the nonpolar outer surface, which is unchanged. The swap alters the pore's lining, which could change which ions pass — one R-group change can alter function.

links: R groups (Mod 2) · Channel proteins · Structure determines function

box: Lysosomal enzymes break proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and complex carbohydrates down into smaller building blocks.
claim: These digestive reactions are condensation reactions, because each bond broken releases a water molecule.
explanation: Breaking polymers apart is hydrolysis: each bond split consumes a water molecule. Condensation is the reverse — it joins monomers and releases water (Module 2).
links: Hydrolysis vs condensation (Mod 2) · Lysosomal digestion

stem: The Golgi adds carbohydrate chains to proteins. How are the sugar units within such a chain linked to one another?
options: By peptide bonds formed through hydrolysis reactions
By glycosidic bonds formed through condensation reactions
By phosphodiester bonds formed through condensation reactions
By hydrogen bonds only, so the chain can easily rearrange
By ionic bonds between charged sugar groups
explanation: Monosaccharides join through glycosidic bonds in condensation reactions (Module 2); the Golgi's enzymes build and attach these chains during glycosylation.
links: Glycosidic bonds (Mod 2) · Golgi glycosylation

title: One ring or two?
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A copying error places an A opposite a G at one site in a DNA double helix.

(나) An RNA molecule folds back on itself, so that two stretches of the same strand pair with each other.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: At the A–G site in (가), the helix would bulge outward, because both bases have two rings.
statements.explanation: A and G are both purines; every normal rung is two rings plus one ring (purine + pyrimidine), which keeps the width constant.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The paired stretches in (나) would contain A–T pairs, since adenine always pairs with thymine.
statements.explanation: RNA has uracil instead of thymine, so its adenines pair with U — and U, like T, is a one-ring pyrimidine.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The folded RNA in (나) would be less chemically stable than a DNA molecule of the same length, because of the 2'-OH on each ribose.
statements.explanation: The 2'-hydroxyl makes RNA more reactive, so RNA is less stable than DNA.

links: Purines vs pyrimidines (Mod 2) · Uracil · Ribose 2'-OH

box: DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, and reverse transcriptase all build nucleic acids by adding nucleotides to the 3' end.
claim: So all three enzymes form phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH of the growing strand and the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide (Module 2).
explanation: Whatever the template (DNA or RNA) and product, chain growth uses the same chemistry: a 3'-OH attacks the incoming nucleotide's 5' phosphate, so every strand grows 5'→3'.
links: Phosphodiester bond (Mod 2) · 5'→3' synthesis

stem: Module 2 listed protein functions such as enzymes, transport, signaling, and support. Which description fits the Na+/K+-ATPase?
options: It is only a transporter; enzymes cannot be embedded in membranes
It is only an enzyme; it merely speeds up ion diffusion
It is a structural anchor linking the membrane to the cytoskeleton
Both a transporter and an enzyme: it moves ions and hydrolyzes ATP
It is a receptor that signals when Na+ levels change
explanation: 'ATPase' names its enzyme activity (hydrolyzing ATP), and it pumps Na+ and K+. Enzymes are one of the four membrane-protein functions, so a single protein can play two roles.
links: Protein functions (Mod 2) · Membrane protein functions · Na+/K+-ATPase

box: Mitochondria resemble proteobacteria, yet Module 1's tree places Eukarya closer to Archaea than to Bacteria.
claim: These facts contradict each other: if mitochondria came from bacteria, eukaryotes must have branched from Bacteria.
explanation: Eukaryotic cells are partnerships: the host lineage (nucleus and cytoplasm) is archaeal, while the mitochondria descend from a bacterium that was engulfed or taken in as a partner. Both facts fit the diagram.
links: Three-domain tree (Mod 1) · Endosymbiosis

box: Most cytosolic proteins fold properly and work near pH 7 (Module 2: pH affects protein structure).
claim: If a lysosome leaked, pH-5 fluid could damage nearby cytosolic proteins by changing the charges on ionizable amino and carboxyl groups, disrupting their folding.
explanation: Extra H+ changes which groups carry charge, disturbing the ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold a protein's shape — one reason lysosomal contents must stay separated from the cytosol.
links: pH and protein structure (Mod 2) · Lysosome compartmentalization

title: Polarity decides the route
prompt: Using Module 2's ideas about polarity, size, and charge, match each molecule to how it can cross a plasma membrane.

pairs.right: Small and nonpolar: dissolves straight through the lipid core
A lipid: crosses by simple diffusion to reach receptors inside the cell
Charged: blocked by the hydrophobic core; needs a channel or pump
Small and uncharged but polar: crosses the bilayer, and faster through aquaporin channels
Too large to cross; acts through a surface receptor instead

explanation: The hydrophobic interior lets small or nonpolar molecules through and stops charged and large ones — polarity, charge, and size (Module 2) predict each route.
links: Selective permeability · Polarity (Mod 2)

box: Many viruses, including influenza, bind specific receptor molecules on a host cell's surface and are brought inside in coated vesicles.
claim: Such a virus is taken up far more efficiently by cells that display its receptor than by cells that could take it in only by pinocytosis.
explanation: Receptor-mediated endocytosis concentrates specific cargo in coated pits, while pinocytosis just samples fluid. Which cells carry the receptor largely determines which cells a virus can infect.
links: Receptor-mediated endocytosis · Viruses (Mod 1)

stem: In E. coli (Module 1), three genes involved in using the sugar lactose sit side by side and are transcribed from one promoter into a single mRNA. What does this imply?
options: The single mRNA is spliced three different ways to make the three proteins
Only the first gene's protein is made, since one mRNA can code for only one protein
The three proteins are switched on together, translated from one polycistronic mRNA
The mRNA must be exported through nuclear pores before any protein is made
Each gene still needs its own separate mRNA before its protein can be made
explanation: Prokaryotic mRNAs can be polycistronic, carrying several genes; a shared promoter lets the cell turn on a whole pathway at once. E. coli has no nucleus and doesn't splice.
links: Polycistronic mRNA · E. coli (Mod 1) · Real-world: the lac genes

title: Energy conversions at membranes
stem: Module 3 lists energy transduction among membrane functions. Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Chloroplast thylakoid membranes hold chlorophyll.

(나) The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because both organelles have membranes that do this work, both belong to the endomembrane system.
statements.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are membranous but not part of the endomembrane system; membership depends on bridge or vesicle connections.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Thylakoid membranes convert light energy into chemical energy, an example of energy transduction.
statements.explanation: Pigments in the thylakoid membrane collect the light energy that the chloroplast uses to make sugars.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The inner mitochondrial membrane converts energy from food molecules into ATP — energy transduction serving the Module 1 property 'acquires and uses energy'.
statements.explanation: The ETC and ATP synthase in the inner membrane harness energy from sugars to make ATP.

links: Energy transduction · Thylakoid · Inner membrane · EMS membership

box: Red blood cells keep their flexible disc shape because membrane proteins tie the plasma membrane to a network of cytoskeleton proteins just beneath it. In hereditary spherocytosis, some of these linking proteins are defective.
claim: Patients' red blood cells would be expected to lose their disc shape and become rounder and more fragile, because the membrane is less firmly anchored to the cytoskeleton.
explanation: Anchoring — linking the membrane to other proteins such as the cytoskeleton, Module 1's protein scaffold — is one of the four membrane-protein functions. Without it, the membrane rounds up into spheres that break easily.
links: Membrane protein functions · Cytoskeleton (Mod 1)

title: Real-world phenomena, cellular explanations
prompt: Match each real-world phenomenon to the Module 1–4 mechanism behind it.

pairs.left: Salting meat keeps bacteria from growing
pairs.right: A hypertonic environment pulls water out of microbial cells by osmosis

pairs.left: Soap and water destroy enveloped viruses
pairs.right: Amphipathic molecules break a lipid membrane apart into micelles
Partial Na+/K+ pump block weakens the Na+ gradient that powers Ca2+ removal

pairs.left: Oral rehydration solution contains both salt and sugar
pairs.right: Na+/glucose symport draws solute into intestinal cells, and water follows

pairs.left: Death-cap mushroom poisoning destroys liver cells
pairs.right: A toxin blocks the eukaryotic polymerase that makes mRNA

pairs.left: Rifampin treats tuberculosis without killing human cells
pairs.right: It blocks the single bacterial RNA polymerase, which differs from human polymerases

explanation: Each case turns on one mechanism from this course: osmosis, amphipathic self-assembly, primary vs secondary active transport, co-transport, and the different RNA polymerases of bacteria and eukaryotes.
links: Osmosis · Amphipathic lipids · Active transport · RNA polymerases

title: One bond type, many jobs
prompt: Match each Module 3–4 structure or process to the Module 2 bond or interaction it depends on.

pairs.left: Holding the two DNA strands together
pairs.right: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases

pairs.left: Linking nucleotides within an RNA strand
pairs.right: Phosphodiester bonds, formed as pyrophosphate is released

pairs.left: Keeping phospholipid tails together in the bilayer
pairs.right: Hydrophobic interactions: water excludes the nonpolar tails

pairs.left: Attaching sugar chains to membrane proteins
pairs.right: Covalent bonds added by Golgi enzymes (glycosylation)

pairs.left: Holding peripheral proteins to the membrane surface
pairs.right: Noncovalent bonds that can break without disrupting the bilayer

explanation: Strong covalent bonds build each polymer, while weak noncovalent forces hold assemblies together — which is why DNA can unzip, bilayers self-heal, and peripheral proteins come off easily.
links: Covalent vs noncovalent (Mod 2) · DNA · Membranes

title: Membranes aren't membership
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Module 1 classified mitochondria, chloroplasts, peroxisomes, ribosomes, the nucleolus, and the cytoskeleton as non-endomembrane structures.

(나) Mitochondria and chloroplasts are semi-autonomous: they grow and divide on their own and contain their own circular genomes.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are excluded from the endomembrane system because they are not linked to it by membrane bridges or vesicle traffic, not because they lack membranes.
statements.explanation: Both have double membranes; what they lack is a physical or vesicle connection to the ER–Golgi network.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Ribosomes and the nucleolus are non-endomembrane for a simpler reason: neither is enclosed by a membrane.
statements.explanation: Ribosomes are RNA–protein machines, and the nucleolus is a region of the nucleus with no membrane of its own.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because both organelles carry their own DNA, they need no proteins or support from the rest of the cell.
statements.explanation: 'Semi'-autonomous means partly independent: they have their own genomes and divide on their own but still depend on the host cell.

links: EMS vs non-EMS (Mod 1) · Semi-autonomous organelles

title: How many genomes in one cell?
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A genome is the genetic material of an organism — for example, a bacterial genome, a nuclear genome, or a mitochondrial genome.

(나) Gene expression is regulated: genes can be turned on or off.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: A human liver cell contains at least two genomes: the nuclear genome and the mitochondrial genome.
statements.explanation: The nucleus holds the nuclear genome, and each mitochondrion carries its own small, circular genome.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Every gene in the nuclear genome is expressed in every cell at all times.
statements.explanation: Gene expression is regulated; different cell types turn on different subsets of genes.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The mitochondrial genome is circular like a typical bacterial chromosome — evidence consistent with endosymbiosis.
statements.explanation: Circular genomes are one of the bacterial features mitochondria retain.

links: Genome types · Endosymbiosis · Regulated gene expression

stem: A drug that blocks transport through nuclear pores is added to cultures of two of Module 1's model organisms, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli. Using the diagram, what is the expected outcome?
options: S. cerevisiae: new mRNA is held in the nucleus and can't be translated; E. coli: unaffected (no nucleus)
Both organisms stop making proteins, since both must export their mRNA to ribosomes
E. coli stops making proteins; S. cerevisiae continues because its ribosomes are inside the nucleus
Neither is affected, because mRNA can diffuse straight through lipid membranes
S. cerevisiae continues, because its transcription and translation are coupled, as in bacteria
explanation: Eukaryotic mRNA is made and processed in the nucleus and must be actively exported through nuclear pores before cytoplasmic ribosomes can translate it. Prokaryotes transcribe and translate in the same compartment.
links: Model organisms (Mod 1) · Nuclear pores · Where transcription happens

box: The nucleolus, where rRNA is made and ribosomes are assembled (Module 1), lies inside the nucleus, the innermost organelle of the endomembrane system (Module 3).
claim: The nucleolus is therefore part of the endomembrane system.
explanation: The nucleolus is a region of the nucleus with no membrane, and Module 1 lists it as non-endomembrane. What belongs to the system is the nuclear envelope, the double membrane continuous with the ER.
links: Nucleolus vs nuclear envelope · EMS membership

box: Electron micrographs of an unknown cell show a plasma membrane, a cell wall, and many ribosomes, but no internal membranes of any kind.
claim: This cell cannot have a nucleus, ER, Golgi apparatus, or lysosomes, which fits a prokaryote such as a bacterium.
explanation: In eukaryotic cells, internal membranes define the organelles; with none, there is no nuclear envelope and no endomembrane compartment. Ribosomes have no membrane, so they can still be present — matching Module 1's prokaryote, which lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
links: Internal membranes define organelles · Prokaryotes (Mod 1)

box: Influenza virus particles can remain infectious for hours on a doorknob.
claim: While on the doorknob, the virus particles slowly carry out metabolism and make new virus particles.
explanation: Viruses are exceptions to the cell theory: outside a host cell they are inert, with no metabolism. They make new particles only after entering a host cell and using its machinery.
links: Viruses as exceptions (Mod 1)

box: ATP (Modules 1–2) consists of adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups.
claim: ATP has the same parts, attached at the same carbons, as the nucleotides RNA polymerase joins into RNA: the base on ribose's 1' carbon and the phosphates on its 3' carbon.
explanation: The phosphates attach at the 5' carbon; the 3' carbon carries the –OH that the next nucleotide bonds to. Otherwise the match is exact: ATP is itself one of RNA polymerase's four building blocks.
links: Nucleotide structure · ATP is a nucleotide (Mod 1–2)

title: Reading eight side chains
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) All eight amino acids are drawn as they exist at physiological pH (about 7.4).

(나) Panels A–G share the same backbone; only the side chain below the α carbon differs.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The side chains in panels C and D carry opposite full charges, so they can form an ionic bond if folding brings them together.
statements.explanation: C's –COO- is negative (acidic) and D's –NH3+ is positive (basic); opposite charges attract.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The side chain in panel B can hydrogen-bond with water through its –OH, even though it carries no full charge.
statements.explanation: Oxygen is electronegative, so the –OH is polar: B is a polar, uncharged, hydrophilic side chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In a folded water-soluble protein, the side chain in panel G would most likely be found buried in the interior.
statements.explanation: A CH2 plus a benzene ring is all carbon and hydrogen — nonpolar and hydrophobic — so it clusters away from water inside the fold.

links: R-group classes · Ionic bonds between side chains · Polarity from electronegativity (Module 2)

title: Which side chain fits?
prompt: Using the diagram, match each description to the side chain that fits it.

pairs.left: Gives the backbone the most freedom to rotate and bend
pairs.right: Panel F: –H

pairs.left: Restricts rotation of the backbone, limiting folding around it
pairs.right: Panel H: ring bonded back to the nitrogen

pairs.left: Can form a covalent cross-bridge with another copy of itself
pairs.right: Panel E: –CH2–SH
Panel D: –(CH2)4–NH3+

pairs.left: Polar but uncharged; hydrogen-bonds with water
pairs.right: Panel B: –CH2–OH

explanation: Panel F is glycine (side chain H): tiny, so the C–N bond rotates freely. H is proline: its side chain loops back to the amino nitrogen and locks rotation. E is cysteine: two –SH groups can join as an S–S disulfide bridge. D is lysine (basic, +). B is serine: its –OH is polar but uncharged.
links: Special amino acids: glycine, proline, cysteine · Charged vs polar side chains

box: A protein designer wants to make a floppy loop on a protein's surface more rigid. One of the loop's amino acids is the one in panel F of the diagram.
claim: Replacing it with the amino acid in panel H would stiffen the loop more than the amino acid in panel D would, even though D's side chain is much longer.
explanation: Rigidity doesn't come from size. D's long chain (lysine) points away from the backbone and has freely rotating bonds of its own, while H's side chain (proline) is bonded to the backbone nitrogen itself, which locks rotation about the C–N bond.
links: Proline restricts rotation · Side chain properties, not size · Real-world: protein design

stem: A protein engineer replaces a glycine in a tight hairpin turn with alanine (side chain –CH3). The protein no longer folds correctly. Which explanation fits best?
options: Alanine's –CH3 hydrogen-bonds to the backbone, pinning the turn open
Alanine's side chain bonds back to its own backbone nitrogen, closing a ring
Alanine's –CH3 limits backbone rotation, so the chain can't bend as sharply
Alanine lacks the H that glycine's side chain uses to hydrogen-bond across the turn
Alanine's –CH3 is nonpolar, so the turn is pulled into the protein's interior
explanation: Glycine's side chain is just H, so the backbone can rotate freely about the C–N bond — the flexibility a tight turn needs. Even a small –CH3 restricts that rotation. Neither glycine's H nor alanine's –CH3 can hydrogen-bond (both are bonded to carbon), alanine has no ring (that's proline), and one small nonpolar group doesn't drag a whole turn into the core.
links: Glycine flexibility · Sequence determines folding

box: Collagen, the main protein of bone and tendon, is a tight triple helix. Every third amino acid is glycine, and each glycine sits at the crowded centre where the three chains meet.
claim: A mutation replacing one of these glycines with a bulkier amino acid can weaken collagen, because only glycine's single H atom fits in that central position.
explanation: Glycine has the smallest side chain (H). A larger side chain can't pack into the helix centre and distorts the triple helix — the cause of many cases of osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease).
links: Glycine: the smallest side chain · Real-world: brittle bone disease

box: A perm breaks the disulfide bonds in hair keratin with a reducing agent, holds the hair around curlers, then re-forms disulfide bonds with an oxidizing agent.
claim: The curl lasts because the disulfide bonds re-form between exactly the same pairs of cysteines as before.
explanation: While the hair is held in its new shape, cysteines that weren't partners before sit side by side, and the oxidizer links them into new S–S bridges. Covalent bridges in new positions hold the new shape; re-forming the old pairs would simply restore the original shape.
links: Disulfide cross-bridges · Real-world: perms

stem: The peptide Val–Gly–Ala–His–Lys is assembled from free amino acids by condensation reactions. How many water molecules are released, and which amino acid carries the free amino group?
options: 5 water molecules; Val
4 water molecules; Lys
5 water molecules; Lys
3 water molecules; Val
4 water molecules; Val
explanation: Five amino acids are joined by 4 peptide bonds, and each dehydration releases one H2O. Sequences are written from the amino (N) end to the carboxyl (C) end, so Val, written first, keeps the free amino group, and Lys keeps the free carboxyl group.
links: Peptide bonds form by dehydration · N- and C-terminus · Writing sequences N→C

box: One lab reports a tripeptide as K-G-V. Another lab reports a tripeptide as V-G-K.
claim: These are the same molecule: both contain lysine, glycine and valine, just written from opposite ends.
explanation: Sequences are written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. K-G-V has lysine at the free amino end; V-G-K has valine there and lysine at the carboxyl end. A backbone has direction (amino end ≠ carboxyl end), so these are different peptides.
links: Primary structure is written N→C · Polypeptides have direction

stem: Using the diagram, a side chain on a protein's surface that forms an ionic bond with a nearby –COO- changes from the one in panel D to the one in panel C. What is the main change at that spot?
options: It becomes nonpolar and tends to move into the folded protein's interior
The attraction becomes a repulsion, since both groups are now negative
It gains the ability to form a disulfide bridge with another copy
Nothing changes, since both side chains are charged and hydrophilic
The ionic bond gets stronger, since C's group carries the larger charge
explanation: D (–(CH2)4–NH3+, lysine) is basic and positive, so it attracts the nearby –COO-; C (–CH2–COO-, aspartate) is acidic and negative, so the two groups now repel and the ionic bond is lost. Both side chains are charged and hydrophilic, so the spot stays at the surface; neither has an –SH, and each carries a single charge.
links: Acidic vs basic side chains · Ionic bonds need opposite charges

box: A protein drug clumps together in its storage vial. Its designers find two valines (side chain –CH(CH3)2) exposed on its surface and replace them with lysines (side chain –(CH2)4–NH3+).
claim: The swap should make the clumping worse, because the new charged side chains will stick to nonpolar patches on neighbouring drug molecules.
explanation: The reverse: exposed nonpolar side chains are what make the molecules stick, since water pushes nonpolar groups together. Charged lysines interact with water (and repel each other), so the swap makes the surface more hydrophilic and the drug clumps less.
links: Hydrophobic vs charged side chains · Real-world: protein drug formulation

box: Proteins are built from 20 kinds of amino acids, like words built from an alphabet.
claim: A chain only 3 amino acids long already has 8,000 possible sequences.
explanation: Each of the 3 positions can hold any of 20 amino acids: 20 × 20 × 20 = 8,000. For a 300-amino-acid protein the number is 20^300 — one reason proteins can be so diverse and versatile.
links: 20 amino acids as an alphabet · Protein diversity

title: One backbone, twenty personalities
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Every amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and an H bonded to its α carbon; only the fourth group, the R group, differs.

(나) At physiological pH, a free amino acid carries H3N+ and COO-.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because of (나), every amino acid in a folded protein carries both an H3N+ and a COO- on its backbone.
statements.explanation: Inside a chain, the amino and carboxyl groups are used up in peptide bonds. Only the first amino acid keeps a free amino group (N-terminus) and only the last keeps a free carboxyl group (C-terminus).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Two different proteins of the same length share the same repeating backbone (N–C–C–N–C–C…); they differ only in the side chains attached to it.
statements.explanation: Peptide bonds always join the same backbone atoms, so sequence differences show up only in the R groups sticking out from the chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Proline is the only amino acid whose α carbon carries two identical groups.
statements.explanation: That's glycine, whose R group is a second H — so its α carbon isn't asymmetric. Proline's α carbon carries four different groups; its side chain loops back to the nitrogen.

links: Amino acid structure · Charged ends at physiological pH · N- and C-terminus

stem: Using the diagram, which pair of side chains, brought together by folding, could join two parts of a protein with a covalent bond?
options: E and E (two –CH2–SH groups)
C and D (–COO- and –NH3+)
B and B (two –CH2–OH groups)
A and G (–CH3 and the ring)
F and F (two –H atoms)
explanation: Two cysteine –SH groups can be joined into an S–S disulfide bond — a covalent cross-bridge, far stronger than the ionic bond C and D can form, the hydrogen bonds between B's –OH groups, or the weak van der Waals contacts between nonpolar A and G.
links: Disulfide bonds are covalent · Bond strengths (Module 2)

box: Proteins are built from only 20 kinds of amino acids, yet they do thousands of different jobs. Two proteins turn out to contain exactly the same number of each kind of amino acid.
claim: So they will fold into the same shape and do the same job.
explanation: What matters is the order of the amino acids, not just which ones are present: the sequence of side chains decides how the chain folds, and the shape decides the job. The same amino acids in a different order make a different protein, just as the same letters can spell different words.
links: Proteins are diverse and versatile · Sequence → shape → function

title: Two backbone patterns
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In each structure, one dashed line is labelled with the two groups it joins.

(나) Each R marks a side chain sticking out from the backbone.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Every dashed bond links a backbone C=O to a backbone N–H; none involves an R group.
statements.explanation: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone groups of nearby amino acids; side chains aren't part of these bonds.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The sheet's two strands are parallel, since they lie side by side.
statements.explanation: Side by side doesn't mean the same direction: the top strand runs N→C left to right and the bottom strand right to left, so they're antiparallel. Sheets can be either.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the helix continued past residue 11, the N–H of residue 12 would bond to the C=O of residue 8.
statements.explanation: Each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues along (1–5, 2–6, 3–7…), so residue 12's N–H pairs with residue 8's C=O, tying each turn of the helix to the next.

links: Secondary structure: backbone H-bonds only · α helix · β sheet

box: An isolated 11-residue segment folds into the helix in the diagram, with residue 1 at its N-terminus.
claim: Residues 8–11 have their N–H groups hydrogen-bonded within the segment, but their C=O groups have no partner.
explanation: Each C=O of residue n pairs with the N–H of residue n + 4. Residues 8–11 would need partners 12–15, which don't exist, while their own N–H groups receive bonds from residues 4–7. At the other end, residues 1–4 have unpaired N–H groups.
links: α helix: residue n bonds to n + 4

stem: Proline's side chain bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, so in a chain that nitrogen carries no H. If residue 7 of the helix in the diagram were proline, which of the helix's hydrogen bonds would be lost?
options: The one between residue 7's C=O and residue 11's N–H
The one between residue 6's C=O and residue 10's N–H
The one between residue 4's C=O and residue 8's N–H
The one between residue 3's C=O and residue 7's N–H
None, since helix H-bonds involve only backbone atoms
explanation: Residue 7's N–H is the partner of residue 3's C=O (n to n + 4). Proline has no N–H to give, so that bond is lost, while its C=O can still bond to residue 11's N–H. Here a side chain matters after all: proline's ring changes a backbone atom itself, one reason proline disrupts helices.
links: α helix pattern · Proline restricts the backbone

title: What holds the fold together?
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) One sample is treated with a reducing agent that turns each –S–S– back into two –SH groups.

(나) A second sample is moved from pH 7 into strong acid (pH 1).

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (나), contact B gets stronger, because the extra H+ adds positive charge to both of its groups.
statements.explanation: COO- picks up H+ and becomes uncharged COOH, so the attraction between opposite charges at B is lost, not strengthened.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In (나), contact D is lost, because its nonpolar groups pick up H+ and become charged.
statements.explanation: Nonpolar groups such as –CH3 can't gain or lose H+, so acid doesn't act on D directly; pH acts on ionizable groups like those at B.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) breaks contact A but leaves the protein's primary structure unchanged.
statements.explanation: A disulfide bridge links two side chains; it isn't part of the backbone, so the amino acid sequence (held by peptide bonds) is untouched.

links: Tertiary interactions · Disulfide vs ionic bonds · pH and ionization (Module 2)

title: Four ways to unfold a protein
prompt: Using the diagram, match each treatment to the contact it most directly disrupts.

pairs.left: A reducing agent that adds H to each sulfur
pairs.right: A: CH2–S–S–CH2

pairs.left: Concentrated salt, whose ions crowd around charged groups
pairs.right: B: COO- facing H3N+

pairs.left: Urea, which hydrogen-bonds to polar groups in place of their partners
pairs.right: C: OH facing O=C

pairs.left: A detergent whose nonpolar tails coat nonpolar groups
pairs.right: D: the clustered nonpolar groups

explanation: Each treatment targets one interaction type: reducing agents split covalent disulfides (A); ions shield the charges of an ionic bond (B); urea competes for hydrogen bonds (C); detergents surround nonpolar groups so they no longer need to hide from water (D).
links: Tertiary interactions · Bond types (Module 2) · Denaturation

box: In the diagram, contact D sits in the middle of the fold, surrounded by the chain, while water lies outside.
claim: D holds together mainly because nonpolar groups attract one another strongly, much as the opposite charges at B do.
explanation: Nonpolar groups attract one another only weakly (van der Waals forces). They cluster mainly because water molecules hydrogen-bond with each other and push nonpolar groups aside (Module 2), so the groups end up hidden in the interior.
links: Hydrophobic interior · Water drives nonpolar clustering (Module 2)

stem: An enzyme is a homodimer: two identical chains held together by side-chain contacts. A mutation changes one amino acid on the surface where the two chains touch. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Nothing changes, since surface amino acids don't affect quaternary structure
The two chains now differ in sequence, so the enzyme becomes a heterodimer
Each chain can still fold, but the pair no longer assembles into the enzyme
The peptide bonds that join the two chains to each other are broken
The chains form a disulfide bridge at that spot, locking them together
explanation: Subunits are held together by the same side-chain interactions as tertiary structure, so a changed contact residue can block pairing. Both chains come from the same mutated gene, so they're still identical (still a homodimer), and subunits aren't joined by peptide bonds.
links: Quaternary structure · Homodimer vs heterodimer

box: Insulin's A and B chains are cut from one longer precursor polypeptide after it has folded. In the folded precursor, two cysteines in the A segment are disulfide-bonded to two cysteines in the B segment.
claim: Once the connecting segment is cut out, only weak noncovalent interactions hold the A and B chains together.
explanation: Cutting out the connecting segment breaks peptide bonds, not disulfides. The two disulfide bonds, each joining a cysteine on chain A to a cysteine on chain B, are covalent and still hold the chains together.
links: Disulfide bridges between chains · Post-translational cleavage

stem: An enzyme is unfolded with chemicals that break its hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds, leaving its peptide bonds intact. When the chemicals are slowly removed, the chain refolds into its active shape. What does this show?
options: The amino acid sequence alone holds the information for the folded shape
The peptide bonds alone hold the folded shape, since they were never broken
The chain refolded at random and happened to find the active shape
Refolding needed a correctly folded copy of the enzyme as a template
Secondary and tertiary structure don't depend on the sequence
explanation: Only the sequence (primary structure) survived, yet the same active shape came back, so the sequence holds the information for secondary and tertiary structure. The peptide bonds just link the chain; the shape itself is held by the interactions that re-formed: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions and disulfides.
links: Primary structure determines higher levels · Denaturation and refolding

box: A peptide alternates nonpolar valine with charged lysine or glutamate: Val–Lys–Val–Glu–Val–Lys–Val–Glu.
claim: If the peptide is stretched out as a strand, replacing the valine at position 3 with lysine would put a charged side chain on the strand's nonpolar face.
explanation: R groups alternate sides along an extended chain, so positions 1, 3, 5 and 7 (all Val) share one face and positions 2, 4, 6 and 8 (Lys, Glu) the other. A lysine at position 3 would sit among the valines, on the nonpolar face that would otherwise pack against the protein's interior.
links: R groups alternate sides · Nonpolar and charged faces

box: In the diagram's sheet, a third strand is added below the bottom strand, running from N at the left to C at the right.
claim: The new strand is antiparallel to the bottom strand and parallel to the top strand.
explanation: The bottom strand runs N→C right to left and the top strand left to right. A strand running left to right is opposite to the bottom strand (antiparallel) and matches the top one (parallel). Both arrangements occur in sheets.
links: β sheets: parallel and antiparallel strands

stem: In the diagram's sheet, R groups alternate between above the sheet (filled) and below it (hollow). The sheet lies against the protein's nonpolar interior on one face, with water on the other. Which pattern along each strand fits best?
options: Nonpolar side chains at every position along the strand
Charged side chains at every position along the strand
Nonpolar side chains on one strand, polar side chains on the other
Glycine at every position so that the sheet can bend
Nonpolar and polar side chains alternating along the strand
explanation: Consecutive residues point to opposite faces, so alternating nonpolar and polar residues put every nonpolar side chain on the interior face and every polar one on the water face. An all-nonpolar strand would leave half its side chains facing water.
links: R groups alternate sides · Faces of a β sheet

title: Which level of structure?
prompt: Match each observation to the level of protein structure it describes.

pairs.left: A mutation swaps the 6th amino acid of the chain for a different one
pairs.right: Primary

pairs.left: In a stretch of keratin, each C=O bonds to the N–H four amino acids along
pairs.right: Secondary

pairs.left: A disulfide bond links cysteine 30 to cysteine 115 of the same chain
pairs.right: Tertiary

pairs.left: An enzyme works only after its α chain and β chain pair up
pairs.right: Quaternary

explanation: Primary = the sequence; secondary = local backbone H-bond patterns (here, the α helix's n to n + 4 bonds); tertiary = the whole folded shape of one chain, held by bonds between side chains far apart in the sequence; quaternary = how separate chains (subunits) assemble.
links: Four levels of protein structure

title: From gene to anticodon
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The four rows show one codon's worth of a gene, its mRNA and the tRNA that reads it.

(나) Unlabelled sequences are written 5'→3'.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: A tRNA with this anticodon would also pair with the codon 5'-ACG-3'.
statements.explanation: Pairing must be antiparallel. Matching 5'-UGC-3' base by base in the same direction gives ACG, but antiparallel pairing matches 3'-CGU-5' to 5'-GCA-3', not to ACG.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Written in the standard 5'→3' direction, the anticodon is UGC.
statements.explanation: The anticodon is 3'-CGU-5'; read from its 5' end it is 5'-UGC-3'.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: For a different gene whose template strand reads 3'-TAC-5', the tRNA that reads its codon has the anticodon 3'-UAC-5'.
statements.explanation: Template 3'-TAC-5' → mRNA codon 5'-AUG-3' → anticodon 3'-UAC-5': the anticodon repeats the template strand, with U for T, because both are complementary to the codon.

links: Codon–anticodon pairing is antiparallel · Template strand (Module 4)

box: In the diagram, the middle base of the DNA template strand (G) is mutated to A. (GCA = Ala, GUA = Val, GAA = Glu)
claim: The mRNA codon becomes GUA, so the protein carries valine in place of alanine.
explanation: The template's middle base pairs with the codon's middle base. Template G → A means the mRNA gets U instead of C: GCA becomes GUA, which codes for Val. One base change in the gene, one amino acid change in the protein.
links: Template strand → codon → amino acid

stem: Using the genetic code table, which single-base change in the mRNA codon CUU would NOT change the amino acid?
options: CUU → CCU
CUU → CUC
CUU → AUU
CUU → CAU
CUU → UUU
explanation: CUU and CUC both code for Leu. The others give Pro (CCU), Ile (AUU), His (CAU) and Phe (UUU). Third-position changes are the ones most often silent, because the code is redundant: many amino acids have codons that differ only in their third base.
links: Redundancy of the genetic code · Silent changes

box: Using the genetic code table, count the codons for each amino acid.
claim: Every amino acid is encoded by at least two codons, which is what makes the code redundant.
explanation: Methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) each have only one codon. The code is still redundant because most amino acids have two to six codons: 61 coding codons for 20 amino acids.
links: Redundancy of the genetic code · AUG start codon

stem: Using the genetic code table, a ribosome starts at the first AUG of the mRNA 5'-CCAUGGUUCAUUGAGC-3'. What polypeptide is made?
options: Met–Val–His–Trp (4 amino acids)
Pro–Trp–Phe–Ile–Glu (5 amino acids)
Met–Val (2 amino acids)
Met–Val–His (3 amino acids)
Met–Val–His–Stop (4 amino acids)
explanation: Starting at AUG sets the reading frame: AUG (Met) GUU (Val) CAU (His) UGA (stop). A stop codon has no amino acid (and UGA is not UGG, Trp), so the chain is 3 long. Reading from the first base would give a different frame (CCA UGG UUC…) and a different protein.
links: Start codon sets the reading frame · Stop codons

stem: In a gene of 300 codons, one nucleotide is inserted just after codon 5, and one nucleotide is deleted from codon 9. Assuming no stop codon appears along the way, what protein is made?
options: Every codon after the insertion is misread, so the rest is garbled
Nothing changes, because the insertion and deletion cancel out
Only codons 6 and 9 change; the codons between them are normal
Codons 6–9 are misread, but the frame is restored from codon 10 on
The chain ends at codon 5, since an extra base acts as a stop signal
explanation: Codons are read three at a time from a fixed start. The insertion shifts the frame, so codons 6–9 are read wrongly; the deletion shifts it back, so codon 10 onward is read normally. Crick and Brenner used exactly this kind of experiment in 1961 to show that the code is read as nonoverlapping triplets.
links: Reading frame · Nonoverlapping triplets · Real-world: Crick and Brenner's experiment

title: Freeze-frame on a ribosome
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) UGG codes for Trp and AAA for Lys; UAG is a stop codon.

(나) The ribosome will keep translating this mRNA until the polypeptide is finished.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The incoming tRNA marked ? must carry the anticodon 3'-ACC-5' and the amino acid Trp.
statements.explanation: The A site holds codon 5'-UGG-3'; its antiparallel partner is 3'-ACC-5', and the tRNA with that anticodon is charged with Trp.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The finished polypeptide will be Met–Ala–Trp–Lys, with Met at its N-terminus.
statements.explanation: AUG GCU UGG AAA, then UAG (stop): Met–Ala–Trp–Lys. Met, the first amino acid, keeps the free amino group.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The tRNA in the E site is uncharged and is about to leave the ribosome.
statements.explanation: It delivered Met, passed it on when the first peptide bond formed, and now exits empty from the E site.

links: A, P and E sites · Codon–anticodon pairing · Start and stop codons

stem: In the diagram, which way is the ribosome moving along the mRNA, and how can you tell?
options: Toward 5': the empty A site marks where the ribosome has just been
Toward 5': Met at the chain's free end was the last amino acid added
Toward 3': the large subunit always sits on the mRNA's 3' side
It stays put while the mRNA slides back and forth through it
Toward 3': AUG, the first codon read, is now under the E site
explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA 5'→3'. The start codon AUG, read first, is now under the E site, and the unread codons lie on the 3' side. Met at the chain's free end was the first amino acid added, not the last, which also shows the ribosome began at the 5' end.
links: Ribosomes move 5'→3' · A, P and E sites · The N-terminus is made first

box: In a classic experiment, the cysteine already attached to a charged tRNA-Cys was chemically converted to alanine, leaving the tRNA's anticodon unchanged. The tRNA was then added to a protein-making system.
claim: Alanine was inserted at cysteine codons, because the ribosome checks only codon–anticodon pairing, not which amino acid the tRNA carries.
explanation: tRNAs are adapters: the anticodon reads the codon, and the amino acid simply rides along. That's why the accuracy of aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which load each tRNA with the right amino acid, matters so much.
links: tRNAs as adapters · Accuracy depends on tRNA synthetases

box: A cell runs short of free leucine, so many tRNAs whose anticodons read leucine codons stay uncharged.
claim: Ribosomes can skip the leucine codons and keep going in frame, making shorter proteins that lack leucine.
explanation: An uncharged tRNA has no amino acid to deliver. A ribosome that reaches a leucine codon waits, with that codon in its A site, until a charged tRNA arrives; it doesn't skip codons.
links: Charged vs uncharged tRNA · The A site

title: Which component is responsible?
prompt: Match each observation to the translation component that best explains it.

pairs.left: A mutant tyrosine tRNA inserts tyrosine at UAG stop codons, so some chains run on past them
pairs.right: The tRNA's anticodon

pairs.left: A tRNA is loaded with the wrong amino acid but still pairs with the correct codon
pairs.right: An aminoacyl tRNA synthetase

pairs.left: An antibiotic binds rRNA in the large subunit and blocks peptide bond formation
pairs.right: The peptidyl transferase center

pairs.left: In an extract missing one protein, finished chains stay attached to tRNAs at stop codons
pairs.right: The release factor

pairs.left: In a human cell extract missing one group of proteins, small subunits never bind capped mRNAs
pairs.right: Eukaryotic initiation factors

explanation: Each component has one job: the anticodon decides which codon a tRNA reads (here, a mutant anticodon pairs with UAG); synthetases load the right amino acid; the rRNA peptidyl transferase center joins amino acids; release factors free the finished chain at a stop codon; eukaryotic initiation factors bring the small subunit to the 5' cap.
links: Components of translation

stem: The standard genetic code has 64 codons. How many of them are read by tRNAs carrying an amino acid?
explanation: Three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons: no tRNA reads them, and a release factor binds instead. That leaves 61 codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons.
links: Stop codons · A redundant code

box: Suppose codons overlapped, so that bases 1-2-3, then 2-3-4, then 3-4-5 were each read as a codon.
claim: A single base substitution would then change up to three neighbouring codons at once, whereas in the real code it changes only the one codon that contains it.
explanation: In an overlapping code each base belongs to three codons. Real codons are a nonoverlapping series of triplets, so each base sits in exactly one codon, and a substitution changes only that codon.
links: Nonoverlapping triplets

stem: A mutation in a cell's rRNA genes changes the amino acid sequence of no protein, yet it slows protein synthesis throughout the cell. Which explanation fits best?
options: rRNA carries amino acids to the ribosome, so fewer arrive at each codon
rRNA is the template for every mRNA, so all mRNAs are made more slowly
rRNA builds the ribosome itself, so every ribosome works more slowly
rRNA forms the 5' cap of each mRNA, so fewer mRNAs are recognized
rRNA pairs with each codon in place of tRNA, so codons are read slowly
explanation: Only mRNA is translated. rRNA is transcribed from DNA but works as RNA: with ribosomal proteins it builds both ribosomal subunits, and it forms the peptidyl transferase center.
