statements.explanation: Eukarya is thought to have descended from within the Archaea, so archaea share a more recent common ancestor with eukaryotes than with bacteria.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because it lives in the gut and not in an extreme environment, M. smithii belongs with the bacteria.
statements.explanation: Archaea often live in extreme environments, but not always; M. smithii's isoprenoid membrane marks it as an archaeon wherever it lives.

links: Archaea are not always extremophiles · Prokaryote features · Eukarya from within Archaea · Real-world: gut methanogens

title: Treating a fungus on human skin
stem: Athlete's foot is a skin infection caused by a fungus. Some antifungal creams work by stopping the fungus from making chitin. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Bacteria living on the same skin are not harmed by the cream.

(나) Suppose another antifungal drug worked by blocking the fungus's ribosomes.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: A drug that blocks chitin synthesis harms the fungus but not the patient, because animal cells have no cell wall.
statements.explanation: Fungal walls contain chitin, a modified polysaccharide; animal cells have no wall, so the drug has no target in them.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The bacteria in (가) escape harm because, like the patient's skin cells, they have no cell wall.
statements.explanation: Bacteria do have cell walls, but theirs contain no chitin (they are built mainly of peptidoglycan), so the cream has nothing to block in them.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The drug in (나) would be more likely than the chitin cream to harm the patient's own cells.
statements.explanation: Fungi and humans are both eukaryotes with similar ribosomes, so a drug against the fungus's ribosomes could also hit the patient's; human cells make no chitin at all.

links: Fungi have chitin walls · Bacteria have walls, but not chitin ones · Animal cells have no wall · Fungi and humans have similar ribosomes · Real-world: antifungal creams

title: Why salt water lights the bulb
stem: In a classroom demonstration, a bulb lights when two wires are dipped into salt water, but not when they're dipped into sugar water, although both solids dissolved completely. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The bulb lights only when the solution contains charged particles that are free to move.

(나) A few spoonfuls of cooking oil are then shaken into each solution.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Sugar dissolves because water breaks its covalent bonds, splitting each molecule into ions.
statements.explanation: Sugar's atoms are held by covalent bonds that stay intact; it dissolves as whole polar molecules hydrogen-bonded to water, so no ions form.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Salt water lights the bulb because dissolving breaks NaCl into Na+ and Cl- ions, each surrounded by water and free to move.
statements.explanation: Water's partial charges pull the ions apart and surround them in hydration shells, leaving charged particles that carry current.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In both solutions the oil will separate into its own layer, because its long nonpolar chains can't form hydrogen bonds with water.
statements.explanation: Nonpolar molecules are excluded by water (the hydrophobic effect), whether or not the water contains salt or sugar.

links: Ionic vs covalent bonds · Hydration shells · Hydrophobic effect · Real-world: a conductivity demonstration

title: Where starch digestion stalls
stem: Salivary amylase starts breaking down the starch in bread while you chew, but it stops working once stomach acid mixes into the swallowed food. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Amylase is a protein made in the salivary glands.

(나) Suppose a medicine held the stomach near pH 6 for a while.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The stomach's H+ concentration is about 5 times higher than the mouth's.
statements.explanation: Each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+, so going from pH 7 to pH 2 means about 10^5 = 100,000 times more H+.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Acid stops amylase by hydrolyzing the peptide bonds that link its amino acids, breaking the enzyme into small fragments.
statements.explanation: A pH change alters the charges on ionizable groups and disrupts the weak bonds holding the protein's shape; it doesn't break the covalent peptide bonds. (Pepsin may later digest the unfolded enzyme, but the acid itself stops it by unfolding it.)

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: With the stomach held near pH 6 as in (나), swallowed salivary amylase would keep digesting starch there for longer.
statements.explanation: The curve shows amylase is still highly active near pH 6, so swallowed amylase would keep working until the pH fell.

links: pH is a log scale · pH changes alter protein shape, not peptide bonds · Enzyme activity depends on pH · Real-world: starch digestion

title: Why ancient DNA outlasts RNA
stem: Scientists have read DNA from Neanderthal bones more than 40,000 years old, but RNA from samples that old is almost never recovered. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Sugar 1 and sugar 2 are the sugars of DNA and RNA, in some order.

(나) DNA and RNA also differ in one base: thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Strands built from sugar 2 break down more easily than strands built from sugar 1, because of sugar 2's -OH on carbon 2'.
statements.explanation: Sugar 2 is RNA's ribose: its 2'-OH makes RNA's backbone reactive, so RNA is far less stable than DNA, whose deoxyribose (sugar 1) lacks it.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: DNA's sugar is sugar 2, the one with an -OH group on carbon 2'.
statements.explanation: 'Deoxy' means one oxygen fewer: DNA's deoxyribose has only H at 2' (sugar 1), while RNA's ribose carries the 2'-OH (sugar 2).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: An RNA strand built with thymine instead of uracil would last as long as DNA, since thymine is what makes DNA the more stable of the two.
statements.explanation: The base swap leaves the backbone unchanged; RNA's instability comes from the 2'-OH on its sugar, which would still be there.

links: Ribose vs deoxyribose · The 2'-OH makes RNA less stable · Thymine vs uracil · Real-world: ancient DNA

title: A milk sugar some babies can't handle
stem: Babies with galactosemia can't properly process galactose, so it builds up to harmful levels when they drink milk. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Lactose, the main sugar in milk, is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose.

(나) Babies with galactosemia are fed formula made without lactose.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Sweetening the formula in (나) with sucrose is safe for these babies, since digesting sucrose releases no galactose.
statements.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose, so hydrolyzing it releases no galactose.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: When lactose formed, the -OH on carbon 1 of galactose and the -OH on carbon 4 of glucose reacted, releasing one water molecule.
statements.explanation: A glycosidic bond forms by condensation between two -OH groups, here at galactose C1 and glucose C4, releasing H2O; digesting lactose adds that water back (hydrolysis).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Since glucose and galactose differ only in the position of one -OH group, enzymes that act on glucose also act on galactose.
statements.explanation: Glucose and galactose are isomers (both C6H12O6), and isomers are functionally different: enzymes are specific to each shape.

links: Isomers are functionally different · Glycosidic bonds form by condensation and break by hydrolysis · Sucrose = glucose + fructose · Real-world: galactosemia

title: A fat your body can't digest
stem: Olestra, a fat substitute once used in potato chips, tastes like fat but adds no calories, because digestive enzymes can't break it down. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In an ordinary fat, digestive enzymes split the fatty acids off the glycerol.

(나) Olestra has a sucrose core carrying six to eight fatty acids.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In both molecules, each fatty acid is attached where the core molecule had a hydroxyl (-OH) group.
statements.explanation: Glycerol and sucrose both carry -OH groups, and each fatty acid's carboxyl group is joined to one of them.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Olestra dissolves readily in water, because its core is sucrose, a sugar that forms hydrogen bonds with water.
statements.explanation: Six to eight long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains surround the small sugar core, so the molecule as a whole is hydrophobic.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Some of the fat-soluble vitamins eaten with olestra dissolve into it and leave the body with it instead of being absorbed.
statements.explanation: Hydrophobic molecules dissolve in other hydrophobic material, so vitamins such as A and E move into the undigested olestra.

links: Triacylglycerol structure · Lipids are grouped by hydrophobicity · Like dissolves like · Real-world: olestra

title: A missing lysosomal enzyme
stem: In Tay-Sachs disease, nerve cells make no working copy of one lysosomal enzyme, so a lipid it normally digests builds up and destroys the cells. For several related diseases, patients receive the missing enzyme by infusion into the blood (enzyme replacement therapy). Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Lipids that a cell no longer needs are broken down inside lysosomes.

(나) An infused enzyme reaches the cells from the blood.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Without the enzyme, the lipid piles up free in the cytosol, outside any organelle.
statements.explanation: The lipid is delivered to lysosomes for digestion; without the enzyme it stays there, so the lysosomes swell.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In a healthy cell, the enzyme is made on the rough ER and passes through the Golgi on its way to the lysosomes.
statements.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes are made in the rough ER, sorted in the Golgi and packaged into lysosomes.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: An infused enzyme helps only if cells take it in by endocytosis, because a protein that large can't cross the lipid bilayer.
statements.explanation: Macromolecules such as proteins can't pass through the lipid bilayer; endocytosis brings them in inside vesicles.

links: Lysosomal enzymes: rough ER → Golgi → lysosome · Endocytosis brings large molecules in · Real-world: Tay-Sachs disease and enzyme replacement therapy

title: Cleaning blood through a membrane
stem: During hemodialysis, a patient's blood flows along one side of a thin membrane while a prepared fluid, the dialysate, flows along the other side, and waste such as urea leaves the blood. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The membrane's pores let water, ions, urea and glucose through, but not blood cells or proteins such as albumin.

(나) Fresh dialysate contains no urea but has normal blood levels of glucose.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Urea crosses the membrane by active transport, which is why it keeps leaving the blood for the whole session.
statements.explanation: Urea diffuses down its concentration gradient into the urea-free dialysate (passive transport); fresh dialysate keeps flowing in, so the gradient, and the net flow, last the whole session.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Albumin stays in the blood because it is hydrophobic and can't pass through the membrane.
statements.explanation: Albumin stays because it is too large for the pores; this membrane sorts molecules by size, letting polar urea, glucose and ions through.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the dialysate contained no glucose, the patient's blood glucose would fall during the session.
statements.explanation: Glucose would then diffuse down its gradient from the blood into the dialysate; matching blood levels prevents a net loss.

links: Diffusion down a concentration gradient · Selectivity by size · Net flux · Real-world: hemodialysis

title: How insulin lets glucose in
stem: After a meal, insulin signals muscle cells to take up glucose from the blood; in type 2 diabetes this response is weakened. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Glucose enters muscle cells through GLUT4, a carrier protein that moves it by facilitated diffusion.

(나) Without insulin, most GLUT4 sits in the membranes of small vesicles inside the cell.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: GLUT4 uses ATP to move glucose into the muscle cell against its concentration gradient.
statements.explanation: In facilitated diffusion a carrier changes shape to move glucose down its gradient, from the blood into the cell, with no ATP.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Insulin raises uptake by making the GLUT4 vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, which adds carriers to the cell surface.
statements.explanation: When a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane (exocytosis), its membrane, with the proteins embedded in it, becomes part of the cell surface.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: GLUT4 can move glucose into the cell even when glucose is more concentrated inside the cell than in the blood.
statements.explanation: Facilitated diffusion only moves solute down its gradient; with the gradient reversed, glucose would leave the cell through GLUT4.

links: Facilitated diffusion by carriers · Exocytosis adds membrane proteins · Real-world: insulin and type 2 diabetes

title: Heartburn pills that switch off a pump
stem: Omeprazole, a common heartburn medicine, blocks the H+/K+ pump of the stomach's parietal cells, which moves H+ out of these cells into the stomach in exchange for K+. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Antacid tablets work by neutralizing acid that is already in the stomach.

(나) Each cycle of the H+/K+ pump hydrolyzes one ATP.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Unlike an antacid, omeprazole does nothing to the acid already in the stomach; it stops new acid from being added.
statements.explanation: Blocking the pump halts further H+ secretion; acid already secreted stays until it's emptied or neutralized.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The pump is an example of primary active transport, because ATP hydrolysis directly powers each cycle.
statements.explanation: Primary active transporters use ATP's chemical energy directly; secondary transporters are driven by an existing ion gradient instead.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Pumping H+ from the cytoplasm at pH 7 into the stomach at pH 1 means working against about a million-fold difference in H+ concentration.
statements.explanation: Six pH units is a 10^6-fold difference in H+, a steep gradient that only an ATP-driven pump can overcome.

links: Primary active transport · Antiport · pH is a log scale (Module 2) · Real-world: proton pump inhibitors

title: A bacterium that hides inside its hunter
stem: Macrophages engulf Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes TB, but the bacteria often survive and even multiply inside them, because they stop their phagosome from fusing with a lysosome. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and keep their interior near pH 5.

(나) In the diagram, step 4 shows the normal route after phagocytosis.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The bacterium gets inside the macrophage without ever passing through the lipid bilayer of its plasma membrane.
statements.explanation: In phagocytosis the membrane wraps around the particle and pinches off, so the bacterium ends up enclosed in a phagosome.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A drug that restored phagosome-lysosome fusion would help the macrophage kill the bacteria.
statements.explanation: Fusion would expose the bacteria to the lysosome's hydrolytic enzymes and low pH, as in the normal route.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Even without fusion, the bacterium in step 3 is already being digested, because the phagosome around it contains hydrolytic enzymes.
statements.explanation: A phagosome holds only what was engulfed; the hydrolytic enzymes and low pH arrive when it fuses with a lysosome to form a secondary lysosome (step 4), the step this bacterium blocks.

links: Phagocytosis · Phagosome-lysosome fusion · Bulk transport keeps membranes continuous · Real-world: tuberculosis

title: When A doesn't equal T
stem: In 1959, base-composition data like those in the diagram showed that the DNA of φX174, a virus that infects E. coli, is unusual. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Sample 1 is DNA from human cells; sample 2 is DNA purified from φX174 virus particles.

(나) Inside an infected E. coli cell, φX174's DNA is copied to make a double-stranded form.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Sample 1's values fit double-stranded DNA, in which every A on one strand pairs with a T on the other, and every G with a C.
statements.explanation: Complementary pairing (A-T, G-C) between the two strands forces %A = %T and %G = %C (Chargaff's rules).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because A + G and T + C are nearly equal in sample 2, φX174's DNA is double-stranded.
statements.explanation: Double-stranded DNA needs A = T and G = C, pair by pair; sample 2 has A 25 vs T 33 and G 24 vs C 18, so its bases aren't paired. A + G (49%) nearly matching T + C (51%) is a coincidence: the DNA in the particles is single-stranded.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The double-stranded form in (나) would still contain more T than A, just like the DNA in the virus particles.
statements.explanation: In any double-stranded DNA each A is paired with a T, so the double-stranded form has equal amounts of A and T (and of G and C).

links: Chargaff's rules · Complementary base pairing · Real-world: φX174, a single-stranded DNA virus

title: Same gene, different cells
stem: Only the beta cells of the pancreas make insulin, yet a muscle cell from the same person carries the very same insulin gene. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Beta cells contain activator proteins that bind an enhancer of the insulin gene; muscle cells lack them.

(나) In an experiment, muscle cells are engineered to make the beta-cell activators.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Deleting the enhancer from a beta cell's DNA would lower its insulin transcription, even with the gene's coding sequence intact.
statements.explanation: The enhancer is the DNA site the activators bind; without it they can't boost transcription, so less mRNA is made from the intact gene.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Muscle cells don't make insulin because they lack the general transcription factors that RNA polymerase II needs at a promoter.
statements.explanation: Muscle cells make many other mRNAs with RNA polymerase II, so they must have the general transcription factors; what they lack, per (가), are the activators that bind the insulin gene's enhancer.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In (나), the engineered muscle cells can start transcribing their own insulin gene.
statements.explanation: Muscle cells carry the gene too; supplying the activators that bind its enhancer is what switches transcription on, as in beta cells.

links: Gene expression is regulated · General transcription factors vs activators · Enhancers are where activators bind · Real-world: insulin is made only in beta cells

title: Sixteen hours to copy one gene
stem: The human dystrophin gene, mutated in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, is one of the largest genes known: RNA polymerase II needs about 16 hours to transcribe it once. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The gene spans about 2.2 million base pairs.

(나) The finished mRNA that leaves the nucleus is about 14,000 nucleotides long.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm begin translating the dystrophin RNA while polymerase II is still transcribing the gene.
statements.explanation: In eukaryotes the nuclear envelope separates the steps: the transcript is processed in the nucleus and only then exported for translation.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: More than 99% of the RNA that polymerase II makes from this gene is removed before the mRNA leaves the nucleus.
statements.explanation: The primary transcript includes the introns; splicing removes them, leaving about 14,000 of 2.2 million nucleotides, under 1%.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Throughout those 16 hours, the polymerase moves along the template strand 3' to 5' while the RNA grows 5' to 3'.
statements.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template 3'→5' and adds each new nucleotide to the RNA's 3' end.

links: The primary transcript includes introns · Template read 3'→5' · Transcription and translation are separated in eukaryotes · Real-world: the dystrophin gene

title: A bacterial heat-shock switch
stem: When E. coli is suddenly moved from 30 °C to 42 °C, it switches on a set of heat-shock genes within minutes by making more of an alternative sigma factor, σ32. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Most E. coli genes are transcribed with the usual sigma factor, σ70.

(나) Human cells can also switch on a whole set of genes when they are heated.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: E. coli switches on its heat-shock genes by making a second type of RNA polymerase.
statements.explanation: Bacteria have a single type of RNA polymerase; swapping the sigma factor changes which promoters it recognizes.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A mutant that can't make σ32 would still switch on its heat-shock genes at 42 °C, because σ70 would recognize their promoters instead.
statements.explanation: σ70 recognizes promoters like those of most genes; the heat-shock genes' -35 and -10 sequences differ, so only σ32 directs RNA polymerase to them.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Human cells switch on their heat-shock genes using transcription factors such as activators, not sigma factors.
statements.explanation: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase II starts at promoters with the help of general transcription factors, activators and mediator, not sigma factors.

links: Sigma factors and promoter recognition · One RNA polymerase in bacteria · Eukaryotic transcription factors · Real-world: the heat-shock response

title: A drug that fixes splicing
stem: Children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) lack a working SMN1 gene. A backup gene, SMN2, makes mostly mRNA that is missing exon 7, and the protein made from that mRNA is quickly broken down. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The drug nusinersen binds SMN2 pre-mRNA in the nucleus.

(나) After treatment, much more of the SMN2 mRNA includes exon 7.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Keeping or skipping exon 7 is a case of alternative splicing, in which one gene's primary transcript gives different mature mRNAs and proteins.
statements.explanation: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same primary transcript, making related but different proteins.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A drug acting only on mRNA already in the cytoplasm would not change whether exon 7 is included.
statements.explanation: Splicing happens in the nucleus before the mRNA is exported, so mRNA in the cytoplasm has already been spliced.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Nusinersen works by permanently changing the DNA sequence of the SMN2 gene, so that its transcripts include exon 7.
statements.explanation: The gene is untouched; the drug acts on the pre-mRNA, changing which exons are joined during splicing.

links: Splicing happens in the nucleus · Alternative splicing · Real-world: spinal muscular atrophy and nusinersen

title: A toxin that damages the ribosome's RNA
stem: Shiga toxin, made by E. coli O157:H7 from undercooked burgers, enters cells lining the gut and kidney and removes a single adenine from the RNA of the ribosome's large subunit. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The damaged adenine lies in a loop of the large subunit's RNA where elongation factors bind as each new tRNA is brought in.

(나) Cells hit by the toxin soon stop making proteins.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because a ribosome is built from RNA as well as protein, a toxin that damages only its RNA still disables it.
statements.explanation: Ribosomes are RNA-protein complexes whose RNA does essential work: even peptide bond formation is catalyzed by the large subunit's rRNA.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Ribosomes already partway along an mRNA, like the one in the diagram, stall, because each new amino acid needs the damaged large subunit.
statements.explanation: Every elongation cycle brings a new tRNA into the A site and needs the large subunit; with it damaged, chains in progress can't grow.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A toxin that blocked transcription instead would stop protein synthesis more slowly, since mRNAs already in the cytoplasm would still be translated for a while.
statements.explanation: Existing mRNAs keep being translated until they're broken down; damaging ribosomes stops translation itself.

links: Ribosomes are RNA + protein · Elongation needs the large subunit · Transcription vs translation (Module 4) · Real-world: Shiga toxin and E. coli O157:H7

title: Rewriting a vaccine's codons
stem: Designers of mRNA vaccines often codon-optimize the gene: they swap many codons for others that human cells read efficiently, while the vaccine still makes the same viral protein. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) One stretch of the original mRNA reads 5'-CUU GAA UGG-3'.

(나) In the optimized mRNA, CUU is replaced by CUG and GAA by GAG.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Replacing CUU with CUG changes the protein, because one base of the codon changed.
statements.explanation: CUU and CUG both code for leucine; the code is redundant, so the amino acid stays the same.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: After both swaps in (나), this stretch still codes for Leu-Glu-Trp.
statements.explanation: CUG is Leu, GAG is Glu and UGG is Trp: the same three amino acids as before.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The designers could also swap UGG for a synonymous codon without changing the protein.
statements.explanation: Tryptophan has only one codon, UGG, so any change there gives a different amino acid or a stop codon.

links: The genetic code is redundant · Reading the codon table · Real-world: codon-optimized mRNA vaccines

title: Reading past an early stop
stem: About one in ten people with cystic fibrosis carries a mutation that turns a codon of the CFTR mRNA into an early stop codon. Drugs such as ataluren were developed to let ribosomes read past early stop codons. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Patient 1's mutation changes codon 542 from GGA to UGA.

(나) Patient 2's mutation deletes one nucleotide from codon 542.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Normally, a tRNA whose anticodon pairs with UGA reads a stop codon and ends translation.
statements.explanation: No tRNA reads a stop codon; a protein release factor binds the A site, and the finished chain is released.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: For patient 1, reading through the early UGA would yield a full-length protein.
statements.explanation: A read-through drug lets a tRNA place an amino acid at the early UGA; the codons after it are still in the original frame, so translation runs on to the normal stop codon.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The same drug would give patient 2 a normal protein, because in both patients only one nucleotide is affected.
statements.explanation: Deleting one nucleotide shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is misread; reading past a single stop can't fix that.

links: Release factors end translation · Reading frame · Real-world: cystic fibrosis and read-through drugs

title: Why sailors' gums bled
stem: On long voyages without fresh fruit, sailors developed scurvy: bleeding gums and wounds that wouldn't heal. Without vitamin C, the collagen that strengthens skin and blood vessels comes out weak. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Collagen is secreted by the cells that make it.

(나) Vitamin C is needed by an enzyme that chemically modifies certain amino acids in newly made collagen chains.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Collagen chains are made by ribosomes that the SRP brings to the rough ER, because collagen is a secreted protein.
statements.explanation: A secreted protein's signal sequence is bound by the SRP, which docks the ribosome on the ER so the chain enters the ER lumen.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Scurvy weakens collagen by changing the order of amino acids in its chains, since the collagen gene is copied incorrectly without vitamin C.
statements.explanation: The gene and the sequence are normal; what fails is a modification made after translation, which needs vitamin C.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Adding citrus fruit to the diet reverses the problem without any change to the sailors' genes.
statements.explanation: With vitamin C back, newly made collagen is modified properly again; the genes were never the problem.

links: Post-translational modification · Secreted proteins enter the rough ER via the SRP · Real-world: scurvy

title: An enzyme sent to the wrong organelle
stem: In one form of primary hyperoxaluria, a cause of kidney stones in children, the liver enzyme AGT still works but ends up in mitochondria instead of in peroxisomes, where it is needed. Changes in AGT, including one near its amino (N) terminus, create a mitochondrial targeting signal there. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) AGT is encoded by a gene in the nucleus.

(나) In mitochondria, AGT can't reach the molecule it normally acts on.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The misdirected AGT is made by ribosomes inside the mitochondria.
statements.explanation: AGT is encoded in the nucleus and made on free ribosomes in the cytosol; its new amino-terminal signal then directs it into mitochondria.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Moved to the carboxyl (C) terminus, the same signal would still send AGT to mitochondria, since a signal works wherever it sits in the chain.
statements.explanation: Mitochondrial signals work at the amino terminus; a signal's position is part of the address.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Changing just a few amino acids near the N-terminus can change where the whole protein goes, because sorting depends on signal sequences.
statements.explanation: A protein's destination is set by its signal sequences, so creating an amino-terminal mitochondrial signal re-addresses the entire protein.

links: Signal sequences direct proteins · Amino-terminal signals target mitochondria · Translation starts on free ribosomes · Real-world: primary hyperoxaluria

title: A warning label on diet soda
stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inherited disease in which the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase doesn't work; newborns are screened for it with a heel-prick blood test. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Untreated, phenylalanine builds up in the blood to levels that harm the developing brain.

(나) Drinks sweetened with aspartame carry the warning "Phenylketonurics: contains phenylalanine".

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Untreated children with PKU often have lighter skin and hair than their relatives, since less tyrosine is made for the route to melanin.
statements.explanation: Linked pathways mean a failed step cuts the supply to everything after it: less tyrosine is made from phenylalanine for the melanin route, and the excess phenylalanine also blocks tyrosinase, the first enzyme on that route, so less pigment is made. (PKU medical formulas are supplemented with tyrosine for this reason.)

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Since the side route's enzyme works normally in PKU, phenylpyruvate is made at its usual low rate even as phenylalanine builds up as in (가).
statements.explanation: That enzyme is unchanged, but far more phenylalanine reaches it, so far more phenylpyruvate is made; these phenylketones spill into the urine and give PKU its name.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The warning in (나) matters because the phenylalanine released when aspartame is digested enters the same pathway as phenylalanine from dietary protein.
statements.explanation: Aspartame is built from aspartate and phenylalanine; digesting it frees phenylalanine, which adds to the load the blocked pathway can't clear.

links: Metabolic pathways are linked: a product of one step is the next step's reactant · Real-world: phenylketonuria (PKU)

box: A food lab burns a whole peanut completely in a calorimeter and measures the heat released. In the body, part of a peanut's fat passes through the gut undigested; the rest, with the digestible carbohydrates, is oxidized to CO2 and H2O.
claim: So the body gets less energy from the peanut than the calorimeter measures, even though no energy is destroyed.
explanation: The calorimeter oxidizes everything, but the undigested fat leaves the body with its energy still in its bonds: energy is conserved; it just isn't released inside the body.
links: First law of thermodynamics · Catabolism releases energy

title: Creatine in a sprinter's muscle
stem: Creatine is one of the most popular sports supplements and modestly improves performance in repeated short sprints. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In the first seconds of intense exercise, phosphocreatine passes its phosphate directly to ADP, making ATP and creatine.

(나) Each value in the diagram is for removing one phosphate from that molecule.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Creatine supplements help because muscle cells oxidize the extra creatine itself for energy, in the same way that they oxidize glucose and fatty acids.
statements.explanation: Creatine is a phosphate carrier, not a fuel: at rest it is recharged to phosphocreatine, and during effort phosphocreatine hands the phosphate to ADP. Extra creatine means a bigger phosphocreatine store for remaking ATP quickly.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Under standard conditions the transfer in (가) has a ΔG of about −3.0 kcal/mol, so it runs forward without any other energy source.
statements.explanation: Coupling phosphocreatine hydrolysis (−10.3) with ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi (+7.3) gives −10.3 + 7.3 = −3.0 kcal/mol.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The reaction creatine + ATP → phosphocreatine + ADP can't run forward in muscle, since its standard ΔG is positive.
statements.explanation: Its standard ΔG is indeed +10.3 − 7.3 = +3.0 kcal/mol, but resting muscle keeps ATP high and ADP very low, and creatine is plentiful after exercise; with reactants held above their equilibrium ratio to products, the actual ΔG is negative, so phosphocreatine is rebuilt.

links: Energetic coupling through a shared phosphate · ATP hydrolysis is exergonic · Real-world: creatine supplements

title: Click, and the pack gets hot
stem: A reusable hand warmer holds a sodium acetate solution that stays liquid at room temperature even though it holds more dissolved salt than would normally stay dissolved. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Clicking a small metal disc inside the pack starts crystals forming, and the pack warms to about 50-55 °C as it turns solid.

(나) To reuse the pack, it is boiled in water until the crystals dissolve, then left to cool without crystallizing.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Clicking the disc supplies the energy that makes the crystallization's ΔG negative, which is why the solution stays liquid until the disc is clicked.
statements.explanation: ΔG is set by the gap between the two plateaus, which the click doesn't change. The click only gets the first crystals past the activation-energy barrier; after that, crystallization carries on by itself.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Crystallizing makes the sodium acetate more ordered, so it is spontaneous only because the heat it releases (negative ΔH) outweighs the drop in entropy.
statements.explanation: In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a negative ΔS makes −TΔS positive; ΔG is still negative because ΔH is more negative.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Resetting the pack in (나) takes an energy input, since going from crystals back to the room-temperature solution has a positive ΔG.
statements.explanation: At room temperature, crystals → solution is the reverse of an exergonic change, so ΔG is positive. Boiling works because at high T the −TΔS term makes dissolving spontaneous; careful cooling then leaves the solution on the higher plateau.

links: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS · Activation energy · Exergonic vs endergonic · Real-world: reusable hand warmers

stem: Refrigerating food slows its spoilage, which depends on enzyme-catalyzed reactions in microbes and in the food itself. Which explanation fits best?
options: The cold lowers the free energy each reaction releases until it reaches zero
The cold makes the spoilage reactions endergonic, so they can no longer proceed
The cold raises the activation energy that each spoilage reaction needs
The cold unfolds the enzymes, so their active sites can no longer bind substrates
The cold leaves fewer molecules with enough kinetic energy to cross the activation barrier
explanation: Reactants must have enough kinetic energy to reach the transition state; cooling slows molecules, so fewer succeed per second. ΔG shifts only slightly and stays negative, the barrier's height is unchanged, and fridge temperatures don't denature enzymes.
links: Activation energy · Kinetic energy · Real-world: refrigeration

title: A cholesterol drug and a look-alike
stem: Statins, the most widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs, inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme for an early step in the liver's cholesterol-making pathway. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Part of each statin molecule is shaped much like HMG-CoA, the enzyme's substrate.

(나) Compound N, an experimental inhibitor, binds the enzyme at a site away from its active site.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The statin cuts the rate by about a fifth at 20 units of HMG-CoA but by nearly half at 5 units, because more substrate outcompetes the drug for the active site.
statements.explanation: At 20 units the rates are about 95% vs 77%; at 5 units about 83% vs 45%. As (가) suggests, the statin and the substrate compete for the same site.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Compound N's curve levels off near 45% because it takes the same share of enzyme molecules out of action at every HMG-CoA concentration.
statements.explanation: Compound N binds a separate site (나), so substrate can't compete it off; the share of enzyme it disables is the same at any HMG-CoA level, which caps the rate.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because the statin curve lies below compound N's at low HMG-CoA, the statin is the stronger inhibitor at every HMG-CoA concentration shown.
statements.explanation: The curves cross near 3-4 units; above that, compound N holds the rate lower, because substrate increasingly outcompetes the statin but can't displace compound N.

links: Competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition · Real-world: statins

title: Pineapple that ruins dessert
stem: Boxes of gelatin dessert mix warn that fresh pineapple or kiwi will keep the gelatin from setting, while canned pineapple is fine. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that hydrolyzes peptide bonds. Gelatin is a protein made from collagen.

(나) Canning heats the fruit to near boiling.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In tube 1 almost no peptide bonds are hydrolyzed even though hydrolysis releases energy, because without an enzyme few of these bonds get over the activation-energy barrier.
statements.explanation: A negative ΔG says a reaction can proceed, not how fast; with a high barrier and no catalyst, the gel stays intact.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Tubes 3 and 4 set because heating made the hydrolysis of gelatin's peptide bonds endergonic, so even a working enzyme could no longer drive it forward.
statements.explanation: Boiling the fruit beforehand doesn't change the ΔG of gelatin hydrolysis in the chilled tube; it is still exergonic. Heating unfolded bromelain, destroying its active site, and without a working enzyme the reaction is too slow to matter.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Comparing tubes 2 and 4 shows that fresh pineapple stops the gel from setting through a heat-sensitive component such as a protein, not through something heat-stable like its sugar or acid.
statements.explanation: The same fruit stops working once boiled; sugars and acids survive boiling, but a protein's fold, and so an enzyme's active site, does not.

links: Enzymes lower activation energy · Heat destroys the active site · ΔG vs rate · Real-world: gelatin and fresh pineapple

box: Dorzagliatin, a diabetes drug approved in China in 2022, makes glucokinase (the liver and pancreas form of hexokinase) phosphorylate glucose faster. Raising the glucose concentration doesn't push the drug off the enzyme.
claim: So dorzagliatin binds glucokinase's active site in place of glucose, since it changes how fast glucose is phosphorylated.
explanation: A drug that took glucose's place would be pushed off by extra glucose, as a competitive inhibitor is. Dorzagliatin binds a separate pocket and changes the enzyme's shape so the active site works better, the opposite of a noncompetitive inhibitor; a molecule needn't occupy the active site to change the rate.
links: Enzyme activators · Competitive inhibition

stem: An enzyme early in an ATP-producing pathway is controlled by small molecules that bind away from its active site. Which pair of controls would best match the cell's energy needs?
options: AMP inhibits the enzyme, and ADP activates it
ATP inhibits the enzyme, and AMP activates it
ATP activates the enzyme, and AMP inhibits it
ATP and AMP both activate the enzyme
ATP and AMP both inhibit the enzyme
explanation: Plenty of ATP means the pathway's product is in surplus, so inhibition saves fuel (feedback); a build-up of AMP signals that ATP has been spent, so activation speeds ATP production.
links: Enzyme activators · Feedback inhibition

title: One drop or many steps
stem: Glucose can be oxidized by O2 in a flame or inside a cell. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Burning releases glucose's energy almost entirely as heat and light.

(나) Cells capture part of the same energy as ATP and reduced electron carriers.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In B, O2 accepts electrons at each small step of the staircase rather than all at once as in A.
statements.explanation: Glucose's electrons go first to NAD+ and FAD; O2 takes them only at the very end of the electron transport chain.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The total free-energy change from glucose + 6 O2 to 6 CO2 + 6 H2O is the same in A and B.
statements.explanation: Both routes start and end with the same molecules, so the overall ΔG is identical; only the path differs.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Releasing the energy in small steps, as in B, lets the cell trap much of it in carriers and ATP instead of losing it all at once as heat.
statements.explanation: Small steps release amounts that enzymes can couple to reducing NAD+ or making ATP; the share that isn't trapped is still released as heat.

links: Energy is released in steps · O2 is the final electron acceptor · Electron carriers

title: Who loses the electrons?
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O

(나) NAD+ + 2 e- + H+ → NADH

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (가), the carbon atoms of glucose are oxidized and the oxygen atoms of O2 are reduced.
statements.explanation: Glucose's carbons lose electrons as they become CO2; O2 gains electrons as it becomes H2O.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In a cell, the electrons glucose loses in (가) reach O2 by way of carriers such as the one in (나), not directly.
statements.explanation: Glucose's electrons go first to NAD+ and FAD; NADH and FADH2 then pass them down the electron transport chain to O2.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In (나), NAD+ is oxidized, since it picks up a hydrogen ion along with the electrons.
statements.explanation: Gaining electrons is reduction: NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The H+ comes along, but the electrons decide it.

links: Oxidation is loss, reduction is gain · NAD+/NADH carry electrons

title: Two ways to make ATP
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In glycolysis, an enzyme moves a phosphate group from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate directly onto ADP.

(나) In the mitochondrion, ATP synthase makes ATP using a proton gradient built by the electron transport chain.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Per glucose, the process in (가) makes most of the cell's ATP, since it happens in more than one stage.
statements.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation gives only about 4 of roughly 32 ATP per glucose; (나), oxidative phosphorylation, makes about 28.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A poison that stopped the electron transport chain would also halt (가) within seconds, because (가) depends on the proton gradient.
statements.explanation: (가) uses no gradient; glycolysis's substrate-level steps keep going if fermentation regenerates NAD+, while (나) stops at once.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) is substrate-level phosphorylation, and it needs neither O2 nor a membrane.
statements.explanation: The phosphate goes straight from a substrate to ADP in one enzyme reaction, so no gradient, membrane or O2 is involved.

links: Substrate-level vs oxidative phosphorylation

title: Where in the pathway?
prompt: Match each event to the stage or pathway where it happens.

pairs.left: Glucose is split into two three-carbon molecules
pairs.right: Glycolysis

pairs.left: A three-carbon molecule loses CO2 and its other two carbons join coenzyme A
pairs.right: Pyruvate oxidation

pairs.left: Oxaloacetate is remade after accepting a two-carbon group
pairs.right: Citric acid cycle

pairs.left: O2 accepts electrons and becomes water
pairs.right: Oxidative phosphorylation

pairs.left: Pyruvate is reduced so NAD+ is regenerated without O2
pairs.right: Fermentation

explanation: Glycolysis splits glucose, pyruvate oxidation makes acetyl-CoA and CO2, the cycle regenerates oxaloacetate, oxidative phosphorylation ends at O2, and fermentation is pyruvate's fate when O2 is absent.
links: Stages of respiration · Fermentation

box: A liver cell like the one in the diagram is given glucose whose carbons are all radioactive.
claim: The first radioactive CO2 is made in the mitochondrial matrix, not in the cytosol where the glucose is first broken down.
explanation: Glycolysis in the cytosol releases no CO2; the first CO2 is released when pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl-CoA in the matrix.
links: Stage locations · Source of CO2

box: Respiration is often summarized as C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O.
claim: The six O2 molecules end up in the six CO2 molecules the cell releases.
explanation: O2 is the final electron acceptor and is reduced to water. The oxygen in exhaled CO2 comes from glucose and water: the equation is a net summary in which the 6 O2 are reduced to 12 H2O while 6 H2O are used up along the way.
links: O2 is reduced to H2O · Glucose is oxidized to CO2

box: A long-distance runner's muscles oxidize a mix of glucose, fatty acids and a little amino-acid fuel.
claim: All three fuels feed the same final stage, oxidative phosphorylation, through reduced electron carriers.
explanation: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins all yield NADH and FADH2 on their way through respiration, and those carriers deliver electrons to the same electron transport chain.
links: Respiration uses several fuels · Electron carriers

box: A cell cut off from O2, and unable to ferment, soon converts most of its NAD+ into NADH.
claim: Glycolysis then slows because NADH, not NAD+, is the form that can accept more electrons from glucose.
explanation: The oxidized form, NAD+, accepts electrons; NADH is already reduced. Glycolysis slows because NAD+ runs short.
links: NAD+ is the oxidized carrier · Redox

box: In the electron transport chain, NADH hands two electrons to complex I and becomes NAD+.
claim: In this step NADH is oxidized and complex I is reduced.
explanation: NADH loses electrons (oxidation) and complex I gains them (reduction); complex I is then oxidized in turn as it passes them on to coenzyme Q.
links: Oxidation is loss, reduction is gain · Electron carriers

box: The table lists what the first three stages of respiration make from each glucose.
claim: If a poison blocked the electron transport chain, the cell would still get the 4 ATP per glucose that the table lists for substrate-level phosphorylation.
explanation: With the chain blocked, NADH isn't reoxidized, so pyruvate oxidation and the cycle stop once their NAD+ runs out; only glycolysis's 2 ATP remain, and only if fermentation regenerates NAD+.
links: Substrate-level phosphorylation · Carriers must be reoxidized

box: A student lists the stages of aerobic respiration as: pyruvate oxidation, glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, citric acid cycle.
claim: Swapping the first two stages and swapping the last two puts the list in the order that glucose's carbon and electrons pass through them.
explanation: The order is glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, then oxidative phosphorylation; both swaps fix the student's list.
links: Order of the four stages

stem: A cell is given radioactive glucose. Using the diagram, where will radioactive pyruvate first appear?
options: Cytosol
Inner mitochondrial membrane
Outer mitochondrial membrane
Intermembrane space
Mitochondrial matrix
explanation: Glycolysis, which makes pyruvate, runs in the cytosol; pyruvate only later enters the matrix for oxidation.
links: Stage locations · Glycolysis

stem: In which of these conversions does the first molecule gain electrons?
options: NADH → NAD+
Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO2
Succinate → fumarate
FAD → FADH2
Glucose → CO2
explanation: FAD gains two electrons (with two H+) to become FADH2: a reduction. The others lose electrons, so they are oxidations.
links: Reduction is gain of electrons · Electron carriers

stem: Why do cells pass glucose's electrons through NADH and a chain of carriers instead of straight to O2?
options: Because O2 accepts electrons from NADH but not from glucose
Because NADH holds more energy than the glucose it came from
Because small steps release energy in amounts cells can capture
Because carriers let the reactions run with no activation energy
Because a longer path releases more total energy from each glucose
explanation: A single drop would release the energy as heat; stepwise transfers let the cell trap it in carriers, a gradient and ATP. The total released is the same by either path.
links: Stepwise energy release

stem: A carbon atom from glucose ends up in exhaled CO2. In which order could it pass through the stages of respiration?
options: Glycolysis → pyruvate oxidation → citric acid cycle
Glycolysis → citric acid cycle → oxidative phosphorylation
Glycolysis → pyruvate oxidation → oxidative phosphorylation
Pyruvate oxidation → glycolysis → citric acid cycle
Glycolysis → citric acid cycle → pyruvate oxidation
explanation: Glucose becomes pyruvate, pyruvate becomes acetyl-CoA (releasing CO2), and the cycle releases the rest as CO2; oxidative phosphorylation handles electrons, not carbon.
links: Order of the stages · Source of exhaled CO2

title: Seeing tumours with a sugar look-alike
stem: FDG-PET scans find many cancers by imaging where FDG, a radioactive look-alike of glucose, collects in the body. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Hexokinase phosphorylates FDG just as it phosphorylates glucose, but the next glycolysis enzyme can't act on FDG 6-phosphate.

(나) Many tumours take up far more glucose than most of the tissue around them.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Tumours in (나) show up as bright spots against the tissue around them, because more FDG enters their cells and is phosphorylated there.
statements.explanation: More uptake through GLUT plus trapping by hexokinase means FDG 6-phosphate accumulates fastest in those cells.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: FDG collects in cells because GLUT carriers move it into cells but not back out of them.
statements.explanation: GLUT carriers work by facilitated diffusion in either direction. FDG is held in the cell because FDG 6-phosphate is charged and no longer fits GLUT; (가) adds that glycolysis can't use it up either.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If a drug blocked hexokinase, FDG would stop building up inside the cells even though it could still enter through GLUT.
statements.explanation: Unphosphorylated FDG can diffuse back out through GLUT; phosphorylation in step 1 is what traps it.

links: Phosphorylation traps glucose in the cell · GLUT facilitated diffusion · Real-world: FDG-PET scans

title: Balancing glycolysis's books
stem: A biochemist follows glucose through glycolysis. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) She tallies every ATP and NADH that the diagram's ten steps use or make for one glucose.

(나) She then repeats the tally starting from fructose 1,6-bisphosphate instead of glucose.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose: 4 are made in steps 7 and 10 and 2 are spent in steps 1 and 3.
statements.explanation: Steps 7 and 10 each make 2 ATP per glucose (4 in all); steps 1 and 3 each spend 1.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Starting from fructose 1,6-bisphosphate as in (나), the net yield would rise to 4 ATP, since the phase 1 cost has already been paid.
statements.explanation: Steps 1 and 3 are skipped, so the 4 ATP from the payoff phase are all net gain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Steps 7 and 10 are substrate-level phosphorylation: an enzyme moves a phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate or phosphoenolpyruvate straight onto ADP.
statements.explanation: No membrane or gradient is involved; the phosphate is transferred within one enzyme reaction.

links: Glycolysis net yield · Investment and payoff phases · Substrate-level phosphorylation

title: What fluoride does to mouth bacteria
stem: Mouth bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans ferment sugars and release acid that dissolves tooth enamel. Assume they run glycolysis exactly as in the diagram. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Fluoride from toothpaste inhibits enolase, step 9 in the diagram, inside these bacteria.

(나) The acid these bacteria make is lactic acid, formed from pyruvate.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The bacteria would still net 2 ATP per glucose, because step 7 lies before the block and still makes ATP.
statements.explanation: Step 7 makes 2 ATP per glucose, exactly offsetting the 2 spent in steps 1 and 3, so the net is 0 without step 10.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: With enolase blocked, 2-phosphoglycerate would pile up and the bacteria would make less ATP from each glucose.
statements.explanation: Step 9's substrate accumulates, and step 10, which makes 2 ATP per glucose, is starved of phosphoenolpyruvate; with no pyruvate to reduce to lactate, NAD+ isn't regenerated either, so even steps 6 and 7 soon stall.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Blocking step 9 also cuts acid production, since less pyruvate is formed for the bacteria to turn into lactic acid.
statements.explanation: Lactic acid comes from pyruvate (나), and pyruvate is made only after steps 9 and 10.

links: Glycolysis payoff phase · Net yield · Real-world: fluoride toothpaste

title: Five reactions, five jobs
prompt: Match each glycolysis reaction to what it achieves.

pairs.right: A phosphate from ATP traps the sugar inside the cell
A six-carbon sugar is split into two three-carbon sugars
Lets both halves of glucose enter the payoff phase
An electron carrier is reduced as the sugar is oxidized
ATP is made as the final product forms

explanation: Phase 1 invests ATP to trap and destabilize the sugar, phase 2 splits it into two G3P, and phase 3 makes NADH and ATP.
links: Three phases of glycolysis

box: Yeast in a sealed jar with no O2 keep running glycolysis for hours, regenerating NAD+ by fermentation.
claim: This shows that no step of glycolysis uses O2 as a reactant.
explanation: Glycolysis is anaerobic in that it consumes no O2; it runs in the cytosol with or without O2, as long as NAD+ is regenerated.
links: Glycolysis needs no O2

box: Glycolysis turns one glucose into two pyruvate molecules.
claim: Some of glucose's carbon leaves as CO2 during glycolysis.
explanation: Two 3-carbon pyruvates hold all 6 carbons of glucose. The first CO2 is released later, in pyruvate oxidation.
links: Glycolysis: 6C → 2 × 3C · Source of CO2

box: In phase 1, glucose gets two phosphate groups from ATP before it is split.
claim: Spending 2 ATP in phase 1 is wasteful: a cell that split glucose without first phosphorylating it would net more ATP per glucose.
explanation: The phosphates added in phase 1 trap glucose and destabilize it so it can be split; unphosphorylated glucose isn't split, and the payoff phase can't happen at all.
links: Glycolysis phase 1 · Phosphorylation traps and destabilizes glucose

box: Phosphofructokinase (step 3) adds a second phosphate before the six-carbon sugar is split in step 4.
claim: If step 3 were skipped and fructose 6-phosphate could be split directly, both three-carbon products would still carry a phosphate.
explanation: Fructose 6-phosphate has only one phosphate, so only one of the two pieces would carry it; adding the second phosphate in step 3 is what lets both halves continue.
links: Glycolysis phases 1 and 2

box: A mitochondrial disease leaves a patient's muscle mitochondria working poorly.
claim: After mild exercise, this patient's blood lactate would be expected to rise more than a healthy person's.
explanation: With oxidative phosphorylation impaired, muscle leans on glycolysis and regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate.
links: Glycolysis works without mitochondria · Lactic acid fermentation · Real-world: mitochondrial disease

box: Most glucose units cut from muscle glycogen are released as glucose 1-phosphate, which becomes glucose 6-phosphate without using ATP.
claim: Each of these units therefore nets 3 ATP in glycolysis instead of 2.
explanation: Skipping step 1 saves the ATP that hexokinase would spend, so the tally becomes 4 made − 1 spent = 3.
links: Glycolysis net yield · Glycogen as stored glucose

box: Step 6 of glycolysis converts G3P to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
claim: If a cell ran out of NAD+, G3P would build up, because step 6 needs NAD+ to accept G3P's electrons.
explanation: Step 6 oxidizes G3P by passing its electrons to NAD+; with no NAD+ to accept them, G3P can't be converted and accumulates.
links: Glycolysis phase 3 · NAD+ as electron acceptor

box: Glycolysis turns glucose into 2 pyruvate, 2 NADH and a net 2 ATP.
claim: Most of glucose's chemical energy has already been released by the end of glycolysis, since glucose has been split in two.
explanation: Glycolysis releases only a small share of the energy; most is still held in the two pyruvates and is released later in the mitochondria.
links: Glycolysis releases a small amount of energy · Stepwise release

stem: A cell given 10 glucose molecules has no O2 and makes ATP only by glycolysis, regenerating NAD+ by fermentation. What is its net ATP gain?
explanation: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP per glucose (4 made − 2 spent), and fermentation adds none: 10 × 2 = 20.
links: Glycolysis net yield · Fermentation yield

stem: A mutation inactivates the enzyme for step 5, so DHAP can no longer become G3P. What is glycolysis's net ATP yield per glucose now?
explanation: Only one G3P per glucose goes through the payoff phase, making 2 ATP, which just repays the 2 spent in phase 1.
links: Glycolysis phase 2 · Net yield

stem: Using the diagram, if step 4 of glycolysis were blocked, what would the net ATP yield per glucose be?
explanation: Steps 1 and 3 have already spent 2 ATP before the split, and no ATP is made until step 7, so each glucose costs the cell 2 ATP.
links: Glycolysis phases 1 and 2

stem: Where is the NADH from glycolysis made, and where must its electrons go in a cell with O2?
options: Matrix; to the ETC in the outer mitochondrial membrane
Matrix; back to step 6 of glycolysis to be reused there
Cytosol; to the ETC in the inner mitochondrial membrane
Intermembrane space; to ATP synthase in the inner membrane
Cytosol; straight to O2 dissolved in the cytosol
explanation: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol; with O2 present, NADH's electrons are ultimately passed to the ETC in the inner membrane.
links: Stage locations · ETC location

stem: Glycolysis is thought to be one of the oldest metabolic pathways. Which of its features best fits an origin before Earth's air held much O2?
options: It has ten enzyme-catalyzed steps
It splits a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon molecules
It spends 2 ATP before it makes any
It makes NADH as well as ATP
It runs in the cytosol and consumes no O2
explanation: All five are true of glycolysis, but only needing no O2 (and no organelle) fits a world with little O2.
links: Glycolysis needs no O2 · Location

title: When a vitamin runs short
stem: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency is common in people with long-term heavy alcohol use; it can damage the brain and raise the level of lactate in the blood. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Thiamine is needed to make TPP, a cofactor of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

(나) The brain gets nearly all of its energy by oxidizing glucose.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because of (가), blood lactate rises: pyruvate that can't be converted to acetyl-CoA is reduced to lactate instead.
statements.explanation: With the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex slowed, pyruvate piles up in the cytosol and is diverted to lactate.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The brain in (나) suffers because each glucose whose pyruvate becomes lactate yields only glycolysis's 2 ATP instead of about 32.
statements.explanation: Without acetyl-CoA from pyruvate, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation can't extract most of glucose's energy.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Giving these patients extra glucose without thiamine would restore the brain's ATP supply, since more glucose means more pyruvate.
statements.explanation: Without TPP the extra pyruvate still can't become acetyl-CoA and mostly becomes lactate, which is why thiamine is given before or with glucose to at-risk patients.

links: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex · Lactate as pyruvate's other fate · ATP yield · Real-world: thiamine deficiency

title: Following the carbons around the cycle
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The two carbons of acetyl-CoA join oxaloacetate to form citrate.

(나) Each turn of the cycle releases two CO2.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The two CO2 leave at isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate and α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA, where the carbon count drops.
statements.explanation: Isocitrate (6C) becomes α-ketoglutarate (5C), and α-ketoglutarate (5C) becomes succinyl-CoA (4C): one CO2 each.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because each turn releases two CO2, the oxaloacetate pool shrinks by one molecule each time an acetyl-CoA enters.
statements.explanation: The two carbons lost balance the two that entered, and oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of each turn.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: One glucose drives two turns of the cycle, so the cycle releases 4 CO2 per glucose.
statements.explanation: Each glucose gives two pyruvate, hence two acetyl-CoA, and each turn releases 2 CO2.

links: The cycle completes oxidation · Oxaloacetate is regenerated · Cycle yield per glucose

title: Borrowing from the cycle
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Cells draw α-ketoglutarate out of the cycle to make the amino acid glutamate.

(나) In these cells, oxaloacetate levels then fall.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) happens because every α-ketoglutarate removed is one less molecule that can go on to be converted back into oxaloacetate.
statements.explanation: Oxaloacetate is regenerated only from the intermediates that complete the turn; drained ones never get there.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If oxaloacetate runs short, acetyl-CoA enters the cycle more slowly, even when plenty of acetyl-CoA is available.
statements.explanation: Acetyl-CoA can enter only by joining oxaloacetate, so oxaloacetate supply limits the cycle's rate.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Supplying extra oxaloacetate, or a molecule that becomes it, could keep the cycle turning while α-ketoglutarate is drawn off.
statements.explanation: Topping up an intermediate replaces what was removed, so acetyl-CoA can keep entering; cells do exactly this, for example by making oxaloacetate from pyruvate.

links: Cycle intermediates feed other pathways · Oxaloacetate is regenerated

title: Where your breath comes from
stem: Breath tests follow labelled carbon from a swallowed fuel into exhaled CO2. Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Fatty acids are cut into acetyl-CoA by beta-oxidation.

(나) In one test, a volunteer drinks glucose labelled with carbon-13 in all six carbons.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The carbon-13 will appear in exhaled CO2, released during pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle.
statements.explanation: Those two stages release glucose's carbons as CO2, which the blood carries to the lungs.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If the volunteer drank carbon-13-labelled fatty acids instead, the label would stay out of exhaled CO2, because fatty acids bypass glycolysis and pyruvate oxidation.
statements.explanation: Their acetyl-CoA (가) is oxidized in the citric acid cycle, which releases the label as CO2.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Of the six labelled carbons in each glucose, four leave as CO2 in pyruvate oxidation and two in the citric acid cycle.
statements.explanation: It is the other way round: pyruvate oxidation releases 2 (one per pyruvate) and the cycle releases 4 (two per turn, two turns).

links: Source of exhaled CO2 · Beta-oxidation feeds the cycle · CO2 per stage · Real-world: carbon-13 breath tests

title: Where it happens
prompt: Match each event to the place where it happens. The diagram shows the compartments.

pairs.left: Glucose enters the cell through GLUT carriers
pairs.right: Plasma membrane

pairs.left: Glucose is split into two pyruvate
pairs.right: Cytosol
Mitochondrial matrix

pairs.left: Electrons pass from carrier to carrier toward O2
pairs.right: Inner mitochondrial membrane
Intermembrane space

explanation: Glycolysis runs in the cytosol; pyruvate oxidation and the cycle in the matrix; the ETC in the inner membrane pumps H+ into the intermembrane space, and ATP synthase, also in the inner membrane, lets it flow back into the matrix.
links: Mitochondrial compartments · Stage locations

title: Who does what
prompt: Match each molecule or enzyme to its role in pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle.

pairs.right: Carries the acetyl group into the citric acid cycle
Accepts the acetyl group and is remade at the end of each turn
Accepts electrons as pyruvate and cycle intermediates are oxidized
Removes CO2 from pyruvate and joins what is left to coenzyme A
Can be drawn off to make the amino acid glutamate

explanation: Each of these has a distinct job: carrier, regenerated acceptor, electron carrier, the converting enzyme and a biosynthetic branch point.
links: Pyruvate oxidation · Cycle intermediates · Electron carriers

box: In the matrix, pyruvate gives up CO2 and two electrons (with an H+) as it becomes an acetyl group, and NAD+ becomes NADH.
claim: In this step pyruvate is oxidized and NAD+ is reduced.
explanation: Pyruvate loses electrons as it becomes CO2 and an acetyl group (oxidation); NAD+ gains them, becoming NADH (reduction).
links: Pyruvate oxidation · Redox

box: A cell completely oxidizes 3 glucose molecules; the table lists what each glucose gives.
claim: Pyruvate oxidation in this cell produces 6 acetyl-CoA, 6 NADH and 6 CO2.
explanation: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate, and each pyruvate gives 1 acetyl-CoA, 1 NADH and 1 CO2: 3 × 2 = 6 of each.
links: Pyruvate oxidation totals

box: In the matrix, the citric acid cycle oxidizes each acetyl group to 2 CO2.
claim: The cycle captures most of that energy as ATP, with only a small share going to NADH and FADH2.
explanation: Per glucose the cycle makes just 2 ATP (as GTP) but 6 NADH and 2 FADH2; most of the energy goes into the carriers, while the carbons leave as CO2.
links: Citric acid cycle yield · Electron carriers

box: Mitochondria isolated from liver cells are placed in a buffer with glucose and O2, but with no cytosol.
claim: They will consume O2 rapidly, since glucose can fuel all four stages.
explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol, so isolated mitochondria can't use glucose; they need pyruvate (or another mitochondrial fuel) to make NADH and use O2.
links: Stage locations · Mitochondrial compartments

box: In 1930s experiments, adding a small amount of a four-carbon cycle intermediate to minced pigeon breast muscle raised its O2 use far more than oxidizing that intermediate alone could explain.
claim: This fits the cycle remaking oxaloacetate every turn, so a small amount of it can process many acetyl groups.
explanation: The added intermediate is recycled turn after turn rather than used up, so it keeps acetyl groups flowing into the cycle.
links: Oxaloacetate is regenerated · Real-world: Krebs's pigeon muscle experiments

box: During moderate exercise, a person breathes out more CO2 than at rest.
claim: The extra CO2 comes mainly from faster pyruvate oxidation and citric acid cycle activity in the working muscles.
explanation: Working muscle oxidizes more fuel; the CO2-releasing steps are pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle.
links: Source of exhaled CO2 · The cycle completes oxidation

box: Per glucose, the citric acid cycle yields 2 ATP (made as GTP).
claim: That ATP is made by ATP synthase, using a proton gradient across the inner membrane.
explanation: The cycle's ATP (as GTP) is made by substrate-level phosphorylation, directly in one enzyme reaction.
links: Substrate-level phosphorylation

box: In human cells, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA mainly when O2 is available.
claim: This is because the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex uses O2 as a reactant when it oxidizes pyruvate.
explanation: NAD+ is the oxidizing agent. O2 is needed indirectly: without it the ETC can't reoxidize NADH, so NAD+ runs out.
links: Pyruvate oxidation · O2 as the final acceptor

stem: Per glucose, how many CO2 are released between pyruvate and the end of the citric acid cycle?
explanation: Pyruvate oxidation releases 2 (one per pyruvate) and the cycle releases 4 (two per turn, two turns): 6 in all, accounting for every carbon of glucose.
links: Pyruvate oxidation totals · Cycle yield · Exhaled CO2

stem: Over a long run, how many oxaloacetate molecules does the citric acid cycle use up, net, while oxidizing 100 acetyl-CoA?
explanation: Each turn uses one oxaloacetate and regenerates one, so the net use is zero; that is what makes it a cycle.
links: Oxaloacetate is regenerated

stem: A high-fat (ketogenic) diet is the standard treatment for children whose pyruvate dehydrogenase complex works poorly. Why does it help?
options: Fats supply NAD+, which restores the faulty enzyme's activity
Fatty acids are broken into acetyl-CoA, bypassing the faulty step
Fats are broken down into glucose, which then skips glycolysis entirely
Fats are fermented to lactate, which then feeds the cycle
Fats are converted to pyruvate, which the cells can then oxidize
explanation: Beta-oxidation turns fatty acids into acetyl-CoA (the liver sends much of it to the brain as ketone bodies), so fat's carbons reach the citric acid cycle without going through pyruvate.
links: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex · Beta-oxidation · Real-world: pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency

stem: A drug blocks the carrier protein that moves pyruvate across the inner mitochondrial membrane. What happens first?
options: Acetyl-CoA builds up in the matrix
Glycolysis stops making pyruvate at all
More NADH is made in the matrix
Pyruvate builds up in the cytosol
Pyruvate builds up in the mitochondrial matrix
explanation: Pyruvate is made in the cytosol but oxidized in the matrix; with the carrier blocked it piles up on the cytosol side, and less acetyl-CoA and NADH are made in the matrix.
links: Mitochondrial compartments · Pyruvate oxidation in the matrix

title: A diet pill that turned people into furnaces
stem: In the 1930s, 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) was sold as a diet pill. It caused rapid weight loss but also fatal overheating, and it still kills people who buy it online. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) DNP picks up H+ in the intermembrane space, crosses the inner membrane, and releases the H+ in the matrix.

(나) People taking DNP breathe faster and burn through their fat stores quickly.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: With DNP, the mitochondria make more ATP for each O2 they use, since electrons flow faster.
statements.explanation: In the diagram ATP made falls to 35 while O2 use rises to 180, so ATP per O2 drops to about a fifth of the untreated value.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because H+ return through DNP instead of through ATP synthase, the gradient's energy is released as heat rather than captured as ATP.
statements.explanation: The gradient still forms and is still used up, but with no machine in the path its energy ends up as heat.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A DNP user who ate enough extra food to cover the extra fuel burned would stop losing weight but would still overheat.
statements.explanation: The heat comes from uncoupled fuel oxidation (가), whatever the energy balance; eating more only replaces the fat in (나).

links: Chemiosmotic coupling · Proton gradient · ATP synthase · Real-world: DNP poisoning

title: Reading an oxygen trace
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase.

(나) Cyanide blocks complex IV.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: O2 use speeds up after ADP is added because ATP synthase can then let H+ flow back, so the ETC can pump faster.
statements.explanation: With ADP present, ATP synthase draws down the gradient; electron transport, coupled to that gradient, speeds up.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: After cyanide is added, O2 stays flat even though DNP is present, since electrons can no longer be passed to O2.
statements.explanation: DNP removes the gradient's brake, but with complex IV blocked (나) there is no path for electrons to O2 at all.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Between minutes 6 and 8, when O2 is used fastest, the mitochondria are also making ATP fastest.
statements.explanation: Oligomycin still blocks ATP synthase (가), and DNP lets H+ bypass it, so almost no ATP is made while O2 use races.

links: Chemiosmotic coupling · O2 is the final acceptor · ATP synthase

title: Rotenone and succinate
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Rotenone, a plant toxin used to kill unwanted fish in lakes, blocks complex I.

(나) Succinate, a citric acid cycle intermediate, is oxidized at complex II, which reduces FAD to FADH2.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Rotenone-poisoned mitochondria given only pyruvate soon stop using O2, even though complex II still works.
statements.explanation: NADH can't be reoxidized at complex I, so NAD+ runs out and the citric acid cycle, which feeds complex II, stops too.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Since complex II pumps no H+, rotenone-poisoned mitochondria given succinate make no ATP at all.
statements.explanation: Electrons from complex II still pass through complexes III and IV, which pump H+, so ATP is still made, just less.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Rotenone-poisoned mitochondria can still pass electrons to O2 if given succinate, since those electrons enter after complex I.
statements.explanation: Complex II hands electrons to Q, downstream of the block, so complexes III and IV still work.

links: FADH2 enters at complex II · Proton pumping by I, III and IV · ETC components · Real-world: rotenone

title: A motor you can watch spin
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In ATP synthase, Fo is the channel in the inner membrane and F1 is the part that sticks into the matrix.

(나) In 1997, researchers attached a fluorescent filament to the rotor of isolated F1 parts and watched it spin when ATP was added.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Given ADP and Pi instead of ATP, the isolated F1 parts in (나) would spin the other way and make ATP.
statements.explanation: With no Fo and no H+ gradient, nothing drives the rotor; isolated F1 can only split ATP, not make it.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In (나), the isolated F1 ran in reverse, using ATP hydrolysis to turn the rotor.
statements.explanation: With no membrane or gradient, F1 can only split ATP; that hydrolysis drives the rotation the researchers saw.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In mitochondria, H+ flowing through Fo from the intermembrane space into the matrix turns the rotor, and F1 uses that rotation to join ADP and Pi.
statements.explanation: H+ flows down its gradient through Fo; the rotation changes the shape of F1's catalytic sites, which make ATP.

links: ATP synthase is a rotary machine · Proton gradient · Real-world: watching single ATP synthase molecules

title: Diagnosing a poison
prompt: Match each poison's observed effect on isolated mitochondria to where it acts.

pairs.left: Stops O2 use with NADH-linked fuels, but adding succinate restores it
pairs.right: Complex I

pairs.left: Stops O2 use with every fuel, and cytochrome c stays oxidized
pairs.right: Complex III

pairs.left: Competes with O2 at the chain's last step
pairs.right: Complex IV

pairs.left: Stops ATP synthesis and slows O2 use, but DNP restores O2 use
pairs.right: The Fo channel of ATP synthase

pairs.left: Speeds O2 use while ATP synthesis falls
pairs.right: No protein: it carries H+ across the bilayer

explanation: These are rotenone (complex I), antimycin A (complex III), carbon monoxide (complex IV), oligomycin (Fo) and DNP (an uncoupler). Where a block sits decides which fuels still work and whether DNP can restore O2 use.
