links: ETC components · FADH2 enters at complex II · ATP synthase · Chemiosmotic coupling · Real-world: mitochondrial poisons

title: If one part were missing
prompt: Match each missing or blocked component to what happens in respiring mitochondria.

pairs.right: Neither complex I nor complex II can pass electrons on
Complex III stays loaded with electrons, but complex IV gets none
Every carrier in the chain stays reduced

pairs.left: The Fo channel of ATP synthase
pairs.right: H+ piles up in the intermembrane space and electron flow slows
Succinate can't be oxidized, but NADH's electrons still reach O2

explanation: Q collects electrons from complexes I and II, cytochrome c links III to IV, O2 is the final acceptor, and Fo is the only path back for H+, so each gap stops the chain at a different place.
links: ETC components · FADH2 at complex II · O2 the final acceptor · Chemiosmotic coupling

box: Newborns keep warm partly with brown fat, whose mitochondria contain a protein called UCP1 in the inner membrane.
claim: These cells make heat because UCP1 lets H+ flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase.
explanation: UCP1 short-circuits the gradient, much like DNP but under the body's control, so the energy is released as heat.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling · Real-world: brown fat

box: Besides blocking O2 transport by hemoglobin, carbon monoxide binds complex IV in place of O2.
claim: In cells where CO occupies complex IV, NADH builds up, because electrons back up behind the block and the chain accepts fewer of them from NADH.
explanation: With complex IV blocked, carriers upstream stay reduced; NADH can't hand off its electrons as fast, so NAD+ runs short.
links: O2 the final acceptor · ETC components · Electron carriers · Real-world: carbon monoxide poisoning

box: A toxin makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to H+.
claim: Electron transport would stop, since the H+ it pumps would leak straight back and no gradient could build.
explanation: Without a gradient to push against, pumping becomes easier and electron transport speeds up, as with DNP; ATP synthesis is what fails.
links: Proton gradient · Proton pumping

box: Inside-out vesicles made from inner mitochondrial membrane have their matrix face on the outside.
claim: Given NADH, these vesicles make the surrounding solution less acidic.
explanation: The complexes pump H+ away from the matrix face, which is now outside, into the vesicles, so H+ falls outside and the pH rises.
links: Proton pumping · Gradient direction

box: Textbook estimates: each NADH yields about 2.5 ATP and each FADH2 about 1.5 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
claim: A mutant complex I that still passed electrons to Q but pumped no H+ would cut NADH's yield to about that of FADH2.
explanation: The 1-ATP gap between NADH and FADH2 comes from complex I's pumping; without it, NADH's electrons drive pumping only at complexes III and IV, as FADH2's do.
links: FADH2 enters at complex II · Proton pumping

box: Per glucose, about 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 reach the electron transport chain. Use 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2.
claim: With these numbers, oxidative phosphorylation makes about 28 ATP per glucose, about seven times as many as substrate-level phosphorylation.
explanation: 10 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 25 + 3 = 28 ATP, against 4 from substrate-level phosphorylation (2 in glycolysis, 2 in the cycle): 28 / 4 = 7.
links: ATP yield · Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation

box: Complete oxidation of one glucose yields about 32 ATP.
claim: The citric acid cycle makes more of these ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation than glycolysis does.
explanation: Per glucose the cycle makes 2 ATP (as GTP); glycolysis makes 4 (2 net). The rest, about 28, come from oxidative phosphorylation.
links: ATP yield · Substrate-level phosphorylation

box: At complex IV, each O2 gains 4 electrons and 4 H+, forming 2 H2O.
claim: The 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 made from one glucose carry exactly enough electrons to reduce the 6 O2 that respiration uses per glucose.
explanation: Each carrier brings 2 electrons: 12 × 2 = 24, and 6 O2 × 4 electrons = 24.
links: O2 is the final acceptor · Electron carriers

box: Electrons lose energy at each step as they pass from NADH to O2.
claim: ATP synthase gets its energy from electrons that complex IV hands on to it.
explanation: The electrons' energy first pumps H+ to build a gradient; ATP synthase then uses the gradient. The gradient is the link.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling

box: Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase.
claim: Adding extra ADP at minute 5 would make O2 use speed up again, as it did at minute 2.
explanation: Oligomycin blocks Fo, so H+ can't flow back through ATP synthase however much ADP is present; the gradient stays steep and keeps holding electron transport back.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling · ATP synthase

stem: A drug stops O2 use by mitochondria given succinate but not by mitochondria given NADH-linked fuel. Where does it most likely act?
options: Complex III
Complex I
Complex IV
Complex II
Cytochrome c
explanation: Succinate's electrons enter at complex II (as FADH2) and join NADH's route at Q; blocking III, IV or cytochrome c would stop both fuels, and blocking I would stop only NADH-linked fuel.
links: FADH2 enters at complex II · ETC components

stem: In some muscle and brain cells, the 2 NADH from glycolysis pass their electrons into the mitochondria as 2 FADH2 instead. Using 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, about how many ATP does each glucose yield in total?
explanation: 8 NADH × 2.5 = 20 and 4 FADH2 × 1.5 = 6 from oxidative phosphorylation, plus 4 by substrate-level phosphorylation: 30.
links: ATP yield · FADH2 enters at complex II

stem: In the trace, why does O2 use jump after DNP is added, even though oligomycin is still present?
options: DNP lets H+ back into the matrix, so the chain can pump freely again
DNP makes ATP synthase pump H+ outward, so the gradient grows
DNP supplies extra electrons to complex I, so more reach O2
DNP replaces O2 as the final acceptor, so the chain speeds up
DNP lets H+ through ATP synthase despite oligomycin, so ATP synthesis restarts
explanation: Oligomycin still blocks ATP synthase, but DNP gives H+ another way back across the bilayer; the gradient falls and electron transport, no longer held back, speeds up.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling · Proton gradient

stem: Brown fat's UCP1 and the drug DNP both make mitochondria release energy as heat. How do they differ?
options: UCP1 pumps H+ out, while DNP pumps H+ into the matrix
UCP1 is a protein the body controls; DNP crosses the bilayer itself
UCP1 blocks complex IV, while DNP blocks the Fo channel
UCP1 makes ATP faster, while DNP makes only heat
UCP1 works in the cytosol, while DNP works in the matrix
explanation: Both let H+ back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase; UCP1 is a regulated channel protein in the inner membrane, while DNP ferries H+ through the lipid bilayer.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling · Proton gradient · Real-world: brown fat and DNP

stem: Which observation best shows that electron transport and ATP synthesis are linked by a gradient, not by direct contact?
options: Mitochondria use more O2 when they are given more fuel
Blocking complex IV stops both electron transport and ATP synthesis at once
An imposed H+ gradient drives ATP synthesis with no electron transport
ATP synthase and complex I sit in the very same membrane
Cells without O2 make their ATP only by glycolysis
explanation: Membrane vesicles with ATP synthase but no working chain make ATP when given an artificial H+ gradient, so the gradient alone is enough to power the synthase.
links: Chemiosmotic coupling · Proton gradient

stem: No step of the citric acid cycle uses O2, yet the cycle stops within minutes when O2 runs out. Why?
options: Glycolysis stops without O2, so no pyruvate reaches the cycle
Acetyl groups can't be carried from the cytosol into the matrix
GDP can't be phosphorylated, so the cycle loses its energy input
There is no source for the carbon in the CO2 the cycle releases
The ETC can't reoxidize NADH and FADH2, so NAD+ and FAD run out
explanation: The cycle needs NAD+ and FAD as electron acceptors; only the ETC, ending at O2, turns NADH and FADH2 back into them. Glycolysis itself needs no O2.
links: O2 the final acceptor · Electron carriers

title: Bread dough and a sprinter's legs
stem: Bakers rely on yeast fermentation to make bread rise, and sprinters rely on lactic acid fermentation in their muscles during an all-out effort. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Both kinds of cell run glycolysis, which reduces NAD+ to NADH.

(나) If dough is mixed with plenty of air, the yeast respire aerobically for a while.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Both cells make their end products for the same reason: to regenerate the NAD+ that glycolysis needs.
statements.explanation: Fermentation's job is to turn the NADH from (가) back into NAD+, so glycolysis, the only ATP source, can continue.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: With air, as in (나), the yeast release more CO2 per glucose than when they ferment.
statements.explanation: Aerobic respiration releases all 6 carbons as CO2; ethanol fermentation releases only 2.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Both the dough and the muscle release CO2 as they ferment, since both start from pyruvate.
statements.explanation: Only ethanol fermentation removes a carbon as CO2; lactic acid fermentation reduces pyruvate directly, so the fermentation itself releases none.

links: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ · Ethanol vs lactic acid fermentation · Real-world: bread and sprinting

title: Fish that survive the winter without O2
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Crucian carp and goldfish can survive days to months without O2 under the ice of frozen-over ponds by turning glucose into ethanol and releasing it through their gills.

(나) In most vertebrates, muscle working without O2 makes lactate, which builds up in the body.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Ethanol fermentation gives the fish more ATP per glucose than lactic acid fermentation, which is why they survive so long.
statements.explanation: Both fermentations net only glycolysis's 2 ATP per glucose; the advantage is disposal of the end product.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Since the fish release their fermentation product as ethanol, none of glucose's carbon leaves them as CO2.
statements.explanation: Ethanol fermentation removes one carbon from each pyruvate as CO2 before NADH reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol: 2 CO2 per glucose.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Making ethanol lets the fish get rid of fermentation's end product, whereas lactate would build up and acidify the body as in (나).
statements.explanation: Ethanol diffuses out across the gills; lactic acid stays in the body, so a long fermentation would be fatal.

links: Ethanol fermentation · Fermentation yield · Lactic acid fermentation · Real-world: crucian carp and goldfish under ice

title: Burning through glucose without O2
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Cultured muscle cells are grown with O2 and then without O2.

(나) Without O2, the cells use glucose many times faster to keep their ATP supply up.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Without O2, the cells' mitochondria keep making ATP by oxidative phosphorylation, with pyruvate as the final electron acceptor.
statements.explanation: Pyruvate accepts electrons in fermentation in the cytosol, which makes no ATP; oxidative phosphorylation needs O2 at complex IV.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Fermentation's far lower ATP yield per glucose explains (나).
statements.explanation: At 2 instead of about 32 ATP per glucose, the cells must use roughly 16 times as much glucose to make the same amount of ATP.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Without O2, the cells stop producing NADH, since NADH is made only by pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondria.
statements.explanation: Glycolysis in the cytosol keeps reducing NAD+ to NADH; fermentation then reoxidizes it.

links: Fermentation yield · O2 the final acceptor · Glycolysis makes NADH in the cytosol

title: Steps without O2
prompt: Match each conversion to the feature that describes it.

pairs.right: NADH reduces pyruvate directly; no carbon is lost
One carbon leaves as CO2
NADH is oxidized to NAD+ as a two-carbon molecule is reduced
The only stage that makes ATP during fermentation
Happens when G3P is oxidized in glycolysis

explanation: Fermentation's extra steps make no ATP; they reoxidize the NADH from glycolysis, either directly on pyruvate (lactate) or after removing CO2 (ethanol).
links: Lactic acid and ethanol fermentation · Fermentation regenerates NAD+

box: Yogurt is made by bacteria that ferment milk sugar into lactic acid.
claim: These bacteria regenerate NAD+ by passing NADH's electrons to pyruvate.
explanation: In lactic acid fermentation, NADH reduces pyruvate to lactate, and the NAD+ formed goes back to glycolysis.
links: Lactic acid fermentation · Fermentation regenerates NAD+ · Real-world: yogurt

box: Wine yeast ferment the sugar in grape juice in a tank closed to air.
claim: The yeast's net 2 ATP per glucose are made in the step that releases CO2.
explanation: The ATP comes from glycolysis; converting pyruvate to acetaldehyde (which releases CO2) and then to ethanol makes none.
links: Ethanol fermentation · Fermentation yield · Real-world: winemaking

box: During a 30-second sprint, a runner's muscle fibres rely heavily on lactic acid fermentation.
claim: Fermentation powers the sprint because it makes more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
explanation: Fermentation makes only 2 ATP per glucose; it helps because glycolysis can run very fast without waiting for O2.
links: Fermentation yield · Real-world: sprinting

box: The steps after pyruvate in fermentation make no ATP of their own.
claim: A cell without O2 could skip the fermentation steps and still keep glycolysis running.
explanation: Without fermentation, NADH would pile up and NAD+ would run out, stopping glycolysis.
links: Fermentation regenerates NAD+

box: Bottle-conditioned beer gets its fizz when yeast ferment a little extra sugar after the bottle is sealed.
claim: The CO2 that carbonates the beer is released in the same step that regenerates NAD+.
explanation: CO2 leaves when pyruvate becomes acetaldehyde; NAD+ is regenerated in the next step, when NADH reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol.
links: Ethanol fermentation · Real-world: bottle-conditioned beer

box: Lactate made by sprinting muscle is carried by the blood to other organs.
claim: This lactate is of little use as fuel, since fermentation has already released most of glucose's energy.
explanation: Fermentation releases only about 7% of glucose's free energy, so the two lactates keep over 90%; the heart can oxidize lactate, and the liver can turn it back into glucose.
links: Fermentation yield · Lactic acid fermentation · Real-world: lactate after exercise

stem: A yeast mutant lacks the enzyme that turns pyruvate into acetaldehyde. Grown without O2, it soon stops making ATP. Why?
options: NADH from glycolysis can't be reoxidized, so glycolysis halts
Acetaldehyde is the molecule that adds phosphate to ADP
Ethanol is needed to keep the yeast's membranes intact
Pyruvate must reach the mitochondria to make any ATP
Without CO2 release, glycolysis loses its energy source
explanation: Ethanol fermentation makes no ATP itself; its job is to reoxidize NADH. Blocking it leaves NAD+ unregenerated, so glycolysis, the only ATP source without O2, stops.
links: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ · Ethanol fermentation

stem: A muscle cell without O2 ferments one glucose. Which list gives the net products?
options: 2 lactate, 2 ATP and 2 CO2
2 ethanol, 2 ATP and 2 CO2
2 lactate and 2 ATP
2 lactate and about 32 ATP
2 pyruvate, 2 ATP and 2 NADH
explanation: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH; reducing the 2 pyruvate to 2 lactate uses up the NADH and releases no CO2.
links: Lactic acid fermentation · Fermentation yield

stem: Which of these releases CO2 as it ferments glucose?
options: Bacteria turning milk into yogurt
Tumour cells in an oxygen-poor core
Human leg muscle during an all-out sprint
Rice seeds germinating under floodwater
Bacteria fermenting sugar on teeth
explanation: Plant cells short of O2 carry out ethanol fermentation, like yeast, releasing CO2 as pyruvate becomes acetaldehyde; the others make lactic acid and release none.
links: Ethanol vs lactic acid fermentation · Real-world: rice under floodwater

stem: A yeast cell with no O2 makes 64 ATP by fermentation. How many CO2 does it release?
explanation: Fermentation nets 2 ATP per glucose, so 32 glucose were used, and each releases 2 CO2: 32 × 2 = 64.
links: Fermentation yield · Ethanol fermentation

title: Running on fat
stem: On a ketogenic diet, people eat very little carbohydrate (often under 50 g a day) and get most of their energy from fat. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Fats are split into glycerol and fatty acids, and the fatty acids are cut into acetyl-CoA by beta-oxidation.

(나) The liver turns some of this acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies, which the brain can take up and use as fuel.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: A drug that blocked beta-oxidation would also stop the liver making most of the brain fuel in (나), even though the dieter still has plenty of stored fat.
statements.explanation: Ketone bodies are made from the acetyl-CoA that beta-oxidation produces (가); with it blocked, the fat can't be turned into brain fuel.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Beta-oxidation is itself a major source of ATP, made by substrate-level phosphorylation.
statements.explanation: Beta-oxidation makes no ATP directly; it makes acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH2, and the ATP comes later from the cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The brain can use the ketone bodies in (나) because its cells turn them back into acetyl-CoA.
statements.explanation: Ketone bodies are a transport form of acetyl-CoA; the brain converts them back and oxidizes them in its mitochondria.

links: Beta-oxidation · Fuels converge on acetyl-CoA · Real-world: ketogenic diets

title: Two glycogen stores, two jobs
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Liver and muscle cells both cut glucose units off glycogen as glucose phosphate.

(나) Muscle cells lack the enzyme that removes that phosphate; liver cells have it.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Glycogen makes a good store because all of its glucose can be released at once when it is needed.
statements.explanation: Glucose units are cut off one at a time and enter glycolysis as glucose 6-phosphate, past step 1.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A person whose liver can't break down glycogen would have low blood glucose between meals, even with normal muscle glycogen.
statements.explanation: Only the liver can remove the phosphate (나) and release free glucose into the blood, so muscle glycogen can't stand in for it.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Muscle glycogen serves that muscle's own contraction, because the glucose phosphate it releases can't leave the cell.
statements.explanation: Phosphorylated sugar is trapped inside the cell, so muscle keeps its glycogen's glucose for itself.

links: Liver vs muscle glycogen · Glycogen releases glucose one unit at a time · Phosphorylation traps glucose

title: Why the body stores fat, not just glycogen
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Fat yields about 9 kcal per gram when fully oxidized; carbohydrate yields about 4.

(나) Glycogen is stored with about 3 g of water per gram, while fat is stored nearly water-free.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Fat yields more energy per gram partly because its fatty acid chains are rich in C-H bonds, whose electrons can be passed to O2.
statements.explanation: Fatty acids are highly reduced, so oxidizing them delivers many electrons to NADH and FADH2 and on to O2.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Storing a day's energy as glycogen would weigh only about twice as much as storing it as fat, since fat gives about twice the energy per gram.
statements.explanation: 9/4 ≈ 2.25 is the dry ratio; with its water (나), glycogen gives about 1 kcal per gram stored, so it weighs about nine times as much as fat.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Fatty acids can be fully oxidized in the cytosol without mitochondria, since they never pass through glycolysis.
statements.explanation: Skipping glycolysis doesn't skip the mitochondria: acetyl-CoA from fatty acids is oxidized by the cycle and the ETC there.

links: Lipids are energy-rich · Beta-oxidation

title: Many fuels, one pathway
prompt: Match each fuel to how it enters cellular respiration.

pairs.right: As free glucose, at the first step of glycolysis
Partway through glycolysis, as a three-carbon sugar phosphate
As acetyl-CoA after beta-oxidation
At several points, such as pyruvate, acetyl-CoA and cycle intermediates
As glucose phosphate cut off one unit at a time, joining glycolysis after its first step

explanation: Every fuel feeds the same central pathway, entering wherever its carbon skeleton fits; fatty acids skip glycolysis entirely.
links: Several fuels feed respiration · Beta-oxidation · Proteins as fuel

box: In McArdle disease, muscle cells can't break down their glycogen, while the liver's glycogen use is normal.
claim: These patients tire quickly in intense exercise, but their blood glucose between meals stays normal.
explanation: Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself, so losing it limits hard exercise; blood glucose depends on liver glycogen, which works normally.
links: Liver vs muscle glycogen · Real-world: McArdle disease

box: Table sugar (sucrose) is digested into glucose and fructose.
claim: Only the glucose half can be used for energy, because glycolysis begins with glucose.
explanation: Fructose is converted into glycolysis intermediates and enters partway along, so both halves are used.
links: Other sugars enter glycolysis · Real-world: table sugar

box: During prolonged starvation, the body breaks down muscle proteins for fuel.
claim: If a poison blocked glycolysis, the amino acids from muscle protein could no longer be used as fuel.
explanation: Amino acids enter at pyruvate, acetyl-CoA and cycle intermediates, all after glycolysis, so they can still be oxidized.
links: Proteins as fuel · Real-world: starvation

box: Beta-oxidation of one fatty acid produces several acetyl-CoA plus NADH and FADH2.
claim: Since beta-oxidation makes no ATP directly, fat is a poor source of ATP.
explanation: Beta-oxidation's acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH2 feed the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, which make large amounts of ATP; per gram, fat yields more than carbohydrate.
links: Beta-oxidation · Lipids are energy-rich

box: A fat with three 16-carbon fatty acids (plus its 3-carbon glycerol) is fully broken down.
claim: Most of this fat's carbon enters respiration as acetyl-CoA rather than through glycolysis.
explanation: 48 of its 51 carbons are in the three fatty acids, which give 24 acetyl-CoA; only glycerol's 3 carbons enter glycolysis.
links: Beta-oxidation · Fuels enter at different points

box: After a large meal, the liver converts excess glucose into fatty acids, which are stored as fat.
claim: Fat made this way stores less energy per gram than fat eaten in food, since it started out as sugar.
explanation: The new fatty acids are the same C-H-rich chains as dietary ones and yield about 9 kcal/g when oxidized.
links: Lipids are energy-rich · Fuels interconvert

stem: Carbon atoms are labelled in glucose, in a fatty acid and in alanine (an amino acid that becomes pyruvate), in three separate experiments. In which molecule could label from all three first appear together?
options: Glycerol
Pyruvate
Oxaloacetate
Glucose
Acetyl-CoA
explanation: Glucose and alanine reach acetyl-CoA through pyruvate, and fatty acids reach it by beta-oxidation; it is the first molecule all three pass through.
links: Fuels converge on acetyl-CoA

stem: Marathon runners 'hit the wall' around km 30, when muscle glycogen runs out, even though their fat stores could fuel many more kilometres. Which explanation fits best?
options: Oxidizing fat produces lactate, which builds up and tires the muscle
Fat is oxidized more slowly, so ATP comes at a lower rate
Fat yields less ATP per gram than glycogen does
Fat must first be converted into glycogen before use
Fatty acids enter respiration through glycolysis, which stalls once glycogen is gone
explanation: Fat holds more energy per gram, but its breakdown and oxidation supply ATP more slowly than glycogen's glucose, so pace drops once muscle glycogen is gone.
links: Glycogen and fat as fuels · Real-world: hitting the wall

stem: Brewers mash malted barley to make wort, which is rich in maltose. How does yeast get energy from the maltose?
options: It ferments maltose without breaking it down first
It splits maltose into glucose and galactose, which enter glycolysis
It splits maltose into glucose and fructose, which enter glycolysis
It splits maltose into two glucose, which enter glycolysis
It sends maltose intact into the citric acid cycle
explanation: Maltose is two glucose units; hydrolyzing it gives glucose, which feeds glycolysis (and, without O2, fermentation).
links: Other sugars enter glycolysis · Real-world: brewing

stem: How many CO2 does the citric acid cycle release in oxidizing all the acetyl-CoA from one 16-carbon fatty acid (palmitate)?
explanation: Palmitate gives 8 acetyl-CoA; each drives one turn of the cycle releasing 2 CO2: 8 × 2 = 16.
links: Beta-oxidation · The cycle completes oxidation

title: Where does the oxygen come from?
stem: In 1941, Samuel Ruben, Martin Kamen and colleagues used the heavy oxygen isotope 18O to find out where the O2 released by photosynthesis comes from. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In each experiment, only one of the two raw materials, water or CO2, was enriched in 18O.

(나) Photosynthesis overall: 6 CO2 + 12 H2O → C6H12O6 + 6 O2 + 6 H2O.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The O2 released matches the label in the water because water is the electron donor that is oxidized in the light reactions.
statements.explanation: Oxidizing water releases electrons, protons and O2, so the O2 carries water's oxygen atoms (experiment 1).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In experiment 2, the extra 18O from the CO2 would end up in the sugar and in the water on the right side of (나).
statements.explanation: CO2's oxygen atoms go into the carbohydrate and the product water; that is why the equation lists water on both sides.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the CO2 in experiment 1 had also been enriched in 18O, the O2 released would have carried much more than 0.84% 18O.
statements.explanation: The O2 comes only from water, so it would still match the water's 0.85%; CO2's oxygen goes into sugar and water.

links: Water is the electron donor · Overall equation · Real-world: Ruben and Kamen's 18O experiments

title: When the lights go out
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) A spinach leaf in bright light is suddenly put in the dark.

(나) CO2 fixation goes on for a few seconds in the dark, then stops.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Extra CO2 supplied when the light went off would keep fixation in (나) going much longer.
statements.explanation: Fixation stops because ATP and NADPH run out, so RuBP can't be regenerated; extra CO2 doesn't replace them.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: O2 links the two stages: the thylakoids release it, and the stroma uses it to fix CO2.
statements.explanation: O2 is a by-product the Calvin cycle doesn't use; the link is ATP and NADPH, made in the thylakoids and spent in the stroma.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Fixation continues briefly in (나) because ATP and NADPH made in the light are still present in the stroma.
statements.explanation: The Calvin cycle runs on ATP and NADPH from the thylakoids; it stops once that supply is used up.

links: The two stages are linked · Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH

title: The same atoms, two directions
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Photosynthesis: 6 CO2 + 12 H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6 O2 + 6 H2O.

(나) Cellular respiration: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (가), carbon is reduced as CO2 becomes carbohydrate, and the oxygen of water is oxidized to O2.
statements.explanation: CO2 gains electrons (reduction) to become sugar; water loses electrons (oxidation), releasing O2.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because (가) and (나) are reverse reactions, cells run (나) using the enzymes of (가) working backward.
statements.explanation: The two processes use different pathways, enzymes and compartments: chloroplast thylakoids and stroma vs cytosol and mitochondria.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Turning CO2 and water into carbohydrate and O2 has a positive ΔG, which is why light energy is needed, while (나) has a negative ΔG.
statements.explanation: Building high-energy carbohydrate from CO2 is endergonic; light supplies the energy that respiration later releases.

links: Photosynthesis is a redox process · Endergonic vs exergonic

title: Life in the sunlit layer
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In clear ocean water, only about 1% of the surface light remains at a depth of about 100-200 m.

(나) Phytoplankton, microscopic photosynthesizers of the ocean's sunlit layer, carry out about half of Earth's photosynthesis.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The O2 that the phytoplankton in (나) release comes from the CO2 dissolved in seawater, which they take apart to make sugar.
statements.explanation: The O2 comes from water split in the light reactions; the CO2 is reduced to carbohydrate.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Most animals living far below the sunlit layer still depend on photosynthesis, eating food that sinks from above.
statements.explanation: Food webs are supported by the biomass of photosynthesizers; deep animals live on organic matter that sinks down.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Phytoplankton carried below about 200 m would photosynthesize far more slowly, even with plenty of CO2 in the seawater.
statements.explanation: Photosynthesis needs light as its energy source; with about 1% of surface light or less, light, not CO2, limits it.

links: Photosynthesis needs light · Energy entry point for food webs · Water is the electron donor

title: Parts of a chloroplast
prompt: Match each part of the chloroplast to the fact that fits it.

pairs.right: Where the herbicide diuron binds and blocks electron flow
Where H+ from split water builds up
Where 14C from 14CO2 first turns up, in 3-phosphoglycerate
Seen in electron micrographs as a pile of coin-like discs
The two membranes a protein made in the cytosol must cross to reach the stroma

explanation: Diuron binds photosystem II in the thylakoid membrane; H+ collects in the lumen; CO2 is fixed into 3-phosphoglycerate in the stroma; grana are stacks of thylakoids; and the double envelope separates the stroma from the cytosol.
links: Chloroplast structure · Stage locations · Thylakoid H+ gradient

box: An oak seedling grows into a tree weighing several tonnes, while the soil around it loses only a little mass.
claim: If the dry wood were burned completely, most of its mass would leave as CO2 and water vapour, with only a small fraction left as mineral ash.
explanation: Wood is mostly carbohydrate that photosynthesis built from CO2 and water; burning oxidizes it back to CO2 and H2O, leaving only the minerals taken from the soil.
links: Photosynthesis builds biomass from CO2

box: The diagram shows what happens to the sunlight reaching a leaf.
claim: Of the sunlight in the range plants can use, at most about a tenth ends up stored in carbohydrate.
explanation: 40% of the sunlight is in the usable range and at most 4% is stored: 4 / 40 = 10%.
links: Efficiency of photosynthesis

box: The diagram shows what happens to the sunlight reaching a leaf.
claim: At least a quarter of the sunlight reaching the leaf ends up as heat.
explanation: Energy isn't destroyed: the 8% converted into heat, plus the 20% 'lost' during carbohydrate synthesis, which is released mostly as heat, already makes 28%.
links: Efficiency of photosynthesis · First law

box: Thylakoids can be separated from the stroma by breaking chloroplasts open and spinning them in a centrifuge.
claim: Isolated thylakoids given light, water and an artificial electron acceptor, but no CO2, can still release O2.
explanation: Water is split by photosystem II in the thylakoid membranes and the acceptor takes its electrons; CO2 is needed only later, in the stroma.
links: Stage locations · Water is the electron donor · Real-world: Hill's experiment

box: Stroma separated from thylakoids, with rubisco and all the Calvin cycle enzymes, is given CO2 and placed in bright light.
claim: It will fix CO2 for as long as the light stays on.
explanation: The stroma's Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH, which only the thylakoids' light reactions make; light alone does nothing for it.
links: The two stages are linked · Stage locations

box: Photosynthesis overall: 6 CO2 + 12 H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6 O2 + 6 H2O.
claim: All 12 hydrogen atoms in the glucose came from water.
explanation: CO2 carries no hydrogen, so every H in the sugar came from water; water's electrons and H+ reach CO2 by way of NADPH.
links: Overall equation · Water is the electron donor

box: In photosynthesis, CO2 is reduced to carbohydrate.
claim: Light supplies the electrons that reduce CO2, so no other molecule has to be oxidized.
explanation: Light supplies energy, not electrons. Reduction always pairs with an oxidation; here water is oxidized, and its electrons (carried by NADPH) reduce CO2.
links: Photosynthesis is a redox process · Water is the electron donor

box: A wolf eats deer, and the deer eat grass.
claim: Since the wolf eats meat rather than plants, the energy it uses doesn't come from photosynthesis.
explanation: The deer got its energy from grass, which captured it from sunlight by photosynthesis; eating the deer passes some of that energy on to the wolf.
links: Photosynthesis is the energy entry point

box: Like mitochondria, chloroplasts are wrapped in two membranes.
claim: The Calvin cycle runs in the narrow space between the chloroplast's inner and outer membranes.
explanation: The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma, the fluid inside the inner membrane that surrounds the thylakoids.
links: Chloroplast structure · Stage locations

stem: Using the diagram, where in the chloroplast are the enzymes that split water and release O2?
options: Thylakoid membrane
Stroma
Outer membrane
Space between the envelope membranes
Inner membrane, which holds the electron transport chain as in mitochondria
explanation: Water is split by photosystem II in the thylakoid membrane, the site of the light-dependent reactions; a chloroplast's inner membrane, unlike a mitochondrion's, holds no electron transport chain.
links: Stage locations · Chloroplast structure

stem: Which pair of molecules does the Calvin cycle return to the light reactions to be recharged?
options: O2 and triose phosphate
ADP and NADP+
ATP and NADPH
CO2 and H2O
ADP and NAD+
explanation: The Calvin cycle spends ATP and NADPH and returns ADP (with Pi) and NADP+, which the light reactions turn back into ATP and NADPH; NAD+ is respiration's carrier.
links: The two stages are linked

stem: Using the overall equation, how many water molecules must be split to release the O2 that goes with one glucose?
explanation: One glucose comes with 6 O2, which hold 12 oxygen atoms; each split water molecule supplies one of them.
links: Overall equation · Water is the electron donor

stem: The O2 in a weedy pond rises during a sunny day and falls overnight. Which explanation fits best?
options: Cool night water holds less dissolved O2, so the O2 escapes into the air
By day respiration releases O2, and at night photosynthesis uses it up
Plants respire only at night, when they use up the O2 that they made by day
At night, photosynthesis runs in reverse and takes O2 back up from the water
By day photosynthesis outpaces respiration; at night only respiration runs
explanation: Photosynthesis releases O2 only in light, while all organisms, plants included, respire day and night. (Cool water holds more dissolved O2, not less.)
links: Photosynthesis needs light · Plants respire day and night

stem: Using the diagram, what is the largest single reason a leaf stores so little of the sunlight it receives?
options: Most of the sunlight's energy is lost during carbohydrate synthesis
Most of the sunlight is turned into heat as soon as the leaf absorbs it
Most of the energy is in wavelengths the pigments can't use
Leaves reflect or transmit most of the light that reaches them
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly green light, which carries little energy
explanation: 60% of the sunlight is outside the usable range, by far the biggest loss; reflection and heat take 8% each, and synthesis losses 20%.
links: Efficiency of photosynthesis

title: Purple light in an indoor farm
stem: Indoor vertical farms often grow lettuce under purple-looking light from panels of red and blue LEDs, which are among the most energy-efficient grow lights. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Each LED colour gives off a narrow band of wavelengths, shown in the diagram.

(나) Many farms also add some green or white LEDs, partly so workers can see the plants' true colour.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Red and blue LEDs are chosen because their wavelengths fall near the peaks of chlorophyll's absorption.
statements.explanation: The blue (450 nm) and red (660 nm) bands sit on the two absorption peaks, so most of their photons are absorbed.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Without the extra light in (나), the lettuce would look dark, having little green light to reflect.
statements.explanation: Leaves look green because they reflect green light; under red and blue light alone there is almost no green to reflect.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Swapping the red LEDs for green LEDs of the same power would not lower photosynthesis, since every visible photon carries energy.
statements.explanation: Only absorbed photons drive photosynthesis. Chlorophyll absorbs 530 nm far more weakly than 660 nm, so a leaf captures green light less completely, and a watt of green light also carries fewer photons than a watt of red.

links: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red · Only absorbed light is used · Real-world: LED grow lights

title: Reading three absorption spectra
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Leaves contain chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and carotenoids.

(나) A dilute suspension of isolated chloroplasts is lit with one wavelength at a time while its O2 release is measured.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: O2 release in (나) would be close to zero at 662 nm, since red light's photons carry less energy than those of the other visible colours.
statements.explanation: Chlorophyll a absorbs strongly at 662 nm, and a red photon carries enough energy to excite it, so red light drives O2 release well.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Carotenoids widen the range of light a leaf can use, absorbing blue-green light near 480 nm that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly.
statements.explanation: At 480 nm the carotenoid curve is high while chlorophyll a's is near zero; accessory pigments fill such gaps.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Chlorophyll b's red peak lies at a longer wavelength than chlorophyll a's, so it extends absorption further into the red.
statements.explanation: Chlorophyll b's red peak (about 642 nm) lies at a shorter wavelength than chlorophyll a's (about 662 nm).

links: Chlorophyll absorption · Accessory pigments

title: Red seaweeds in deep water
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Seawater absorbs red light within the top several metres, but blue and green light reach much deeper.

(나) Red algae that grow deep on reefs carry accessory pigments (phycoerythrins) that absorb green and blue-green light, and this light drives their photosynthesis.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Seen in white light (for example, at the surface), these algae look red because their pigments absorb green and blue-green light and reflect relatively more red.
statements.explanation: An object's colour is the light it doesn't absorb; phycoerythrins absorb green and blue-green, so relatively more red is reflected.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: At depth, these algae still get most of their energy from red light absorbed at chlorophyll's red peak, as land plants do.
statements.explanation: Red light is absorbed by the water near the surface (가), so very little reaches deep algae; they rely on green and blue-green light.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The pigments in (나) pass on absorbed energy, not electrons, to chlorophyll, as antenna pigments do.
statements.explanation: Accessory pigments act like antenna pigments, transferring excitation energy toward the reaction center.

links: Accessory pigments · Antenna energy transfer · Light limits where photosynthesis can occur · Real-world: deep red algae

title: Across the spectrum
prompt: Match each kind of light to the description that fits it.

pairs.right: More energy per photon than any visible light
Absorbed strongly by both chlorophylls and carotenoids
The visible light chlorophyll absorbs least
Absorbed strongly by chlorophyll a but not by carotenoids
Less energy per photon than visible light, and plant pigments barely absorb it

explanation: Photon energy rises as wavelength shortens; within the visible range, chlorophyll's peaks are blue and red, and carotenoids absorb only in the blue to blue-green.
links: Wavelength and energy · Chlorophyll absorption · Accessory pigments

title: After a photon is absorbed
prompt: Match each situation to what happens to the absorbed energy.

pairs.left: A chlorophyll molecule just struck by a red photon
pairs.right: An electron is raised to an excited state

pairs.left: Laundry brightener glowing blue under an ultraviolet lamp
pairs.right: Light is given off again, at a longer wavelength

pairs.left: A leaf in full sun absorbing more light than it can use
pairs.right: Much of the extra energy is released as heat

pairs.left: An antenna chlorophyll packed among others
pairs.right: The excitation passes to a neighbouring pigment

pairs.left: The reaction-center pair of a photosystem
pairs.right: The excited electron itself leaves for an acceptor molecule

explanation: Absorbing a photon raises an electron to an excited state; the pigment then loses the energy as heat or fluorescence, or passes it on. In a photosystem, antenna pigments pass energy along and the reaction-center pair passes an electron to an acceptor.
links: Photon excitation · Fates of an excited state · Antenna and reaction center

box: A plant absorbs one blue photon (450 nm) and one red photon (680 nm).
claim: Since both photons are absorbed by chlorophyll and both drive photosynthesis, they carry the same energy.
explanation: Energy per photon rises as wavelength gets shorter, so the 450 nm photon carries more energy than the 680 nm one; the extra is lost as heat before the energy is used.
links: Wavelength and photon energy

box: A highlighter dye absorbs light and quickly re-emits light (fluorescence).
claim: A dye that absorbs mainly green light (about 530 nm) could fluoresce blue (about 450 nm).
explanation: Some absorbed energy is lost as heat first, so fluorescence has a longer wavelength, with less energy per photon, than the light absorbed.
links: Fates of an excited state

box: Chlorophylls a and b have the same tail and differ only in one side group on the porphyrin ring shown in the diagram.
claim: The two would be expected to absorb somewhat different wavelengths.
explanation: The porphyrin ring is the light-absorbing part, so changing one of its side groups shifts the absorption peaks (chlorophyll a near 430 and 662 nm, chlorophyll b near 455 and 642 nm).
links: Chlorophyll structure

box: Crops grown in soil low in magnesium develop yellowing leaves.
claim: Adding magnesium to the soil would be expected to let new leaves make normal amounts of chlorophyll again.
explanation: Every chlorophyll molecule has a Mg ion at the centre of its porphyrin ring, so without enough Mg the plant can't make enough chlorophyll; with Mg restored, new leaves can green up.
links: Chlorophyll structure · Real-world: magnesium deficiency

box: In autumn, many leaves break down their chlorophyll before they fall, and they turn yellow and orange.
claim: The yellow and orange are pigments the leaf makes fresh in autumn, after its chlorophyll is gone.
explanation: The yellow-orange carotenoids were in the leaf all summer, absorbing light alongside chlorophyll; they show once the green chlorophyll is broken down.
links: Accessory pigments · Real-world: autumn leaves

box: In the diagram, many antenna chlorophylls surround one reaction-center pair. A mutant alga has normal reaction centers but only a small fraction of the usual antenna.
claim: In dim light, the mutant would photosynthesize about as fast as a normal alga, since its reaction centers are normal.
explanation: In dim light, few photons strike a reaction center directly; the antenna gathers light over a much larger area and passes the energy on, so with a small antenna each reaction center is excited less often.
links: Antenna energy transfer

box: An intact leaf absorbs most of the visible light that strikes it, even though a chlorophyll solution absorbs green light poorly. The diagram shows the absorption of three leaf pigments.
claim: Accessory pigments and the many layers of chlorophyll-filled cells in a leaf help explain this.
explanation: Carotenoids fill in the blue-green (about 470-520 nm), and light scattered back and forth through many cell layers has many chances to be absorbed, so even weakly absorbed green light is mostly captured.
links: Leaves absorb most of the spectrum · Accessory pigments

box: Sunlight includes a great deal of infrared light, with wavelengths longer than about 750 nm.
claim: Each infrared photon has too little energy to raise chlorophyll to an excited state, so even very bright infrared light drives almost no photosynthesis.
explanation: A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a jump to an excited state. Infrared photons carry less energy than red ones, and adding more of them doesn't give any single photon enough.
links: Photon excitation · Wavelength and photon energy

stem: In 1882, Theodor Engelmann lit a strand of green alga with light spread into a spectrum and watched O2-seeking bacteria gather along it. Where did most bacteria gather?
options: At the blue and red parts of the strand
At the violet end, where photons carry the most energy
Past the red end, in the infrared
At the green and yellow parts of the strand
Evenly along the whole strand
explanation: O2 is released fastest where photosynthesis is fastest, which is where chlorophyll absorbs best: blue and red.
links: Chlorophyll absorbs blue and red · Real-world: Engelmann's experiment

stem: Five LED lamps of equal power each give off one colour. Which lamp gives off the fewest photons per second?
options: Blue, 450 nm
Green, 530 nm
Amber, 590 nm
Red, 660 nm
Far-red, 730 nm
explanation: Equal power means equal energy per second; each blue photon carries the most energy, so the blue lamp needs the fewest photons to deliver it.
links: Wavelength and photon energy

stem: Chlorophyllide is chlorophyll without the hydrocarbon tail shown in the diagram. Compared with chlorophyll, what would you expect of it?
options: It no longer absorbs light, since the tail is the light-absorbing part
It loses its Mg ion, since the tail is what holds the ion in the ring
It is unchanged, since the tail plays no part in where chlorophyll sits
It moves deeper into the membrane, since the tail was its water-loving part
It still absorbs light but is no longer anchored in the thylakoid membrane
explanation: The porphyrin ring absorbs light and holds the Mg, so both stay; the hydrophobic tail is what anchors chlorophyll in the membrane's lipid bilayer.
links: Chlorophyll structure

stem: An antenna chlorophyll in an intact leaf absorbs a photon. What usually happens next?
options: An electron leaves it and travels straight on to NADP+
It uses the energy to split a water molecule itself
Its excited electron hops from pigment to pigment to the reaction center
The energy passes from pigment to pigment to a reaction center
Most of the energy is given off again as red fluorescence
explanation: The excitation energy, not the electron, is handed between antenna pigments until it reaches the reaction center; little is lost as fluorescence, and only the reaction-center pair passes an electron on.
links: Antenna energy transfer · Fates of an excited state

stem: A corn mutant can't make carotenoids. In bright sunlight its seedlings turn white and die. Which explanation fits best?
options: Without carotenoids, the seedlings can no longer absorb red light well
Carotenoids carry the electrons from photosystem II across to photosystem I
Without carotenoids, excess light damages the photosynthetic machinery
Carotenoids form the porphyrin ring at the core of chlorophyll
Without carotenoids, the leaves reflect most of the blue light falling on them
explanation: Carotenoids protect the photosynthetic components from damage; without them, bright light destroys chlorophyll (photobleaching).
links: Accessory pigments protect

title: Weed killers that jam photosystem II
stem: Atrazine and diuron, two widely used weed killers, kill plants by binding photosystem II in the pocket where plastoquinone normally docks. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) With the pocket blocked, electrons can't pass from photosystem II to plastoquinone.

(나) Some weeds have become resistant to atrazine through a single amino-acid change in the pocket that greatly weakens its binding.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Treated plants die mainly because the herbicide stops their chlorophyll from absorbing light, so no energy can enter the leaf.
statements.explanation: The pigments still absorb light, but the energy can't leave photosystem II as electron flow; it forms reactive oxygen that wrecks membranes, which kills the weed faster than starvation would.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: With the QB pocket blocked, the plastoquinone pool in the diagram gets no electrons from photosystem II, so linear electron flow stops making NADPH and the Calvin cycle stalls.
statements.explanation: PSII and PSI work in series, so no electrons from water reach PSI and NADP+ (가); without NADPH the cycle can't run, even though cyclic flow around PSI can still make some ATP.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In a resistant weed from (나), plastoquinone still docks in the pocket, so electrons keep flowing even when atrazine is present.
statements.explanation: If atrazine can't bind well, plastoquinone still docks and electrons keep flowing, though usually a little more slowly than in unaltered weeds.

links: Photosystems in series · NADPH from PSI · Real-world: PSII herbicides

title: Reading the Z
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) An asterisk (*) marks a photosystem whose reaction center has just been excited by light.

(나) The cytochrome b6f complex sits between plastoquinone (PQ) and plastocyanin (PC).

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Electrons reach PSI with more energy than they had at PSII*, because the b6f complex adds energy.
statements.explanation: Energy falls from PSII* through PQ, b6f and PC, so electrons arrive at PSI lower than they were at PSII*.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Electrons end at NADP+ with more energy than they had in H2O, so their overall flow needs an input of light energy.
statements.explanation: NADP+ sits above H2O on the energy axis; light absorbed at the two photosystems supplies the difference.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The energy released as electrons fall from PQ to PC is simply lost as heat.
statements.explanation: Much of it is used at the b6f complex (나) to move H+ into the lumen, building the gradient that drives ATP synthase.

links: Z scheme · Thylakoid H+ gradient

title: ATP from an acid bath
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In 1966, isolated thylakoids were soaked in pH 4 buffer until their lumens were acidic, then moved quickly into pH 8 buffer containing ADP and Pi, in the dark.

(나) The thylakoids made a burst of ATP without any light.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) shows that an H+ gradient alone, with more H+ inside the lumen, is enough to drive ATP synthase.
statements.explanation: With no light and no electron flow, the only energy source was the imposed gradient.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The burst soon stops because, in the dark, nothing pumps H+ back into the lumen.
statements.explanation: In a leaf, light-driven electron flow keeps refilling the lumen with H+; here the gradient was used up and not replaced.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Once the thylakoids were in the pH 8 buffer, the ATP was made as H+ flowed through ATP synthase from the buffer into the acidic lumen.
statements.explanation: H+ flows down its gradient, from the acidic lumen (high H+) out to the pH 8 buffer (low H+), through ATP synthase.

links: Photophosphorylation · Thylakoid H+ gradient · Real-world: Jagendorf's acid-bath experiment

title: Electrons that loop back to b6f
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Linear electron flow: H2O → PSII → PQ → b6f → PC → PSI → ferredoxin → NADP+.

(나) In cyclic electron flow, electrons leaving PSI pass back to the b6f complex and then return to PSI.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Cyclic flow in (나) still moves H+ into the lumen, so it can make ATP.
statements.explanation: Electrons still pass through the b6f complex, which builds the H+ gradient that drives ATP synthase.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: A chloroplast running only cyclic flow would soon stop fixing CO2, even in bright light.
statements.explanation: Cyclic flow makes no NADPH, so 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate can't be reduced to triose phosphate and the Calvin cycle stalls.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Cells can use cyclic flow to make extra ATP when the Calvin cycle needs more ATP than linear flow supplies alongside its NADPH.
statements.explanation: The Calvin cycle uses 3 ATP for every 2 NADPH; cyclic flow adds ATP without adding NADPH.

links: Cyclic electron transport · Calvin cycle needs NADPH

title: Knocking out the thylakoid chain
prompt: Match each blocked component to its most direct effect in the light.

pairs.right: Water is no longer split, so no O2 is released
Electrons can't leave PSII for the b6f complex
PSI's oxidized reaction center isn't refilled
Electrons reach plastocyanin but aren't raised high enough to reduce NADP+
H+ piles up in the lumen, but no ATP is made

explanation: Electrons go water → PSII → plastoquinone → b6f → plastocyanin → PSI → NADP+, so blocking a carrier stops the step it serves; blocking ATP synthase leaves the H+ gradient unused.
links: PSII takes electrons from water · PQ and PC carriers · PSI makes NADPH · Photophosphorylation

title: Inputs and outputs
prompt: Match each molecule to its role in the light reactions.

pairs.right: The electron donor oxidized at photosystem II
The by-product released when water is split
The final electron acceptor of linear electron flow
Made on the stroma side as H+ leaves the lumen
Not used by the light reactions; reduced later in the stroma

explanation: The light reactions take electrons from water (releasing O2), deliver them to NADP+, and make ATP with the H+ gradient; CO2 enters only in the Calvin cycle.
links: PSII takes electrons from water · NADP+ the final acceptor · Photophosphorylation · Two linked stages

box: In the chain shown in the diagram, a mutant plant's plastocyanin cannot pass electrons to PSI.
claim: In light, its PSII keeps splitting water at the normal rate, since PSII hands its electrons to plastoquinone, not to plastocyanin.
explanation: With plastocyanin stuck, electrons back up through b6f and the plastoquinone pool, so PSII has nowhere to send them and soon stops splitting water.
links: Plastoquinone and plastocyanin · Photosystems in series

box: The diagram shows the thylakoid membrane. In bright light, electron flow keeps the lumen far more acidic than the stroma.
claim: A chemical that lets H+ leak freely across the thylakoid membrane would stop ATP synthesis, but electron flow from water to NADP+ would continue.
explanation: ATP synthase runs on the H+ gradient, which the leak collapses; electron flow doesn't depend on making ATP, so it continues (as with DNP in mitochondria).
links: Photophosphorylation · Thylakoid H+ gradient

box: Chloroplast ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane.
claim: The ATP made here has to cross the thylakoid membrane before the Calvin cycle can use it.
explanation: CF1, the part that makes ATP, faces the stroma, so the ATP is released right where the Calvin cycle runs.
links: Photophosphorylation · Stage locations

box: In bright light, a leaf cell's chloroplasts are making ATP quickly.
claim: Blocking the cell's mitochondria would still cut the ATP supply for work in the cytosol, such as making proteins.
explanation: Chloroplast ATP stays in the chloroplast for the Calvin cycle, so the cytosol relies on respiration for most of its ATP.
links: Chloroplast ATP stays in the chloroplast

box: The cells of a carrot root are not green and carry out no photosynthesis.
claim: These cells get most of their ATP from respiration in their mitochondria, by oxidizing sugar made in the leaves.
explanation: Roots don't photosynthesize; like all plant cells they respire, using sugar carried down from the leaves.
links: Non-green cells respire sugar from the leaves · Real-world: carrot roots

box: Each time PSII's reaction center is excited, it loses an electron to an acceptor.
claim: If PSII could not take electrons from water, it would soon stop passing electrons on, even in bright light.
explanation: An oxidized reaction center must get an electron back from a donor before it can work again, and water is PSII's donor.
links: Reaction center · PSII takes electrons from water

box: Photosystem I's reaction center also loses an electron each time it is excited.
claim: Like photosystem II, it replaces the lost electron by splitting water.
explanation: Only PSII splits water. PSI's reaction center gets its replacement electron from plastocyanin, that is, from the chain coming from PSII.
links: Reaction center · Plastocyanin feeds PSI

box: Linear electron flow carries electrons from water all the way to NADP+.
claim: For each O2 released, 4 electrons pass along the chain, enough to reduce 2 NADP+ to NADPH.
explanation: 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e−, and each NADP+ takes 2 electrons, so 4 electrons reduce 2 NADP+.
links: PSII takes electrons from water · Electrons per NADPH

box: A mutant alga lacks photosystem II but can still run cyclic electron flow through photosystem I and the b6f complex.
claim: In light, the mutant would still release some O2, though more slowly than a normal alga.
explanation: Only PSII splits water, so without it no O2 is released; cyclic flow still makes ATP because its electrons pass through b6f.
links: Cyclic electron transport · PSII splits water

stem: Thylakoids supplied with NADP+ and ferredoxin are treated with diuron (which blocks electron flow from PSII to plastoquinone) and given an artificial donor that feeds electrons straight into plastocyanin. In light, what happens?
options: Neither O2 release nor NADPH formation resumes
NADPH forms again, but no O2 is released
O2 is released again, but no NADPH forms
NADPH forms again, and O2 is now released at photosystem I
Both O2 release and NADPH formation resume
explanation: The donor feeds PSI, which can still reduce NADP+ by way of ferredoxin; PSII stays blocked, so it stops splitting water and no O2 is released.
links: Photosystems in series · PSII splits water · PSI makes NADPH · Real-world: diuron and artificial electron donors

stem: A leaf is moved from darkness into bright light. Within a minute, how do the pH values of the thylakoid lumen and the stroma change?
options: Both fall, since the light reactions release H+
The lumen's pH falls and the stroma's rises
Neither changes, since H+ is moved between them rather than made
Both rise, since the light reactions use up H+
The lumen's pH rises and the stroma's falls
explanation: Electron flow moves H+ from the stroma into the lumen, and splitting water adds H+ to the lumen, so the lumen becomes more acidic and the stroma more alkaline.
links: Thylakoid H+ gradient · pH

stem: Why do the light reactions need two photosystems working in series?
options: One photosystem absorbs only blue light and the other only red
Two photosystems can split water twice as fast as one
Energy lost along the chain must be restored by a second light input
PSII makes all of the ATP, while PSI releases all of the O2
PSI splits water, while PSII reduces NADP+ at the very end of the chain
explanation: Electrons lose energy from PSII through PQ, b6f and PC; PSI's second boost lifts them high enough to reduce NADP+ (the Z scheme). Both photosystems absorb red and blue light, and water is split at PSII, not PSI.
links: Z scheme · Two photosystems in series

stem: Linear electron flow releases one O2 and reduces 2 NADP+. At least how many photons must the two photosystems absorb to do this?
explanation: One O2, or 2 NADPH, means 4 electrons, and each is boosted once at PSII and once at PSI: 4 × 2 = 8. Four would count only one photon per electron.
links: Two photosystems in series · PSII takes electrons from water

stem: A mutant plant that can't run cyclic electron flow is grown in bright light. Which imbalance would you expect in its chloroplasts?
options: No O2 release, because photosystem II stops working
CO2 can no longer bind to rubisco in the stroma
Too little NADPH for the Calvin cycle, while ATP builds up
Too little ATP for the Calvin cycle, while NADPH builds up
No H+ gradient at all across the thylakoid membrane
explanation: Cyclic flow normally adds ATP without NADPH to meet the cycle's 3 ATP : 2 NADPH need; linear flow alone still splits water and pumps H+, but makes too little ATP for its NADPH.
links: Cyclic electron transport · Calvin cycle stoichiometry

stem: The herbicide paraquat takes electrons from photosystem I before they reach ferredoxin. Which process of the light reactions does it stop most directly?
options: Release of H+ into the lumen from water
Splitting of water at photosystem II
Reduction of plastoquinone at photosystem II
Absorption of light by antenna pigments
Reduction of NADP+ to NADPH
explanation: Electrons diverted after PSI never reach ferredoxin and NADP+, so NADPH formation stops; the earlier steps can still run.
links: PSI makes NADPH · Real-world: paraquat

title: Pumping CO2 into a greenhouse
stem: Commercial greenhouse growers often pump in extra CO2, raising it to about 1000 ppm, more than twice the outdoor level. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Rubisco, the enzyme that adds CO2 to RuBP, works well below its top speed at outdoor CO2 levels.

(나) In winter, many growers set a higher CO2 target on bright days than on dull ones.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In bright light, enrichment from 420 to 1000 ppm raises the rate from about 65% to over 90% of maximum, because rubisco gets more of its substrate.
statements.explanation: The bright-light curve is still climbing at 420 ppm, so carboxylation is limited by CO2 there (가).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In bright light, enrichment speeds photosynthesis mainly because the extra CO2 supplies more of the NADPH the Calvin cycle needs to reduce 3-phosphoglycerate.
statements.explanation: CO2 is rubisco's substrate in carboxylation; NADPH comes from the light reactions, not from CO2.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: On dull days, extra CO2 adds much less than on bright days, because the light reactions limit how fast ATP and NADPH are supplied.
statements.explanation: The dim-light curve rises only from about 33% to 40%; in dim light the cycle is short of ATP and NADPH more than of CO2, which fits (나).

links: Rubisco carboxylation · Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH · Real-world: greenhouse CO2 enrichment

title: Following a radioactive carbon
stem: In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Melvin Calvin's team fed radioactive 14CO2 to illuminated algae (Chlorella), killed samples from a few seconds to a minute later, and identified which compounds were radioactive. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Rubisco joins CO2 to RuBP, a five-carbon sugar.

(나) When the light was switched off, 3-phosphoglycerate levels rose and RuBP levels fell.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Since 3-phosphoglycerate holds most of the label at first, it is the carbohydrate the cycle exports to the rest of the plant.
statements.explanation: It is the first stable product, but it is then reduced to triose phosphate; the label moves on into sugar phosphates, and triose phosphate is what leaves the cycle.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The data fit CO2 joining a five-carbon acceptor whose six-carbon product splits at once into two 3-phosphoglycerate.
statements.explanation: Rubisco adds CO2 to RuBP (5C); the unstable 6C product splits into two 3-phosphoglycerate, one of which carries the new 14C, so 3-phosphoglycerate is labelled first.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (나) happens because carboxylation continues briefly in the dark, while turning 3-phosphoglycerate back into RuBP needs light-made ATP and NADPH.
statements.explanation: Carboxylation uses up RuBP and makes 3-phosphoglycerate without ATP, but the steps that reduce 3-phosphoglycerate and remake RuBP need ATP and NADPH.

links: Carboxylation by rubisco · Reduction and regeneration need ATP and NADPH · Real-world: Calvin's 14C experiments

title: Counting carbons around the cycle
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In steady light, a chloroplast keeps its RuBP pool at a constant size.

(나) Suppose a chloroplast starts exporting triose phosphate faster than usual.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Of the 6 triose phosphates made, only 3 are needed to rebuild the 3 RuBP, so half of the product can leave the cycle.
statements.explanation: 3 RuBP hold 15 carbons, which takes 5 triose phosphates (5 × 3 = 15); only 1 in 6 can leave if the RuBP pool is to stay the same size (가).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If the chloroplast in (나) exported 2 of every 6 triose phosphates, RuBP would be regenerated faster and the cycle would speed up.
statements.explanation: The 4 triose phosphates left (12 C) can't rebuild 3 RuBP (15 C), so the RuBP pool shrinks and the cycle slows.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Fixing 3 CO2 uses 3 RuBP and produces 6 molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.
statements.explanation: Each CO2 joins one RuBP, and each six-carbon product splits into two 3-phosphoglycerate: 3 × 2 = 6.

links: Calvin cycle stoichiometry · Regeneration of RuBP · Carboxylation

title: Saving sugar for the night
stem: Read (가) and (나). Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Leaves store some of the day's triose phosphate as starch inside their chloroplasts.

(나) Mutants of the small plant Arabidopsis that can't make leaf starch grow normally in continuous light but poorly in short days with long nights.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The mutants in (나) struggle in long nights because they run out of sugar to respire before dawn.
statements.explanation: With no light there is no ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle; starch made by day is the leaf's night-time sugar supply.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Starch stored by day is broken down to glucose at night, which leaf cells can respire in their mitochondria.
statements.explanation: Starch is a glucose polymer; its glucose units feed glycolysis and respiration for the night-time ATP supply.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: At night, the Calvin cycle keeps running on stored starch, which supplies the ATP and NADPH it needs.
statements.explanation: The Calvin cycle's ATP and NADPH come from the light reactions; starch is broken down for respiration, not to run the cycle.

links: Starch stores carbohydrate for the night · Calvin cycle needs light-made ATP and NADPH · Glucose stores · Real-world: starchless Arabidopsis mutants

title: Steps of the Calvin cycle
prompt: Match each step to what happens in it.

pairs.right: A five-carbon sugar gains a carbon from the air
3-phosphoglycerate gains a phosphate from ATP
1,3-bisphosphoglycerate gains electrons from NADPH
Fifteen carbons are reshuffled into three five-carbon acceptors
Three carbons leave for every three CO2 fixed

explanation: Carboxylation adds CO2 to RuBP; ATP then phosphorylates 3-phosphoglycerate, and NADPH reduces the product to triose phosphate; regeneration rebuilds three RuBP (15 C) from five triose phosphates, so one triose phosphate (3 C) leaves for every 3 CO2 fixed.
links: Carboxylation · Reduction · Regeneration · Stoichiometry

box: Rubisco makes up as much as half of the soluble protein in a leaf, yet each of its active sites fixes only about 3 CO2 per second.
claim: Since each rubisco molecule is reused over and over, halving a leaf's rubisco would barely slow its CO2 fixation in bright light.
explanation: Reuse doesn't make any one enzyme faster. Each active site fixes only about 3 CO2 per second, so in bright light total fixation depends on how much rubisco there is, and halving it cuts fixation a lot.
links: Rubisco carboxylation · Enzymes are reused

box: In algae given 14CO2 in the light, the label shows up first in 3-phosphoglycerate, then in sugar phosphates, and within a minute in RuBP as well.
claim: The label reaching RuBP shows that some of the newly fixed carbon is used to rebuild the CO2 acceptor.
explanation: Five of every six triose phosphates are rearranged back into RuBP, so carbon fixed a few seconds earlier soon turns up in RuBP; this is what makes the pathway a cycle.
links: Regeneration of RuBP · Calvin cycle overview

box: In the reduction step, 3-phosphoglycerate becomes triose phosphate, a three-carbon sugar with more potential energy.
claim: If NADPH ran out but ATP stayed plentiful, the cycle could still make triose phosphate using ATP alone.
explanation: ATP only adds a phosphate, giving 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; it takes electrons from NADPH to reduce that to higher-energy triose phosphate.
links: Reduction step

box: The Calvin cycle fixes 3 CO2 for each triose phosphate it exports.
claim: For every 3 CO2 fixed, the cycle uses 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
explanation: 6 ATP and 6 NADPH reduce 6 3-phosphoglycerate, and 3 more ATP regenerate 3 RuBP: 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.
links: Calvin cycle stoichiometry

box: In the regeneration step, triose phosphates are rearranged to rebuild RuBP.
claim: Regeneration of RuBP is powered by NADPH rather than ATP.
explanation: Regeneration uses ATP (3 per 3 RuBP); NADPH is spent only in the reduction step.
links: Regeneration of RuBP

box: A leaf in bright light is suddenly given air with no CO2.
claim: RuBP builds up and 3-phosphoglycerate falls, because carboxylation stops while regeneration continues.
explanation: Without CO2, rubisco can no longer carboxylate RuBP, but the light reactions still power reduction and regeneration for a while, so RuBP accumulates and 3-phosphoglycerate is used up.
links: Carboxylation · Regeneration of RuBP

box: Leaves picked from one plant at dusk and at dawn are tested with iodine, which stains starch blue-black.
claim: The dawn leaves stain darker, because starch keeps building up overnight while the Calvin cycle rests.
explanation: Starch made by day is broken down at night for the leaf's respiration, so the dusk leaves stain darker.
links: Starch is stored by day and used at night

stem: How many turns of the Calvin cycle (one CO2 fixed per turn) are needed to make the carbon for one glucose?
explanation: Glucose has six carbons and each turn fixes one CO2, so 6 turns; two exported triose phosphates make one glucose.
links: Calvin cycle stoichiometry

stem: How many NADPH does the Calvin cycle use to make the carbon for one glucose?
explanation: Each CO2 fixed needs 2 NADPH (6 NADPH per 3 CO2), so 6 CO2 need 12. 18 is the ATP count (9 per 3 CO2), not the NADPH count.
links: Calvin cycle stoichiometry · Reduction step

stem: A leaf in the light takes up 14CO2. At which step does the 14C first become part of an organic molecule (fixed)?
options: 14CO2 dissolves in the fluid of the stroma
Rubisco joins 14CO2 to RuBP
ATP phosphorylates 3-phosphoglycerate
NADPH reduces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate
Triose phosphate leaves the cycle
explanation: Carbon is fixed when inorganic CO2 is attached to an organic molecule, which rubisco does by joining it to RuBP; the later steps reduce and move carbon that is already fixed.
links: Carboxylation by rubisco

stem: Where does rubisco work, and where do the ATP and NADPH used by the Calvin cycle come from?
options: Stroma; made on the stroma side of the thylakoids
Envelope space; imported from the cytosol
Stroma; imported into the chloroplast from the mitochondria
Thylakoid lumen; made inside the lumen
Cytosol; made by glycolysis in the cytosol
explanation: The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma, and the light reactions release ATP and NADPH on the stroma side; chloroplast ATP isn't imported.
links: Stage locations · Chloroplast ATP stays in the chloroplast · Two linked stages

stem: A potato tuber grows underground and fills with starch. Which sequence traces one of its carbon atoms from the air into that starch?
options: CO2 → 3-phosphoglycerate → triose phosphate → sugar sent from the leaf → starch in the tuber
Carbon from soil minerals → roots → sugar in the tuber → starch
CO2 → fixed by the tuber's own cells underground → starch in the tuber
CO2 → 3-phosphoglycerate → glycogen stored in the leaf → sugar sent to the tuber → starch in the tuber
CO2 → triose phosphate → 3-phosphoglycerate → sugar sent from the leaf → starch in the tuber
explanation: Rubisco fixes CO2 into 3-phosphoglycerate, which is reduced to triose phosphate in the leaf; sugar made from it travels to the tuber, which can't photosynthesize underground, and is stored as starch.
links: Calvin cycle makes carbohydrate · Reduction step · Real-world: potato tubers

title: Why electrons fall toward oxygen
stem: Cellular respiration moves electrons from the C-H bonds of fuel molecules to oxygen. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Oxygen is far more electronegative than carbon or hydrogen.

(나) In respiration, glucose's carbons end up in CO2, and the oxygen atoms of O2 end up in H2O.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: As electrons pass from glucose's C-H bonds into the O-H bonds of water, they end up held more tightly by a more electronegative atom, which releases energy.
statements.explanation: Electrons shared nearly equally in C-H bonds have high potential energy; pulled toward oxygen in polar O-H bonds, they have less, and the difference is released.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Fats need more O2 per gram to oxidize than sugars do, because their chains carry many C-H bonds and few oxygen atoms.
statements.explanation: Sugars already hold many O atoms, so they are partly oxidized; fatty acid chains are mostly C-H, so more O2 is needed to accept their electrons, which is also why fats yield more energy per gram.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If the chain's final acceptor pulled on electrons less strongly than O2 does, less energy would be released per pair of electrons passed along it.
statements.explanation: The energy released depends on how far the electrons fall; a weaker acceptor means a shorter fall and less energy for pumping H+.

links: Electronegativity (Module 2) · O2 is the final electron acceptor (Module 7) · Lipids are energy-rich

title: A vitamin inside an electron carrier
stem: NAD+ carries electrons from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle to the electron transport chain. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The body makes the nicotinamide part of NAD+ from the vitamin niacin (B3).

(나) Pellagra, caused by severe niacin deficiency, damages the skin, the gut and the brain.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: NAD+ is built from two nucleotides joined through their phosphate groups, one carrying adenine and one carrying nicotinamide.
statements.explanation: Each half is a base + ribose + phosphate, and the two phosphates link the halves, which is why it is called a dinucleotide.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Extra dietary adenine would cure pellagra, since an adenine nucleotide makes up half of NAD+.
statements.explanation: The missing part is nicotinamide, which comes from niacin (or the amino acid tryptophan); cells can make adenine nucleotides themselves.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Without enough niacin, as in (나), cells run short of NAD+, slowing glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, which need it to accept electrons.
statements.explanation: Both pathways stall without an oxidized carrier to accept electrons, so tissues with high energy demand suffer.

links: Nucleotide structure (Module 2) · NAD+ as an electron carrier (Module 7) · Real-world: pellagra

title: Two organelles, two gradients
stem: Mitochondria and chloroplasts both make ATP using an H+ gradient across a membrane. Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In both organelles, electron transport moves H+ across a membrane.

(나) In both, H+ flows back down its gradient through ATP synthase.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In both organelles, ATP is released into the compartment where H+ is high.
statements.explanation: H+ flows from the high-H+ side through ATP synthase, and ATP is made on the other side: the matrix (4) and the stroma (F).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: H+ builds up in compartment 2 of the mitochondrion and in compartment D of the chloroplast.
statements.explanation: The ETC pumps H+ from the matrix (4) into the intermembrane space (2); in chloroplasts H+ moves from the stroma (F) into the lumen (D).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Membranes 3 and C each hold an electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
statements.explanation: The inner mitochondrial membrane (3) and the thylakoid membrane (C) are the energy-converting membranes; the outer membranes are leaky.

links: Double-membrane organelles (Module 3) · H+ gradients in mitochondria and chloroplasts (Modules 7-8)

title: A bacterium's power plant
